Primitive of x by Arcsecant of x over a: \int x \operatorname{arcsec} \frac x a \ \mathrm d x = \begin{cases} \frac {x^2} 2 \operatorname{arcsec} \frac x a - \frac {a \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} } 2 + C & : 0 < \operatorname{arcsec} \dfrac x a < \dfrac \pi 2 \\ \frac {x^2} 2 \operatorname{arcsec} \frac x a + \frac {a \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} } 2 + C & : \dfrac \pi 2 < \operatorname{arcsec} \dfrac x a < \pi \\ \end{cases}

Primitive of x by Arccosecant of x over a: \int x \arccsc \frac x a \rd x = \begin{cases} \frac {x^2} 2 \arccsc \frac x a + \frac {a \sqrt {x^2 - a^2} } 2 + C & : 0 < \arccsc \dfrac x a < \dfrac \pi 2 \\ \frac {x^2} 2 \arccsc \frac x a - \frac {a \sqrt {x^2 - a^2} } 2 + C & : -\dfrac \pi 2 < \arccsc \dfrac x a < 0 \\ \end{cases}

Primitive of Arcsecant of x over a over x squared: \int \frac {\operatorname{arcsec} \frac x a} {x^2} \ \mathrm d x = \begin{cases} \frac {-\operatorname{arcsec} \frac x a} x + \frac {\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} } {a x} + C & : 0 < \operatorname{arcsec} \dfrac x a < \dfrac \pi 2 \\ \frac {-\operatorname{arcsec} \frac x a} x - \frac {\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} } {a x} + C & : \dfrac \pi 2 < \operatorname{arcsec} \dfrac x a < \pi \\ \end{cases}

Primitive of Arccosecant of x over a over x squared: \int \frac {\arccsc \frac x a} {x^2} \rd x = \begin{cases} \frac {-\arccsc \frac x a} x - \frac {\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} } {a x} + C & : 0 < \arccsc \dfrac x a < \dfrac \pi 2 \\ \frac {-\arccsc \frac x a} x + \frac {\sqrt{x^2 - a^2} } {a x} + C & : -\dfrac \pi 2 < \arccsc \dfrac x a < 0 \\ \end{cases}
Primitive of Power of x by Arcsine of x over a: \int x^m \arcsin \frac x a \rd x = \frac {x^{m + 1} } {m + 1} \arcsin \frac x a - \frac 1 {m + 1} \int \frac {x^{m + 1} \rd x} {\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} } + C
Primitive of Exponential of a x: \int e^{a x} \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} } a + C
Primitive of x by Exponential of a x: \int x e^{a x} \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} } a \paren {x - \frac 1 a} + C
Primitive of x squared by Exponential of a x: \int x^2 e^{a x} \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} } a \paren {x^2 - \frac {2 x} a + \frac 2 {a^2} } + C
Primitive of Power of x by Exponential of a x/Lemma: Let n be a positive integer. Then: : \int x^n e^{a x} \rd x = \frac {x^n e^{a x} } a - \frac n a \int x^{n - 1} e^{a x} \rd x + C
Primitive of Exponential of a x over x: \int \frac {e^{a x} \rd x} x = \ln \size x + \sum_{k \mathop \ge 1} \frac {\paren {a x}^k} {k \times k!} + C

Primitive of Exponential of a x over Power of x: \int \frac {e^{a x} \rd x} {x^n} = \frac {-e^{a x} } {\paren {n - 1} x^{n - 1} } + \frac a {n - 1} \int \frac {e^{a x} \rd x} {x^{n - 1} } + C where n \ne 1.
Primitive of Reciprocal of p plus q by Exponential of a x: \int \frac {\d x} {p + q e^{a x} } = \frac x p - \frac 1 {a p} \ln \size {p + q e^{a x} } + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of p plus q by Exponential of a x: \int \frac {\d x} {\paren {p + q e^{a x} }^2} = \frac x {p^2} + \frac 1 {a p \paren {p + q e^{a x} } } - \frac 1 {a p^2} \ln \size {p + q e^{a x} } + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of p by Exponential of a x plus q by Exponential of -a x: \int \frac {\d x} {p e^{a x} + q e^{-a x} } = \begin{cases} \frac 1 {a \sqrt {p q} } \map \arctan {\sqrt {\frac p q} e^{a x} } & : \sqrt {p q} > 0 \\ \frac 1 {2 a \sqrt {-p q} } \ln \size {\frac {e^{a x} - \sqrt {-\frac q p} } {e^{a x} + \sqrt {-\frac q p} } } & : \sqrt {p q} < 0 \\ \end{cases}
Primitive of Exponential of a x by Sine of b x: \int e^{a x} \sin b x \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} \paren {a \sin b x - b \cos b x} } {a^2 + b^2} + C
Primitive of Exponential of a x by Cosine of b x: \int e^{a x} \cos b x \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} \paren {a \cos b x + b \sin b x {a^2 + b^2} + C

Primitive of x by Exponential of a x by Sine of b x: \int x e^{a x} \sin b x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x e^{a x} \left({a \sin b x - b \cos bx}\right)} {a^2 + b^2} - \frac {e^{a x} \left({\left({a^2 - b^2}\right) \sin b x - 2 a b \cos bx}\right)} {\left({a^2 + b^2}\right)^2} + C

Primitive of x by Exponential of a x by Cosine of b x: \int x e^{a x} \cos b x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x e^{a x} \left({a \cos b x + b \sin bx}\right)} {a^2 + b^2} - \frac {e^{a x} \left({\left({a^2 - b^2}\right) \cos b x - 2 a b \sin bx}\right)} {\left({a^2 + b^2}\right)^2} + C
Primitive of Exponential of a x by Logarithm of x: \int e^{a x} \ln x \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} \ln x} a - \frac 1 a \int \frac {e^{a x} } x \rd x + C

Primitive of Exponential of a x by Power of Sine of b x: \int e^{a x} \sin^n b x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {e^{a x} \sin^{n - 1} b x} {a^2 + n^2 b^2} \left({a \sin b x - n b \cos b x}\right) + \frac {n \left({n - 1}\right) b^2} {a^2 + n^2 b^2} \int e^{a x} \sin^{n - 2} b x \ \mathrm d x + C

Primitive of Exponential of a x by Power of Cosine of b x: \int e^{a x} \cos^n b x \rd x = \frac {e^{a x} \cos^{n - 1} b x} {a^2 + n^2 b^2} \paren {a \cos b x + n b \sin b x} + \frac {n \paren {n - 1} b^2} {a^2 + n^2 b^2} \int e^{a x} \cos^{n - 2} b x \rd x + C
Primitive of Logarithm of x: \int \ln x \rd x = x \ln x - x + C
Primitive of x by Logarithm of x: \int x \ln x \rd x = \frac {x^2} 2 \left({\ln x - \frac 1 2}\right) + C
Primitive of Power of x by Logarithm of x: \int x^m \ln x \rd x = \frac {x^{m + 1} } {m + 1} \left({\ln x - \frac 1 {m + 1} }\right) + C where m \ne -1.
Primitive of Logarithm of x over x: \int \frac {\ln x} x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\ln^2 x} 2 + C
Primitive of Logarithm of x over x squared: \int \frac {\ln x} {x^2} \ \mathrm d x = \frac {-\ln x} x - \frac 1 x + C
Primitive of Square of Logarithm of x: \int \ln^2 x \ \mathrm d x = x \ln^2 x - 2 x \ln x + 2 x + C
Primitive of Power of Logarithm of x over x: \int \frac {\ln^n x} x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\ln^{n + 1} x} {n + 1} + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of x by Logarithm of x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {x \ln x} = \ln \left({\ln x}\right) + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of Logarithm of x: \int \frac {\d x} {\ln x} = \map \ln {\ln x} + \ln x + \sum_{k \mathop \ge 2}^n \frac {\paren {\ln x}^k} {k \times k!} + C

Primitive of Power of x over Logarithm of x: \int \frac {x^m \rd x} {\ln x} = \map \ln {\ln x} + \paren {m + 1} \ln x + \sum_{k \mathop \ge 2}^n \frac {\paren {m + 1}^k \paren {\ln x}^k} {k \times k!} + C
Primitive of Power of Logarithm of x: \int \ln^n x \rd x = x \ln^n x - n \int \ln^{n - 1} x \rd x + C
Primitive of Power of x by Power of Logarithm of x: \int x^m \ln^n x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x^{m + 1} \ln^n x} {m + 1} - \frac n {m + 1} \int x^m \ln^{n - 1} x \ \mathrm d x + C where m \ne -1.
Primitive of Logarithm of x squared plus a squared: \int \map \ln {x^2 + a^2} \rd x = x \map \ln {x^2 + a^2} - 2 x + 2 a \arctan \frac x a + C
Primitive of Logarithm of x squared minus a squared: \int \ln \left({x^2 - a^2}\right) \rd x = x \ln \left({x^2 - a^2}\right) - 2 x + a \ln \left({\frac {x + a} {x - a} }\right) + C for x^2 > a^2.

Primitive of Power of x by Logarithm of x squared plus a squared: \int x^m \map \ln {x^2 + a^2} \rd x = \frac {x^{m + 1} \map \ln {x^2 + a^2} } {m + 1} - \frac 2 {m + 1} \int \frac {x^{m + 2} } {x^2 + a^2} \rd x

Primitive of Power of x by Logarithm of x squared minus a squared: \int x^m \, \map \ln {x^2 - a^2} \rd x = \frac {x^{m + 1} \, \map \ln {x^2 - a^2} } {m + 1} - \frac 2 {m + 1} \int \frac {x^{m + 2} } {x^2 - a^2} \rd x
Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int \sinh a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\cosh a x} a + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int \cosh a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\sinh a x} a + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Tangent of a x: \int \tanh a x \rd x = \frac {\ln \size {\cosh a x} } a + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x: \int \coth a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {\ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert} a + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosecant of a x: \int \csch a x \rd x = \frac 1 a \ln \size {\tanh \frac {a x} 2} + C
Primitive of x by Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int x \sinh a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x \cosh a x} a - \frac {\sinh a x} {a^2} + C
Primitive of x by Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int x \cosh a x \rd x = \frac {x \sinh a x} a - \frac {\cosh a x} {a^2} + C
Primitive of x squared by Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int x^2 \sinh a x \ \mathrm d x = \left({\frac {x^2} a + \frac 2 {a^3} }\right) \cosh a x - \frac {2 x \sinh a x} {a^2} + C
Primitive of x squared by Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int x^2 \cosh a x \ \mathrm d x = \left({\frac {x^2} a + \frac 2 {a^3} }\right) \sinh a x - \frac {2 x \cosh a x} {a^2} + C

Primitive of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x over x: {{begin-eqn \int \frac {\coth a x \ \mathrm d x} x \sum_{k \mathop \ge 0} \frac {\left({-1}\right)^k 2^{2 k} B_k \left({a x}\right)^{2 k - 1} } {\left({2 k - 1}\right) \left({2 k}\right)!} + C r = -\frac 1 {a x} + \frac {a x} 3 - \frac {\left({a x}\right)^3} {135} + \cdots + C {{end-eqn where B_k denotes the kth Bernoulli number.

Primitive of Hyperbolic Secant of a x over x: {{begin-eqn \int \frac {\operatorname{sech} a x \ \mathrm d x} x \ln \left\vert{x}\right\vert + \sum_{k \mathop \ge 1} \frac {\left({-1}\right)^k E_k \left({a x}\right)^{2 k} } {\left({2 k}\right) \left({2 k}\right)!} + C r = \ln \left\vert{x}\right\vert - \frac {\left({a x}\right)^2} 4 + \frac {\left({a x}\right)^4} {96} - \frac {\left({a x}\right)^6} {4320} + \cdots + C {{end-eqn where E_k denotes the kth Euler number.

Primitive of Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int \frac {\d x} {\cosh a x} = \frac {2 \map \arctan {e^{a x} } } a + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\coth a x} = \frac {\ln \left\vert {\cosh a x} \right\vert} a + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Secant of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\operatorname{sech} a x} = \frac {\sinh a x} a + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Cosecant of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\operatorname{csch} a x} = \frac {\cosh a x} a + C

Primitive of x over Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int \frac {x \ \mathrm d x} {\sinh a x} = \frac 1 {a^2} \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {2 \left({2^{2 n - 1} - 1}\right) B_{2 n} \left({a x}\right)^{2 n + 1} } {\left({2 n + 1}\right)!} + C

Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int \sinh^2 a x \rd x = \dfrac {\sinh a x \cosh a x} {2 a} - \frac x 2 + C
Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int \cosh^2 a x \rd x = \frac {\sinh a x \cosh a x} {2 a} + \frac x 2 + C
Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Tangent of a x: \int \tanh^2 a x \rd x = x - \frac {\tanh a x} a + C
Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x: \int \coth^2 a x \ \mathrm d x = x - \frac {\coth a x} a + C
Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Secant of a x: \int \sech^2 a x \rd x = \frac {\tanh a x} a + C
Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Cosecant of a x: \int \operatorname{csch}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {-\coth a x} a + C
Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Sine of a x/Corollary: \int \sinh^2 a x \rd x = \frac {\sinh 2 a x} {4 a} - \frac x 2 + C

Primitive of Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x/Corollary: \int \cosh^2 a x \rd x = \frac {\sinh 2 a x} {4 a} + \frac x 2 + C
Primitive of x by Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int x \cosh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x \sinh 2 a x} {4 a} - \frac {\cosh 2 a x} {8 a^2} + \frac {x^2} 4 + C
Primitive of x by Square of Hyperbolic Tangent of a x: \int x \tanh^2 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x^2} 2 - \frac {x \tanh a x} a + \frac 1 {a^2} \ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert + C
Primitive of x by Square of Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x: \int x \coth^2 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x^2} 2 - \frac {x \coth a x} a + \frac 1 {a^2} \ln \left\vert{\sinh a x}\right\vert + C
Primitive of x by Square of Hyperbolic Secant of a x: \int x \operatorname{sech}^2 a x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x \tanh a x} a - \frac 1 {a^2} \ln \left\vert{\cosh a x}\right\vert + C
Primitive of x by Square of Hyperbolic Cosecant of a x: \int x \csch^2 a x \rd x = \frac {-x \coth a x} a + \frac 1 {a^2} \ln \size {\sinh a x} + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\sinh^2 a x} = - \frac {\coth a x} a + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\cosh^2 a x} = \frac {\tanh a x} a + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Hyperbolic Sine of p x: \int \sinh a x \sinh p x \rd x = \frac {\map \sinh {a + p} x} {2 \paren {a + p} } - \frac {\map \sinh {a - p} x} {2 \paren {a - p} } + C

Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x by Hyperbolic Cosine of p x: \int \cosh a x \cosh p x \rd x = \frac {\map \sinh {a + p} x} {2 \paren {a + p} } + \frac {\map \sinh {a - p} x} {2 \paren {a - p} } + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Sine of p x: \int \sinh a x \sin p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \cosh a x \sin p x - p \sinh a x \cos p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Sine of a x by Cosine of p x: \int \sinh a x \cos p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \cosh a x \cos p x + p \sinh a x \sin p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x by Sine of p x: \int \cosh a x \sin p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \sinh a x \sin p x - p \cosh a x \cos p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C
Primitive of Hyperbolic Cosine of a x by Cosine of p x: \int \cosh a x \cos p x \ \mathrm d x = \frac {a \sinh a x \cos p x + p \cosh a x \sin p x} {a^2 + p^2} + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of p plus q by Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int \frac {\d x} {p + q \sinh a x} = \frac 1 {a \sqrt{p^2 + q^2} } \ln \size {\frac {q e^{a x} + p - \sqrt {p^2 + q^2} } {q e^{a x} + p + \sqrt {p^2 + q^2} } } + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of p plus q by Hyperbolic Cosine of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \cosh a x} = \begin{cases} \frac 2 {a \sqrt{q^2 - p^2} } \arctan \frac {q e^{a x} + p} {\sqrt {q^2 - p^2} } + C & : p^2 < q^2 \\ \frac 1 {a \sqrt{p^2 - q^2} } \ln \left\vert{\frac {q e^{a x} + p - \sqrt {p^2 - q^2} } {q e^{a x} + p + \sqrt {p^2 - q^2} } }\right\vert + C & : p^2 > q^2 \end{cases}

Primitive of Reciprocal of p plus q by Hyperbolic Tangent of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \tanh a x} = \frac {p x} {p^2 - q^2} - \frac q {a \left({p^2 - q^2}\right)} \ln \left\vert{q \sinh a x + p \cosh a x}\right\vert + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of p plus q by Hyperbolic Cotangent of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \coth a x} = \frac {p x} {p^2 - q^2} - \frac q {a \left({p^2 - q^2}\right)} \ln \left\vert{p \sinh a x + q \cosh a x}\right\vert + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of q plus p by Hyperbolic Secant of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {q + p \operatorname{sech} a x} = \frac x q - \frac p q \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \cosh a x} + C
Primitive of Reciprocal of q plus p by Hyperbolic Cosecant of a x: \int \frac {\d x} {q + p \csch a x} = \frac x q - \frac p q \int \frac {\d x} {p + q \sinh a x} + C

Primitive of Reciprocal of Square of p plus q by Hyperbolic Sine of a x: \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {\left({p + q \sinh a x}\right)^2} = \frac {-q \cosh a x} {a \left({p^2 + q^2}\right) \left({p + q \sinh a x}\right)} + \frac p {p^2 + q^2} \int \frac {\mathrm d x} {p + q \sinh a x} + C

Primitive of Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine of x over a over x squared: \int \frac {\cosh^{-1} \dfrac x a \ \mathrm d x} {x^2} = \begin{cases} \frac {-\cosh^{-1} \dfrac x a} x - \frac 1 a \ln \left({\frac {a + \sqrt {x^2 + a^2} } x}\right) & : \cosh^{-1} \dfrac x a > 0 \\ \frac {-\cosh^{-1} \dfrac x a} x + \frac 1 a \ln \left({\frac {a + \sqrt {x^2 + a^2} } x}\right) & : \cosh^{-1} \dfrac x a < 0 \\ \end{cases}

Primitive of Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent of x over a over x squared: \int \frac {\tanh^{-1} \dfrac x a \rd x} {x^2} = \frac {-\tanh^{-1} \dfrac x a} x + \frac 1 {2 a} \map \ln {\frac {x^2} {a^2 - x^2} } + C

Primitive of Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent of x over a over x squared: \int \frac {\coth^{-1} \dfrac x a \rd x} {x^2} = \frac {-\coth^{-1} \dfrac x a} x + \frac 1 {2 a} \map \ln {\frac {x^2} {x^2 - a^2} } + C

Primitive of Power of x by Inverse Hyperbolic Sine of x over a: \int x^m \sinh^{-1} \frac x a \ \mathrm d x = \frac {x^{m + 1} } {m + 1} \sinh^{-1} \frac x a- \frac 1 {m + 1} \int \frac {x^{m + 1} } {\sqrt {x^2 + a^2} } \ \mathrm d x + C

Primitive of Power of x by Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent of x over a: \int x^m \coth^{-1} \frac x a \rd x = \frac {x^{m + 1} } {m + 1} \coth^{-1} \frac x a - \frac a {m + 1} \int \frac {x^{m + 1} } {a^2 - x^2} \rd x + C

Primitive of Power of x by Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant of x over a: \int x^m \operatorname{csch}^{-1} \frac x a \rd x = \begin{cases} \frac {x^{m + 1} } {m + 1} \operatorname{csch}^{-1} \frac x a + \frac 1 {m + 1} \int \frac {x^m} {\sqrt {x^2 + a^2} } \rd x + C & : x > 0 \\ \frac {x^{m + 1} } {m + 1} \operatorname{csch}^{-1} \frac x a - \frac 1 {m + 1} \int \frac {x^m} {\sqrt {x^2 + a^2} } \rd x + C & : x < 0 \\ \end{cases}
Hyperbolic Tangent Half-Angle Substitution: \int \map F {\sinh x, \cosh x} \rd x = 2 \int \map F {\frac {2 u} {1 - u^2}, \frac {1 + u^2} {1 - u^2} } \frac {\d u} {1 - u^2} where u = \tanh \dfrac x 2.
Reciprocal of One Plus Cosine: \dfrac 1 {1 + \cos x} = \dfrac 1 2 \sec^2 \dfrac x 2
Reciprocal of One Minus Cosine: \dfrac 1 {1 - \cos x} = \dfrac 1 2 \csc^2 \left({\dfrac x 2}\right)
Irrationality of Logarithm: Let a, b \in \N_{>0} such that both \nexists m, n \in \N_{>0}: a^m = b^n. Then \log_b a is irrational.
Tangent of 22.5 Degrees: \tan 22.5^\circ = \tan \dfrac \pi 8 = \sqrt 2 - 1
Tangent of 67.5 Degrees: \tan 67.5 \degrees = \tan \dfrac {3 \pi} 8 = \sqrt 2 + 1
Sine of x plus Cosine of x/Cosine Form: \sin x + \cos x = \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {x - \dfrac \pi 4}
Sine of x minus Cosine of x/Sine Form: \sin x - \cos x = \sqrt 2 \sin \left({x - \dfrac \pi 4}\right)
Sine of x minus Cosine of x: === Sine Form === {{:Sine of x minus Cosine of x/Sine Form === Cosine Form === {{:Sine of x minus Cosine of x/Cosine Form
Sine of x minus Cosine of x/Cosine Form: \sin x - \cos x = \sqrt 2 \, \map \cos {x - \dfrac {3 \pi} 4}
Multiple of Sine plus Multiple of Cosine: === Cosine Form === {{:Multiple of Sine plus Multiple of Cosine/Cosine Form === Sine Form === {{:Multiple of Sine plus Multiple of Cosine/Sine Form
Multiple of Sine plus Multiple of Cosine/Cosine Form: p \sin x + q \cos x = \sqrt {p^2 + q^2} \map \cos {x + \arctan \dfrac {-p} q}
Multiple of Sine plus Multiple of Cosine/Sine Form: p \sin x + q \cos x = \sqrt {p^2 + q^2} \sin \left({x + \arctan \dfrac q p}\right)

Primitive of Cosine of a x over Sine of a x plus phi: \int \frac {\cos a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } = \frac {\ln \size {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } } {a \cos \phi} + \tan \phi \int \frac {\sin a x \rd x} {\map \sin {a x + \phi} } + C

Primitive of Sine of a x over Sine of a x plus phi: \int \frac {\sin a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)} = \frac x {\cos \phi} - \tan \phi \int \frac {\cos a x \ \mathrm d x} {\sin \left({a x + \phi}\right)} + C
Reciprocal of One Plus Hyperbolic Cosine: \dfrac 1 {1 + \cosh x} = \dfrac 1 2 \operatorname{sech}^2 \dfrac x 2
Reciprocal of Hyperbolic Cosine Minus One: \dfrac 1 {\cosh x - 1} = \dfrac 1 2 \csch^2 \dfrac x 2

Steiner-Lehmus Theorem: Let ABC be a triangle. Denote the lengths of the angle bisectors through the vertices A and B by \omega_\alpha and \omega_\beta. Let \omega_\alpha = \omega_\beta. Then ABC is an isosceles triangle.

Triangle Right-Angle-Hypotenuse-Side Equality: If two triangles have: : one right angle each : the sides opposite to the right angle equal : another two respective sides equal they will also have: : their third sides equal : the remaining two angles equal to their respective remaining angles.
Internal Angles of Regular Polygon: The size A of each internal angle of a regular n-gon is given by: :A = \dfrac {\paren {n - 2} 180 \degrees} n
Sum of Internal Angles of Polygon: The sum S of all internal angles of a polygon with n sides is given by the formula S = \paren {n - 2} 180 \degrees.

Five Platonic Solids: There exist exactly five platonic solids: :\paren 1: \quad the regular tetrahedron :\paren 2: \quad the cube :\paren 3: \quad the regular octahedron :\paren 4: \quad the regular dodecahedron :\paren 5: \quad the regular icosahedron. {{:Euclid:Proposition/XIII/18/Endnote

Space in which All Convergent Sequences have Unique Limit not necessarily Hausdorff: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space. Let T be such that all convergent sequences have a unique limit point. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is a Hausdorff space.

Geometric Sequence with Coprime Extremes is in Lowest Terms: Let G_n = \sequence {a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let: :a_0 \perp a_n where \perp denotes coprimality. Then G_n is in its lowest terms.
Measurements of Common Angles/Straight Angle: The measurement of a straight angle is \dfrac{360^\circ} 2 = 180^\circ or \dfrac {2 \pi} 2 = \pi.
Measurements of Common Angles/Right Angle: The measurement of a right angle is \dfrac {180 \degrees} 2 = 90 \degrees or \dfrac \pi 2.
Measurements of Common Angles/Full Angle: A full angle is equal to one full rotation.
Measurements of Common Angles/Acute Angle: An acute angle measures \theta, where: :0 \degrees < \theta < 90 \degrees or: :0 < \theta < \dfrac \pi 2
Measurements of Common Angles/Obtuse Angle: An obtuse angle measures \theta, where: : 90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ or: : \dfrac \pi 2 < \theta < \pi
Measurements of Common Angles/Reflex Angle: A reflex angle measures \theta, where: : 180^\circ < \theta < 360^\circ or: : \pi < \theta < 2 \pi

Supplementary Interior Angles implies Parallel Lines: Given two infinite straight lines which are cut by a transversal, if the interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary, then the lines are parallel.
Equal Corresponding Angles implies Parallel Lines: Given two infinite straight lines which are cut by a transversal, if the corresponding angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.

Equivalence of Definitions of Tangent Vector: Let M be a smooth manifold. Let m \in M be a point. Let V be an open neighborhood of m. Let C^\infty \left({V, \R}\right) be defined as the set of all smooth mappings f: V \to \R. {{TFAE|def = Tangent Vector
Parallelism implies Equal Alternate Angles: Given two infinite straight lines which are cut by a transversal, if the lines are parallel, then the alternate angles are equal.
Parallelism implies Equal Corresponding Angles: Given two infinite straight lines which are cut by a transversal, if the lines are parallel, then the corresponding angles are equal.
Proportion is Reflexive: Proportion is a reflexive relation. That is, every real variable is proportional to itself: :\forall x \in \R: x \propto x
Proportion is Symmetric: Proportion is a symmetric relation. That is: :\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto y \implies y \propto x
Proportion is Transitive: Proportion is a transitive relation. That is: :\forall x,y,z \in \R: x \propto y \land y \propto z \implies x \propto z

Parallelism implies Supplementary Interior Angles: Given two infinite straight lines which are cut by a transversal, if the lines are parallel, then the interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary.
Proportion of Power: Let x and y be proportional. {{explain|Establish what types of object x and y are. As it stands here, they could be anything. Let n \in \Z. Then x^n \propto y^n.
Sine of 18 Degrees: \sin 18 \degrees = \sin \dfrac \pi {10} = \dfrac {\sqrt 5 - 1} 4 where \sin denotes the sine function.
Cosine of 72 Degrees: \cos 72 \degrees = \cos \dfrac {2 \pi} 5 = \dfrac {\sqrt 5 - 1} 4
Sine of 72 Degrees: \sin 72 \degrees = \sin \dfrac {2 \pi} 5 = \dfrac {\sqrt{10 + 2 \sqrt 5} } 4 where \sin denotes the sine function.
Cosine of 18 Degrees: \cos 18^\circ = \cos \dfrac \pi {10} = \dfrac {\sqrt{10 + 2 \sqrt 5 4 where \cos denotes the cosine function.

Sine of 3 Degrees: \sin 3^\circ = \sin \dfrac \pi {60} = \dfrac {\sqrt{30} + \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 - \sqrt 2 - 2 \sqrt {15 + 3 \sqrt 5} + 2 \sqrt {5 + \sqrt 5} } {16} where \sin denotes the sine function.

Cosine of 3 Degrees: \cos 3^\circ = \cos \dfrac {\pi} {60} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{30} - \sqrt{10} - \sqrt 6 + \sqrt 2 + 2 \sqrt{15 + 3 \sqrt 5} + 2 \sqrt{5 + \sqrt 5} } {16} where \cos denotes the cosine function.
Square Root of Sum as Sum of Square Roots: Let a, b \in \R, a \ge b. Then: :\sqrt {a + b} = \sqrt {\dfrac a 2 + \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2 2} + \sqrt {\dfrac a 2 - \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2 2}
Sine of 1 Degree: \sin 1^\circ = \sin \dfrac {\pi} {180} = where \sin denotes the sine function.
Rectangle is Parallelogram: Let ABCD be a rectangle. Then ABCD is a parallelogram.

Condition for Denesting of Square Root: Let a, b \in \Q_{\ge 0}. Suppose \sqrt b \notin \Q. Then: :\exists p, q \in \Q: \sqrt {a + \sqrt b} = \sqrt p + \sqrt q {{iff: :\exists n \in \Q: a^2 - b = n^2.
Characteristic Function of Union/Variant 1: \chi_{A \mathop \cup B} = \min \set {\chi_A + \chi_B, 1}
Characteristic Function of Union/Variant 2: \chi_{A \mathop \cup B} = \chi_A + \chi_B - \chi_{A \mathop \cap B}
Characteristic Function of Union/Variant 3: \chi_{A \mathop \cup B} = \max \set {\chi_A, \chi_B}
Characteristic Function of Intersection/Variant 1: \chi_{A \cap B} = \chi_A \chi_B
Characteristic Function of Intersection/Variant 2: \chi_{A \cap B} = \min \left\{{\chi_A, \chi_B}\right\}

Tangent Space is Vector Space: Let M be a smooth manifold of dimension n \in \N. Let m \in M be a point. Let \left({U, \kappa}\right) be a chart with m \in U. Let T_m M be the tangent space at m. Then T_m M is a real vector space of dimension n, spanned by the basis: :\left\{ {\left.{\dfrac \partial {\partial \kappa^i} }\right\vert_m : i \in \left\{{1, \dotsc, n}\right\} }\right\} that is, the set of partial derivatives with respect to the ith coordinate function \kappa^i evaluated at m.
Multiplication of Real Numbers is Right Distributive over Subtraction: {{:Euclid:Proposition/V/6 That is, for any number a and for any integers m, n: :m a - n a = \paren {m - n} a
Sum of Square Roots as Square Root of Sum: \sqrt a + \sqrt b = \sqrt {a + b + \sqrt {4 a b} }

Divisor of One of Coprime Numbers is Coprime to Other: Let a, b \in \N be numbers such that a and b are coprime: :a \perp b Let c > 1 be a divisor of a: :c \divides a Then c and b are coprime: :c \perp b {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/23
Integer Coprime to all Factors is Coprime to Whole/Proof 1: Let a, b \in \Z. Let b = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^r b_j Let a be coprime to each of b_1, \ldots, b_r. Then a is coprime to b.
Integer Coprime to all Factors is Coprime to Whole/Proof 2: Let a, b, c \in \Z. Let c be coprime to each of a and b. Then c is coprime to a b. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/24
Square of Coprime Number is Coprime: Let a and b be coprime integers: :a, b \in \Z: a \perp b Then: :a^2 \perp b {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/25

Product of Coprime Pairs is Coprime: Let a, b, c, d be integers. Let: :a \perp c, b \perp c, a \perp d, b \perp d where a \perp c denotes that a and c are coprime. Then: :a b \perp c d {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/26
Powers of Coprime Numbers are Coprime: Let a, b be coprime integers: :a \perp b Then: :\forall n \in \N_{>0}: a^n \perp b^n {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/27
Numbers are Coprime iff Sum is Coprime to Both: Let a, b be integers. Then: :a \perp b \iff a \perp \paren {a + b} where a \perp b denotes that a and b are coprime. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/28
Composite Number has Prime Factor: Let a be a composite number. Then there exists a prime number p such that: :p \divides a where \divides means is a divisor of. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/31

Natural Number is Prime or has Prime Factor: Let a be a natural number greater than 1. Then either: :a is a prime number or: :there exists a prime number p \ne a such that p \divides a where \divides denotes is a divisor of. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/32
LCM of Three Numbers: Let a, b, c \in \Z: a b c \ne 0. The lowest common multiple of a, b, c, denoted \lcm \set {a, b, c}, can always be found. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/36

Negative of Real Function that Increases Without Bound: Let f: \R \to \R be a real function. Then: :(1): \quad \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} -\map f x = -\infty :(2): \quad \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = +\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} -\map f x = -\infty
Integer Divided by Divisor is Integer: Let a, b \in \N. Then: :b \divides a \implies \dfrac 1 b \times a \in \N where \divides denotes divisibilty. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/37
Divisor is Reciprocal of Divisor of Integer: Let a, b, c \in \Z_{>0}. Then: :b = \dfrac 1 c \times a \implies c \divides a where \divides denotes divisibilty. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VII/38

Negative of Real Function that Decreases Without Bound: Let f: \R \to \R be a real function. Then: :(1): \quad \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to +\infty} -\map f x = +\infty :(2): \quad \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} \map f x = -\infty \implies \lim_{x \mathop \to -\infty} -\map f x = +\infty

Construction of Geometric Sequence in Lowest Terms: It is possible to find a geometric sequence of integers G_n of length n + 1 with a given common ratio such that G_n is in its lowest terms. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/2
Geometric Sequence in Lowest Terms has Coprime Extremes: A geometric sequence of integers in lowest terms has extremes which are coprime. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/3

General Associativity Theorem/Formulation 3: Let \struct {S, \circ} be a semigroup. Let a_i denote elements of S. Let \circ be associative. Let n \in \Z be a positive integer such that n \ge 3. Then all possible parenthesizations of the expression: :a_1 \circ a_2 \circ \cdots \circ a_n are equivalent.

First Element of Geometric Sequence not dividing Second: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers of length n. Let a_0 not be a divisor of a_1. Then: :\forall j, k \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, n}, j \ne k: a_j \nmid a_k That is, if the initial term of P does not divide the second, no term of P divides any other term of P. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/6

First Element of Geometric Sequence that divides Last also divides Second: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers of length n. Let a_0 be a divisor of a_n. Then a_0 is a divisor of a_2. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/7

Geometric Sequences in Proportion have Same Number of Elements: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers of length n. Let r be the common ratio of P. Let Q = \sequence {b_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le m} be a geometric sequence of integers of length m. Let r be the common ratio of Q. Let b_0 and b_m be such that \dfrac {b_0} {b_m} = \dfrac {a_0} {a_n}. Then m = n. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/8

Elements of Geometric Sequence between Coprime Numbers: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers of length n + 1. Let a_0 be coprime to a_n. Then there exist geometric sequences of integers Q_1 and Q_2 of length n + 1 such that: :the initial term of both Q_1 and Q_2 is 1 :the final term of Q_1 is a_0 :the final term of Q_2 is a_n. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/9

Product of Geometric Sequences from One: Let Q_1 = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} and Q_2 = \sequence {b_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be geometric sequences of integers of length n + 1. Let a_0 = b_0 = 1. Then the sequence P = \sequence {p_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} defined as: :\forall j \in \set {0, \ldots, n}: p_j = b^j a^{n - j} is a geometric sequence. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/10

Powers of Elements of Geometric Sequence are in Geometric Sequence: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers. Then the sequence Q = \sequence {b_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} defined as: :\forall j \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, n}: b_j = a_j^m where m \in \Z_{>0}, is a geometric sequence. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/13
Number divides Number iff Square divides Square: Let a, b \in \Z. Then: :a^2 \divides b^2 \iff a \divides b where \divides denotes integer divisibility. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/14
Number divides Number iff Cube divides Cube: Let a, b \in \Z. Then: :a^3 \divides b^3 \iff a \divides b where \divides denotes integer divisibility. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/15

Number does not divide Number iff Square does not divide Square: Let a, b \in \Z be integers. Then: :a 
mid b \iff a^2 
mid b^2 where a 
mid b denotes that a is not a divisor of b. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/16

Number does not divide Number iff Cube does not divide Cube: Let a, b \in \Z be integers. Then: :a 
mid b \iff a^3 
mid b^3 where a 
mid b denotes that a is not a divisor of b. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/17
Numbers between which exists one Mean Proportional are Similar Plane: Let a, b \in \Z such that the geometric mean is an integer. Then a and b are similar plane numbers. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/20

Numbers between which exist two Mean Proportionals are Similar Solid: Let a, b \in \Z be the extremes of a geometric sequence of integers whose length is 4: :\tuple {a, m_1, m_2, b} That is, such that a and b have 2 mean proportionals. Then a and b are similar solid numbers. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/21

If First of Three Numbers in Geometric Sequence is Square then Third is Square: Let P = \tuple {a, b, c} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let a be a square number. Then c is also a square number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/22

If First of Four Numbers in Geometric Sequence is Cube then Fourth is Cube: Let P = \tuple {a, b, c, d} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let a be a cube number. Then d is also a cube number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/23

If Ratio of Square to Number is as between Two Squares then Number is Square: Let a, b, c, d \in \Z be integers such that: :\dfrac a b = \dfrac {c^2} {d^2} Let a be a square number. Then b is also a square number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/24

If Ratio of Cube to Number is as between Two Cubes then Number is Cube: Let a, b, c, d \in \Z be integers such that: :\dfrac a b = \dfrac {c^3} {d^3} Let a be a cube number. Then b is also a cube number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/VIII/25
Square of Cube Number is Cube: Let a \in \N be a natural number. Let a be a cube number. Then a^2 is also a cube number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/3
Cube Number multiplied by Cube Number is Cube: Let a, b \in \N be natural numbers. Let a and b be cube numbers. Then a b is also a cube number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/4
Number Squared making Cube is itself Cube: Let a \in \Z be an integer. Let a^2 be a cube number. Then a is a cube number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/6
Product of Composite Number with Number is Solid Number: Let a, b \in \Z be positive integers. Let a be a composite number. Then a b is a solid number. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/7
Square Numbers are Similar Plane Numbers: Let a and b be square numbers. Then a and b are similar plane numbers.

Elements of Geometric Sequence from One which are Powers of Number: Let G_n = \sequence {a_n}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let a_0 = 1. Then: :\forall m, k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}: k \divides m \implies a_m is a power of k where \divides denotes divisibility. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/8

Elements of Geometric Sequence from One where First Element is Power of Number: Let G_n = \sequence {a_n}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let a_0 = 1. Let m \in \Z_{> 0}. Let a_1 be the mth power of an integer. Then all the terms of G_n are mth powers of integers. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/9

Elements of Geometric Sequence from One where First Element is not Power of Number: Let G_n = \sequence {a_n}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let a_0 = 1. Let k \in \Z_{> 1}. Let a_1 not be a power of k. Then a_m is not a power of k except for: :\forall m, k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: k \divides m where \divides denotes divisibility. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/10

Elements of Geometric Sequence from One which Divide Later Elements: Let G_n = \sequence {a_n}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} be a geometric Sequence of integers. Let a_0 = 1. Let m \in \Z_{> 0}. Then: :\forall r \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, m}: a_k \divides a_m where \divides denotes divisibility. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/11

Elements of Geometric Sequence from One Divisible by Prime: Let G_n = \sequence {a_n}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers. Let a_0 = 1. Let p be a prime number such that: :p \divides a_n where \divides denotes divisibility. Then p \divides a_1. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/12

Divisibility of Elements of Geometric Sequence from One where First Element is Prime: Let Q_n = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of length n consisting of integers only. Let a_0 = 1. Let a_1 be a prime number. Then the only divisors of a_n are a_j for j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/13

Sum of Pair of Elements of Geometric Sequence with Three Elements in Lowest Terms is Coprime to other Element: Let P = \tuple {a, b, c} be a geometric sequence of integers in its lowest terms. Then \paren {a + b}, \paren {b + c} and \paren {a + c} are all coprime to each of a, b and c. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/15

Two Coprime Integers have no Third Integer Proportional: Let a, b \in \Z_{>0} be integers such that a and b are coprime. Then there is no integer c \in \Z such that: :\dfrac a b = \dfrac b c {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/16

Last Element of Geometric Sequence with Coprime Extremes has no Integer Proportional as First to Second: Let G_n = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of integers such that a_0 \ne 1. Let a_0 \perp a_n, where \perp denotes coprimality. Then there does not exist an integer b such that: :\dfrac {a_0} {a_1} = \dfrac {a_n} b {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/17

Condition for Existence of Third Number Proportional to Two Numbers: Let a, b, c \in \Z be integers. Let \tuple {a, b, c} be a geometric sequence. In order for this to be possible, both of these conditions must be true: :(1): \quad a and b cannot be coprime :(2): \quad a \divides b^2 where \divides denotes divisibility. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/18

Odd Divisor of Even Number also divides its Half: Let a, b \in \Z be integers. Let a be odd and b be even. Let: :a \divides b where \divides denotes divisibility. Then: :a \divides \dfrac b 2 {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/30

Odd Number Coprime to Number is also Coprime to its Double: Let a, b \in \Z be integers. Let a be odd. Let: : a \perp b where \perp denotes coprimality. Then: : a \perp 2 b {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/31
Power of Two is Even-Times Even Only: Let a > 2 be a power of 2. Then a is even-times even only. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/32
Number whose Half is Odd is Even-Times Odd: Let a \in \Z be an integer such that \dfrac a 2 is an odd integer. Then a is even-times odd. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/33

Number neither whose Half is Odd nor Power of Two is both Even-Times Even and Even-Times Odd: Let a \in \Z be an integer such that: :(1): \quad a is not a power of 2 :(2): \quad \dfrac a 2 is an even integer. Then a is both even-times even and even-times odd. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/34

Existence of Fraction of Number Smaller than Given: Let a, b \in \R_{>0} be two (strictly) positive real numbers, such that a > b. Let the sequence \left\langle{a_n}\right\rangle be defined recursively as: :a_i = \begin{cases} a & : i = 1 \\ a_{i - 1} - c: \dfrac {a_{i - 1} } 2 < c < a_{i - 1} & : i > 1 \end{cases} Then: : \exists n \in \N_{>0}: a_n < b {{:Euclid:Proposition/X/1

Restriction of Continuous Mapping is Continuous/Topological Spaces: Let T_1 = \left({S_1, \tau_1}\right) and T_2 = \left({S_2, \tau_2}\right) be topological spaces. Let M_1 \subseteq S_1 be a subset of S_1. Let f: S_1 \to S_2 be a mapping which is continuous. Let M_2 \subseteq S_2 be a subset of S_2 such that f\left[{M_1}\right] \subseteq M_2. Let f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2: M_1 \to M_2 be the restriction of f to M_1 \times M_2. Then f {\restriction_{M_1 \times M_2 is continuous, where M_1 and M_2 are equipped with the respective subspace topologies.

Restriction of Continuous Mapping is Continuous/Metric Spaces: Let M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1} and M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2} be metric spaces. Let S \subseteq M_1 be a subset of M_1. Let f: M_1 \to M_2 be a mapping which is continuous at a point \alpha \in S. Let f \restriction_S = g: S \to M_2 be the restriction of f to S. Then g is continuous at \alpha.

Restriction of Inverse is Inverse of Restriction: Let S_1 and S_2 be sets. Let f: S_1 \to S_2 be a bijection. Let S \subseteq S_1 be a subset of S_1. Let f^{-1} be the inverse of f. Let f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right] be the restriction of f to S \times f\left[{S}\right]. Let f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S be the restriction of f^{-1} to f \left[{S}\right] \times S. Then: : f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right] is a bijection and: : {\left({f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right] }\right)}^{-1} = f^{-1} {\restriction_{f \left[{S}\right] \times S

Restriction of Homeomorphism is Homeomorphism: Let T_1 = \left({S_1, \tau_1}\right), T_2 = \left({S_2, \tau_2}\right) be topological spaces. Let f: S_1 \to S_2 be a homeomorphism between T_1 and T_2. Let S be a subset of S_1. Let f {\restriction_{S \times f\left[{S}\right] : S \to f \left[{S}\right] be the restriction of f to S \times f \left[{S}\right]. Let S and f \left[{S}\right] bear their respective subspace topologies. Then f {\restriction_{S \times f \left[{S}\right] is a homeomorphism.
Theorem of Even Perfect Numbers/Sufficient Condition: Let n \in \N be such that 2^n - 1 is prime. Then 2^{n - 1} \paren {2^n - 1} is perfect. {{:Euclid:Proposition/IX/36
Theorem of Even Perfect Numbers/Necessary Condition: Let a \in \N be an even perfect number. Then a is in the form: :2^{n - 1} \paren {2^n - 1} where 2^n - 1 is prime.

Condition for Commensurability of Roots of Quadratic Equation: Consider the quadratic equation: :(1): \quad a x - x^2 = \dfrac {b^2} 4 Then x and a - x are commensurable {{iff \sqrt{a^2 - b^2} and a are commensurable. {{:Euclid:Proposition/X/17

Condition for Incommensurability of Roots of Quadratic Equation: Consider the quadratic equation: :(1): \quad a x - x^2 = \dfrac {b^2} 4 Then x and a - x are incommensurable {{iff \sqrt {a^2 - b^2} and a are incommensurable. {{:Euclid:Proposition/X/18

Product of Rationally Expressible Numbers is Rational: Let a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q} be the lengths of rational line segments. Furthermore, let \dfrac a b \in \Q. Then, a b \in \Q. {{:Euclid:Proposition/X/19

otin \Q \land \paren { rac a b}^2 \in \Q} \implies \paren {\paren {a - b} 
otin \Q \land \paren {a - b}^2 
otin \Q} {{:Euclid:Proposition/X/73

Construction of Apotome is Unique: Let D be the domain \left\{{x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}\right\}, the rationally expressible numbers. Let a, b \in D be two rationally expressible numbers such that a - b is an apotome. Then, there exists only one x \in D such that a - b + x and a are commensurable in square only. {{:Euclid:Proposition/X/79
Lower Bound of Natural Logarithm: \forall x \in \R_{>0}: 1 - \dfrac 1 x \le \ln x where \ln x denotes the natural logarithm of x.
Bounds of Natural Logarithm: Let \ln y be the natural logarithm of y where y \in \R_{>0}. Then \ln satisfies the compound inequality: : 1 - \frac 1 y \le \ln y \le y - 1
Definition:Elevated/Point: Let P be a plane. An elevated point (relative to P) is a point in space which does not lie on P.
Definition:Elevated/Line: Let P be a plane. An elevated line (relative to P) is a line in space which does not lie entirely in P.
Mordell's Theorem: Let C be an elliptic curve over \Q. Then the group of rational points on C is a finitely generated abelian group.
Common Ratio in Rational Geometric Sequence is Rational: Let \sequence {a_k} be a geometric sequence whose terms are rational. Then the common ratio of \sequence {a_k} is rational.
Common Ratio in Integer Geometric Sequence is Rational: Let \sequence {a_k} be a geometric sequence whose terms are all integers. Then the common ratio of \sequence {a_k} is rational.

Form of Geometric Sequence of Integers: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of length n + 1 consisting of integers only. Then the jth term of P is given by: :a_j = k p^{n - j} q^j where: : the common ratio of P expressed in canonical form is \dfrac q p : k is an integer.

Geometric Sequence of Integers with Integer Common Ratio: Let P = \sequence {a_j}_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} be a geometric sequence of length n consisting entirely of integers. Let r be the common ratio of P. Then r is an integer {{iff: :\forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}, i \le j: a_i \divides a_j That is, terms of P divide later terms of P {{iff r is an integer.

Integers are Coprime iff Powers are Coprime: Let a, b \in \Z be integers. Then: :a \perp b \iff \forall n \in \N: a^n \perp b^n That is, two integers are coprime {{iff all their positive integer powers are coprime.
Successor Mapping of Peano Structure has no Fixed Point: Let \PP = \struct {P, s, 0} be a Peano structure. Then: :\forall n \in P: \map s n \ne n That is, the successor mapping has no fixed points.
Integer Addition is Cancellable: The operation of addition on the set of integers \Z is cancellable: :\forall x, y, z \in \Z: x + z = y + z \implies x = y

Open Real Interval is Subset of Closed Real Interval: Let a, b \in \R be real numbers. Then: :\openint a b \subseteq \closedint a b where: :\openint a b is the open interval between a and b :\closedint a b is the closed interval between a and b.
Complement Relative to Subset is Subset of Complement Relative to Superset: Let A, B, C be sets such that A \subseteq B \subseteq C. Then: :\relcomp B A \subseteq \relcomp C A
Complement of Relative Complement is Union with Complement: Let A, B, C be sets such that A \subseteq B \subseteq C. Then: :\relcomp C {\relcomp B A} = A \cup \relcomp C B

Set Union Preserves Subsets/Families of Sets: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {A_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} and \family {B_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be indexed families of subsets of a set S. Let: :\forall \beta \in I: A_\beta \subseteq B_\beta Then: : \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in I} A_\alpha \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in I} B_\alpha

Set Union Preserves Subsets/General Result: Let \mathbb S, \mathbb T be sets of sets. Suppose that for each S \in \mathbb S there exists a T \in \mathbb T such that S \subseteq T. Then \bigcup \mathbb S \subseteq \bigcup \mathbb T.

Intersection of Family is Subset of Intersection of Subset of Family: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {A_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be an indexed family of subsets of a set S. Let J \subseteq I. Then: : \bigcap_{\alpha \mathop \in I} A_\alpha \subseteq \bigcap_{\alpha \mathop \in J} A_\alpha where \bigcap_{\alpha \mathop \in I} A_\alpha denotes the intersection of \family {A_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I}.

Union of Subset of Family is Subset of Union of Family: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {A_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be an indexed family of subsets of a set S. Let J \subseteq I Then: : \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in J} A_\alpha \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in I} A_\alpha where \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in I} A_\alpha denotes the union of \family {A_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I}.

Intersection of Open Intervals of Positive Reals is Empty: Let \R_{> 0} be the set of strictly positive real numbers. For all x \in \R_{> 0}, let A_x be the open real interval \openint 0 x. Then: : \bigcap_{x \mathop \in \R_{> 0} } A_x = \O

Union of Open Intervals of Positive Reals is Set of Strictly Positive Reals: Let \R_{> 0} be the set of strictly positive real numbers. For all x \in \R_{> 0}, let A_x be the open real interval \openint 0 x. Then: : \bigcup_{x \mathop \in \R_{> 0} } A_x = \R_{> 0}

Intersection of Closed Intervals of Positive Reals is Zero: Let \R_{> 0} be the set of strictly positive real numbers. For all x \in \R_{> 0}, let B_x be the closed real interval \closedint 0 x. Then: : \bigcap_{x \mathop \in \R_{> 0} } B_x = \set 0

Union of Closed Intervals of Positive Reals is Set of Positive Reals: Let \R_{> 0} be the set of strictly positive real numbers. For all x \in \R_{> 0}, let B_x be the closed real interval \closedint 0 x. Then: : \bigcup_{x \mathop \in \R_{> 0} } B_x = \R_{\ge 0}

Relative Complement of Cartesian Product: Let A and B be sets. Let X \subseteq A and Y \subseteq B. Then: :\relcomp {A \mathop \times B} {X \times Y} = \paren {A \times \relcomp B Y} \cup \paren {\relcomp A X \times B}

Subset of Cartesian Product not necessarily Cartesian Product of Subsets: Let A and B be sets. Let A and B both have at least two distinct elements. Then there exists W \subseteq A \times B such that W is not the cartesian product of a subset of A and a subset of B.

Subset equals Preimage of Image implies Injection: Let f: S \to T be a mapping. Let f^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T be the direct image mapping of f. Similarly, let f^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S be the inverse image mapping of f. Let: :\forall A \in \powerset S: A = \map {\paren {f^\gets \circ f^\to} } A Then f is an injection.

Preimage of Image of Subset under Injection equals Subset: Let f: S \to T be an injection. Then: :\forall A \subseteq S: A = \paren {f^{-1} \circ f} \sqbrk A where: :f \sqbrk A denotes the image of A under f :f^{-1} denotes the inverse of f :f^{-1} \circ f denotes composition of f^{-1} and f.

Subset equals Image of Preimage implies Surjection: Let f: S \to T be a mapping. Let: :\forall B \subseteq T: B = \paren {f \circ f^{-1} } \sqbrk B where f \sqbrk B denotes the image of B under f. Then f is a surjection.

Image of Preimage of Subset under Surjection equals Subset: Let f: S \to T be a surjection. Then: :\forall B \subseteq T: B = \left({f \circ f^{-1} }\right) \sqbrk B where: :f \sqbrk B denotes the image of B under f :f^{-1} denotes the inverse of f :f \circ f^{-1} denotes composition of f and f^{-1}.
Intersection of Image with Subset of Codomain: Let S and T be sets. Let f: S \to T be a mapping. Let A \subseteq S and B \subseteq T. Then: :f \sqbrk {A \cap f^{-1} \sqbrk B} = f \sqbrk A \cap B

Projection is Injection iff Factor is Singleton: Let S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n be non-empty sets. Let S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i be the cartesian product of S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n. Let \pr_j: S \to S_j be the jth projection on S. Then \pr_j is an injection {{iff S_k is a singleton for all k \in \set {1, 2, \dotsc, n} where k \ne j.

Preimage of Element under Projection: Let A and B be sets. Let A \times B be the cartesian product of A and B. Let \pr_1: A \times B \to A be the first projection of A \times B. Let a \in A. Then: :\pr_1^{-1} \sqbrk {\set a} = \set {\tuple {a, b}: b \in B} that is: :\pr_1^{-1} \sqbrk {\set a} = \set a \times B
Divisors of Factorial: Let n \in \N_{>0}. Then all natural numbers less than or equal to n are divisors of n!: :\forall k \in \left\{{1, 2, \ldots, n}\right\}: n! \equiv 0 \pmod k

Positive Difference Relation on Reals is Transitive: Let P \subseteq \R be a subset of the real numbers such that: :(1): \quad 1 \in P :(2): \quad a, b \in P \implies a + b \in P :(3): \quad For all x \in \R, exactly one of these is true: :::x \in P :::x = 0 :::-x \in P Let Q \subseteq \R \times \R be the relation on \R defined as: :Q = \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \R: a - b \in P} Then Q is a transitive relation.

Repeated Composition of Injection is Injection: Let S be a set. Let f: S \to S be an injection. Let the sequence of mappings: :f^0, f^1, f^2, \ldots, f^n, \ldots be defined as: :\forall n \in \N: \map {f^n} x = \begin {cases} x & : n = 0 \\ \map f x & : n = 1 \\ \map f {\map {f^{n - 1} } x} & : n > 1 \end{cases} Then for all n \in \N, f^n is an injection.

Composition of Repeated Compositions of Injections: Let S be a set. Let f: S \to S be an injection. Let the sequence of mappings: :f^0, f^1, f^2, \ldots, f^n, \ldots be defined as: :\forall n \in \N: f^n \left({x}\right) = \begin{cases} x & : n = 0 \\ f \left({x}\right) & : n = 1 \\ f \left({f^{n-1} \left({x}\right)}\right) & : n > 1 \end{cases} Then: :\forall m, n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: f^n \circ f^m = f^{m + n} where f^n \circ f^m denotes composition of mappings.

Derivative Function on Set of Functions induces Equivalence Relation: Let X be the set of real functions f: \R \to \R which possess continuous derivatives. Let \mathcal R \subseteq X \times X be the relation on X defined as: :\mathcal R = \set {\tuple {f, g} \in X \times X: D f = D g} where D f denotes the first derivative of f. Then \mathcal R is an equivalence relation.

Factorial Divides Product of Successive Numbers: Let m, n \in \N_{\ge 1} be natural numbers Let m^{\overline n} be m to the power of n rising. Then: :m^{\overline n} \equiv 0 \bmod n! That is, the factorial of n divides the product of n successive numbers.
Binomial Coefficient is Integer: Let \dbinom n k be a binomial coefficient. Then \dbinom n k is an integer.

Set of Mappings which map to Same Element induces Equivalence Relation: Let X and Y be sets. Let E be the set of all mappings from X to Y. Let b \in X. Let \mathcal R \subseteq E \times E be the relation on E defined as: :\mathcal R := \set {\tuple {f, g} \in \mathcal R: \map f b = \map g b} Then \mathcal R is an equivalence relation.

Renaming Mapping from Set of Mappings on Single Element: Let X and Y be sets. Let E be the set of all mappings from X to Y. Let b \in X. Let \mathcal R \subseteq E \times E be the relation on E defined as: :\mathcal R := \set {\tuple {f, g} \in \mathcal R: \map f b = \map g b} Let e_b: E / \mathcal R \to Y be the renaming mapping induced by \mathcal R. Then e_b is a bijection.
Equivalence of Definitions of Inverse Mapping: Let S and T be sets. {{TFAE|def = Inverse Mapping
Inverse Mapping is Bijection: Let S and T be sets. Let f: S \to T and g: T \to S be inverse mappings of each other. Then f and g are bijections.

Mapping is Injection and Surjection iff Inverse is Mapping/Proof 2: Let S and T be sets. Let f: S \to T be a mapping. Then: : f: S \to T can be defined as a bijection in the sense that: ::(1): \quad f is an injection ::(2): \quad f is a surjection. {{iff: :the inverse f^{-1} of f is such that: ::for each y \in T, the preimage \map {f^{-1} } y has exactly one element. :That is, such that f^{-1} \subseteq T \times S is itself a mapping.

Mapping is Extension iff Composite with Inclusion: Let S and T be sets. Let A \subseteq S. Let f: S \to T and g: A \to T be mappings. Then f is an extension of g {{iff: :f = g \circ i_A where i_A is the inclusion mapping on A. This can be illustrated using a commutative diagram as follows: ::\begin {xy} \xymatrix@L + 2mu@ + 1em { A \ar[r]^*{i_A} \ar@{-->}[rd]_*{f = g \circ i_A} & S \ar[d]^*{g} \\ & T } \end {xy}

Cardinality of Set of Restrictions of Mapping: Let S and T be sets. Let f: S \to T be a mapping. Let the cardinality of S be n. Let F be the set of restrictions of f to a subset of S. Then there are 2^n elements of F.

Projection is Surjection/Family of Sets: Let \family {S_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of sets. Let \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha be the Cartesian product of \family {S_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of S_\alpha be non-empty. For each \beta \in I, let \pr_\beta: \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha \to S_\beta be the \betath projection on S = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} S_\alpha. Then \pr_\beta is a surjection.
Taxicab Metric on Real Vector Space is Metric: The taxicab metric on the real vector space \R^n is a metric.

Chebyshev Distance on Real Vector Space is Metric: The Chebyshev distance on \R^n: : \forall x, y \in \R^n: d_\infty \left({x, y}\right):= \max_{i \mathop = 1}^n {\left\vert{x_i - y_i}\right\vert} is a metric.

Positive Multiple of Metric is Metric: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let k \in \R_{>0} be a (strictly) positive real number. Let d_k: A \times A \to \R be the function defined as: :\forall \left({x, y}\right) \in A: d_k \left({x, y}\right) = k \cdot d \left({x, y}\right) Then M_k = \left({A, d_k}\right) is a metric space.

Set of Successive Numbers contains Unique Multiple: Let m \in \Z_{\ge 1}. Then \set {m, m + 1, \ldots, m + n - 1} contains a unique integer that is a multiple of n. That is, in any set containing n successive integers, n divides exactly one of those integers.

Taxicab Metric is Topologically Equivalent to Chebyshev Distance on Real Vector Space: For n \in \N, let \R^n be a real vector space. Let d_1 be the taxicab metric on \R^n. Let d_\infty be the Chebyshev distance on \R^n. Then :\forall x, y \in \R^n: d_\infty \left({x, y}\right) \le d_1 \left({x, y}\right) \le n \cdot d_\infty \left({x, y}\right) It follows that d_1 and d_\infty are Lipschitz equivalent.

L1 Metric on Closed Real Interval is Metric: Let S be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]. Let d: S \times S \to \R be the L^1 metric on \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]: : \forall f, g \in S: d \left({f, g}\right) := \int_a^b \left\vert{f \left({t}\right) - g \left({t}\right)}\right\vert \ \mathrm d t Then d is a metric.

Euclidean Metric is Metric: Let M_{1'} = \left({A_{1'}, d_{1'\right), M_{2'} = \left({A_{2'}, d_{2'\right), \ldots, M_{n'} = \left({A_{n'}, d_{n'\right) be metric spaces. Let \mathcal A = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'} be the cartesian product of A_{1'}, A_{2'}, \ldots, A_{n'}. The Euclidean metric on \mathcal A is a metric.
Euclidean Space is Normed Space: The Euclidean norm is a norm on the Euclidean space \R^n.

Number of Multiples less than Given Number: Let m, n \in \N_{\ge 1}. The number of multiples of m not greater than n is given by: :q = \floor {\dfrac n m} where \floor {\cdot} denotes the floor function

Restriction of Non-Continuous Mapping on Metric Space to Subspace may be Continuous: Let M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right) and M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right) be a metric spaces. Let f: A_1 \to A_2 be a mapping. Let Y \subseteq A_1. Let f {\restriction_Y}: Y \to A_2 be the restriction of f to Y. Let f {\restriction_Y} be \left({d_Y, d_2}\right)-continuous. Then it is not necessarily the case that f is also \left({d_1, d_2}\right)-continuous.

Supremum Metric on Bounded Real Functions on Closed Interval is Metric: Let \closedint a b \subseteq \R be a closed real interval. Let A be the set of all bounded real functions f: \closedint a b \to \R. Let d: A \times A \to \R be the supremum metric on A. Then d is a metric.

Supremum Metric on Continuous Real Functions is Subspace of Bounded: Let \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R be a closed real interval. Let \mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] be the set of all continuous functions f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R. Let \mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right) be the set of all bounded real functions f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R. Let d be the supremum metric on \mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right). Then \left({\mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], d_{\mathscr C} }\right) is a subspace of \left({\mathscr B \left({\left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right], \R}\right), d}\right).

Zero Definite Integral of Nowhere Negative Function implies Zero Function: Let \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R be a closed real interval. Let h: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R be a continuous real function such that: :\forall x \in \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]: h \left({x}\right) \ge 0 Let: : \int_a^b h \left({x}\right) \rd x = 0 Then: :\forall x \in \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]: h \left({x}\right) = 0

L2 Metric on Closed Real Interval is Metric: Let S be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval \closedint a b. Let d: S \times S \to \R be the L^2 metric on \closedint a b: : \forall f, g \in S: \map {d_2} {f, g} := \paren {\int_a^b \paren {\map f t - \map g t}^2 \rd t}^{\frac 1 2} Then d_2 is a metric.

Element in Bounded Metric Space has Bound: Let M = \left({X, d}\right) be a metric space. Let M' = \left({Y, d_Y}\right) be a subspace of M. Let M' be bounded in M. Then: :\forall a' \in X: \exists K' \in \R: \forall x \in Y: d \left({x, a}\right) \le K' That is, if there is one element of X which satisfies the condition for Y to be bounded in M, they all do.

Convergence of Square of Linear Combination of Sequences whose Squares Converge: Let \sequence {x_i} and \sequence {y_i} be real sequences such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 and \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} y_i^2 are convergent. Let \lambda, \mu \in \R be real numbers. Then \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i}^2 is convergent.

Hilbert Sequence Space is Metric Space: Let A be the set of all real sequences \left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \left({A, d_2}\right) be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is a metric space.

Supremum Metric on Bounded Real-Valued Functions is Metric: Let X be a set. Let A be the set of all bounded real-valued functions f: X \to \R. Let d: A \times A \to \R be the supremum metric on A. Then d is a metric.
Supremum Metric on Bounded Real Sequences is Metric: Let A be the set of all bounded real sequences. Let d: A \times A \to \R be the supremum metric on A. Then d is a metric.

Supremum Metric is Metric: Let S be a set. Let M = \left({A', d'}\right) be a metric space. Let A be the set of all bounded mappings f: S \to M. Let d: A \times A \to \R be the supremum metric on A. Then d is a metric.

Supremum Metric on Bounded Continuous Mappings is Metric: Let M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right) and M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right) be metric spaces. Let A be the set of all continuous mappings f: M_1 \to M_2 which are also bounded. Let d: A \times A \to \R be the supremum metric on A. Then d is a metric.
Harmonic Number is not Integer: Let H_n be the nth harmonic number. Then H_n is not an integer for n \ge 2. That is, the only harmonic numbers that are integers are H_0 and H_1.

Supremum Metric on Differentiability Class is Metric: Let \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R be a closed real interval. Let r \in \N be a natural number. Supremum Metric on Continuous Real Functions is Metric: Let \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \subseteq \R be a closed real interval. Let \mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] be the set of all continuous functions f: \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right] \to \R. Let d be the supremum metric on \mathscr C \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]. Then d is a metric.

Subspace of Metric Space is Metric Space: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let H \subseteq A. Let d_H: H \times H \to \R be the restriction d \restriction_{H \times H} of d to H. Let \left({H, d_H}\right) be a metric subspace of \left({A, d}\right). Then d_H is a metric on H.

Lp Metric on Closed Real Interval is Metric: Let S be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]. Let p \in \R_{\ge 1}. Let d_p: S \times S \to \R be the L^p metric on \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]: : \forall f, g \in S: d \left({f, g}\right) := \left({\int_a^b \left\vert{f \left({t}\right) - g \left({t}\right)}\right\vert^p \ \mathrm d t}\right)^{\frac 1 p} Then d_p is a metric.

P-Sequence Space of Real Sequences is Metric Space: Let A be the set of all real sequences \left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let d_p be the p-sequence metric on \R. Then \ell^p := \left({A, d_p}\right) is a metric space.

P-adic Metric is Metric: Let p \in \N be a prime. Let \norm{\,\cdot\,}_p: \Q \to \R_{\ge 0} be the p-adic norm on \Q. Let d_p be the p-adic metric on \Q: :\forall x, y \in \Q: \map {d_p} {x, y} = \norm{x - y}_p Then d_p is a metric.

Constant Function is Continuous/Real Function: Let f_c: \R \to \R be the constant mapping: :\exists c \in \R: \forall a \in \R: \map {f_c} a = c Then f_c is continuous on \R.

Identity Mapping is Continuous/Metric Space: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. The identity mapping I_A: A \to A defined as: :\forall x \in A: I_A \left({x}\right) = x is a continuous mapping.

Identity Mapping on Real Vector Space from Chebyshev to Euclidean Metric is Continuous: Let \R^n be an n-dimensional real vector space. Let d_2 be the Euclidean metric on \R^n. Let d_\infty be the Chebyshev distance on \R^n. Let I: \R^n \to \R^n be the identity mapping from \R^n to itself. Identity Mapping on Real Vector Space from Euclidean to Chebyshev Distance is Continuous: Let \R^n be an n-dimensional real vector space. Let d_2 be the Euclidean metric on \R^n. Let d_\infty be the Chebyshev distance on \R^n. Let I: \R^n \to \R^n be the identity mapping from \R^n to itself. Then the mapping: :I: \left({\R^n, d_2}\right) \to \left({\R^n, d_\infty}\right) is \left({d_2, d_\infty}\right)-continuous.

Composite of Continuous Mappings at Point between Metric Spaces is Continuous at Point: Let M_1 = \left({X_1, d_1}\right), M_2 = \left({X_2, d_2}\right), M_3 = \left({X_3, d_3}\right) be metric spaces. Let f: M_1 \to M_2 be continuous at a \in X_1. Let g: M_2 \to M_3 be continuous at f \left({a}\right) \in X_2. Then their composite g \circ f: M_1 \to M_3 is continuous at a \in X_1.

Composite of Continuous Mappings between Metric Spaces is Continuous: Let M_1 = \left({X_1, d_1}\right), M_2 = \left({X_2, d_2}\right), M_3 = \left({X_3, d_3}\right) be metric spaces. Let f: M_1 \to M_2 and g: M_2 \to M_3 be continuous mappings. Then their composite g \circ f: M_1 \to M_3 is continuous.

Metric Space Completeness is not Preserved by Homeomorphism: Let M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1} and M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2} be metric spaces. Let \phi: M_1 \to M_2 be a homeomorphism. If M_1 is complete then it is not necessarily the case that so is M_2.

Let I: X \to \R be the real-valued function defined as: : \forall f \in X: I \left({f}\right) := \int_a^b f \left({t}\right) \ \mathop d t Then the mapping: :I : \left({X, d_1}\right) \to \left({\R, d}\right) is continuous.

Addition of Coordinates on Cartesian Plane under Chebyshev Distance is Continuous Function: Let \R^2 be the real number plane. Let d_\infty be the Chebyshev distance on \R^2. Addition of Coordinates on Euclidean Plane is Continuous Function: Let \struct {\R^2, d_2} be the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let f: \R^2 \to \R be the real-valued function defined as: :\forall \tuple {x_1, x_2} \in \R^2: \map f {x_1, x_2} = x_1 + x_2 Then f is continuous.

Open Ball is Neighborhood of all Points Inside: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let a \in A. Let B_\epsilon \left({a}\right) be an open \epsilon-ball of a in M. Let x \in B_\epsilon \left({a}\right). Then B_\epsilon \left({a}\right) is a neighborhoods of x in M.

Then the following are equivalent: :(1): \quad G \subseteq X is an open set of \left({X, d}\right) :(2): \quad \forall x \in G: \forall \left\langle{x_n}\right\rangle \in X: x_n \to x: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n \ge n_0: \left\langle{x_n}\right\rangle \in G

Metric Space Continuity by Inverse of Mapping between Neighborhoods: Let M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1} and M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2} be metric spaces. Let f: A_1 \to A_2 be a mapping from A_1 to A_2. Point in Metric Space has Neighborhood: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let a \in A be a point in M. Then there exists some neighborhood of a in M.
Point in Metric Space is Element of its Neighborhood: Let N be a neighborhood of a in M. Then a \in N.
Superset of Neighborhood in Metric Space is Neighborhood: Let N be a neighborhood of a in M. Let N \subseteq N' \subseteq A. Then N' is a neighborhood of a in M.
Intersection of Neighborhoods in Metric Space is Neighborhood: Let N, N' be neighborhoods of a in M. Then N \cap N' is a neighborhood of a in M.

Neighborhood in Metric Space has Subset Neighborhood: Let N be a neighborhood of a in M. Then there exists a neighborhood N' of a such that: :(1): \quad N' \subseteq N :(2): \quad N' is a neighborhood of each of its points.
Basic Properties of Neighborhood in Metric Space: This page gathers together the basic properties of a neighborhood in a metric space.

Basis for Element of Real Number Line: Let M = \struct {\R, d} denote the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let a \in \R be a point in M. Then the set of all open intervals containing a is a basis for the neighborhood system of a.

Open Ball in Real Number Line is Open Interval: Let \struct {\R, d} denote the real number line \R with the usual (Euclidean) metric d. Let x \in \R be a point in \R. Let \map {B_\epsilon} x be the open \epsilon-ball at x. Then \map {B_\epsilon} x is the open interval \openint {x - \epsilon} {x + \epsilon}.

Open Real Interval is Open Ball: Let \R denote the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let I := \openint a b \subseteq \R be an open real interval. Then I is the open \epsilon-ball \map {B_\epsilon} \alpha of some \alpha \in \R.

Neighborhoods in Standard Discrete Metric Space: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space where d is the standard discrete metric. Let a \in A. Then \left\{ {a}\right\} is a neighborhood of a which forms a basis for the system of neighborhoods of a.

Subset of Standard Discrete Metric Space is Neighborhood of Each Point: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space where d is the standard discrete metric. Let S \subseteq A. Let a \in S. Then S is a neighborhood of a. That is, every subset of A is a neighborhood of each of its points.

Continuity of Heaviside Step Function: Let \mu_c: \R \to \R be the Heaviside step function: :\mu_c \left({x}\right) = \begin{cases} 0 & : x < c \\ 1 & : x > c \\ \text{arbitrary} & : x = c \end{cases} Then \mu_c is continuous at every point of \R except at c.

Metric Space Continuity by Neighborhood Basis: Let M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1} and M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2} be metric spaces. Let f: A_1 \to A_2 be a mapping from A_1 to A_2. Let a \in A_1 be a point in A_1. Closed Intervals form Neighborhood Basis in Real Number Line: Let \R be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let a \in \R be a point in \R. Let \BB_a be defined as: :\BB_a := \set {\closedint {a - \epsilon} {a + \epsilon}: \epsilon \in \R_{>0} } that is, the set of all closed intervals of \R with a as a midpoint. Then \BB_a is a basis for the neighborhood system of a.

Open Rational-Number Balls form Neighborhood Basis in Real Number Line: Let \R be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let a \in \R be a point in \R. Let \BB_a be defined as: :\BB_a := \set {\map {B_\epsilon} a: \epsilon \in \Q_{>0} } that is, the set of all open \epsilon-balls of a for rational \epsilon. Then the \BB_a is a basis for the neighborhood system of a.

Open Reciprocal-N Balls form Neighborhood Basis in Real Number Line: Let \R denote the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let a \in \R be a point in \R. Let \BB_a be defined as: :\BB_a := \set {\map {B_\epsilon} a: \epsilon \in \set {\dfrac 1 n: n \in \N} } that is, the set of all open \epsilon-balls of a for \epsilon which are reciprocals of integers. Then \BB_a is a basis for the neighborhood system of a.

Subset of Open Reciprocal-N Balls forms Neighborhood Basis in Real Number Line: Let \R denote the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let a \in \R be a point in \R. Let k \in \Z be some fixed integer. Let \BB_a be defined as: :\BB_a := \set {\map {B_\epsilon} a: \epsilon \in \set {\dfrac 1 n: n \in \N, n > k} } that is, the set of all open \epsilon-balls of a for \epsilon which are reciprocals of integers greater than k. Then the \BB_a is a basis for the neighborhood system of a.

Neighborhood Basis in Real Number Line is Infinite: Let \R be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let a \in \R be a point in \R. Let \BB_a be a basis for the neighborhood system of a. Then \BB_a is an infinite set.

Distinct Points in Metric Space have Disjoint Neighborhoods: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let x, y \in M: x \ne y. Then there exist neighborhoods N_x and N_y of x and y respectively such that N_x \cap N_y = \varnothing, that is, that are disjoint.
Point in Metric Space has Countable Neighborhood Basis: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let a \in A. Then there exists a basis for the neighborhood system of a which is countable.

Positive Image of Point of Continuous Real Function implies Positive Closed Interval of Domain: Let f: \R \to \R be a continuous real function. Let a \in \R such that f \left({a}\right) > 0. Then: :\exists k \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \left[{a - \delta \,.\,.\, a + \delta}\right]: f \left({x}\right) \ge k

Limit of Sequence in Metric Space in Neighborhood: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let \left\langle{a_n}\right\rangle be a sequence in A. Then \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} a_n = a iff for each neighborhood V of a: :\exists N \in \N: n > N \implies a_n \in V
Square of Real Number is Non-Negative: Let x \in \R. Then: : 0 \le x^2
Real Number between Zero and One is Greater than Square: Let x \in \R. Let 0 < x < 1. Then: : 0 < x^2 < x
Real Number Greater than One is Less than Square: Let x \in \R. Let x > 1. Then: : x^2 > x
Power of Real Number greater than One is Unbounded Above: Let x \in \R be a real number such that x > 1. Let set S = \set {x^n: n \in \N}. Then S is unbounded above.

Power of Real Number between Zero and One is Bounded: Let x \in \R be a real number. Let 0 < x < 1. Let set S = \set {x^n: n \in \N}. Then: :\inf S = 0 and: :\sup S = 1 where \inf S and \sup S are the infimum and supremum of S respectively.

Continuity of Mapping between Metric Spaces by Convergent Sequence: Let M_1 = \left({A_1, d_1}\right) and M_2 = \left({A_2, d_2}\right) be metric spaces. Let f: A_1 \to A_2 be a mapping. Then f is continuous at a \in X iff: : whenever \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = a for a sequence \left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle of points of A_1 it is true that: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} f \left({x_n}\right) = f \left({a}\right)

Limit of Image of Sequence/Real Number Line: Let f be a real function which is continuous on the interval \Bbb I. Let \left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle be a sequence of points in \Bbb I such that: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = \xi where: : (1): \quad \xi \in \Bbb I : (2): \quad \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n denotes the limit of x_n. Infimum of Subset of Real Numbers is Arbitrarily Close: Let A \subseteq \R be a subset of the real numbers. Let b be an infimum of A. Let \epsilon \in \R_{>0}. Then: :\exists x \in A: x - b < \epsilon

Existence of Sequence in Set of Real Numbers whose Limit is Infimum: Let A \subseteq \R be a non-empty subset of the real numbers. Let b be an infimum of A. Then there exists a sequence \sequence {a_n} in \R such that: :(1): \quad \forall n \in \N: a_n \in A :(2): \quad \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} a_n = b

Existence of Sequence in Subset of Metric Space whose Limit is Infimum: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a metric space. Let a \in A. Let S \subseteq A be a non-empty subset of A. Then there exists a sequence \sequence {a_n} of points of S such that: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map d {a, a_n} = \map d {a, S}
Recurrence Formula for Sum of Sequence of Fibonacci Numbers: Let g_n be the sum of the first n Fibonacci numbers. Then: :\forall n \ge 2: g_n = g_{n - 1} + g_{n - 2} + 1

Limit of Subsequence equals Limit of Sequence/Metric Space: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let \left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle be a sequence in A. Then: : \lim_{r \mathop \to \infty} x_{n_r} = l

Convergent Real Sequence is Bounded: Let \left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle be a sequence in \R. Let l \in A such that \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = l. Then \left \langle {x_n} \right \rangle is bounded.
Monotone Convergence Theorem (Real Analysis)/Decreasing Sequence: Let \sequence {x_n} be decreasing and bounded below. Then \sequence {x_n} converges to its infimum.
Monotone Convergence Theorem (Real Analysis)/Increasing Sequence: Let \sequence {x_n} be increasing and bounded above. Then \sequence {x_n} converges to its supremum.

Triangle Inequality for Distance from Element to Set: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a metric space. Let S \subseteq A be a non-empty subset of A. Let x, y \in A. Then: :\map d {x, S} \le \map d {x, y} + \map d {y, S} where \map d {x, S} is the distance from x to S.

Open Ball in Euclidean Plane is Interior of Circle: Let \R^2 be the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) metric. Let x = \tuple {x_1, x_2} \in \R^2 be a point in \R^2. Let \map {B_\epsilon} x be the open \epsilon-ball at x. Then \map {B_\epsilon} x is the interior of the circle whose center is x and whose radius is \epsilon.

Open Ball in Euclidean 3-Space is Interior of Sphere: Let \R^3 be the real Euclidean 3-space considered as a metric space under the usual metric. Let x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, x_3} \in \R^3 be a point in \R^3. Let \map {B_\epsilon} x be the open \epsilon-ball at x. Then \map {B_\epsilon} x is the interior of the sphere whose center is x and whose radius is \epsilon.

Open Ball in Real Number Plane under Chebyshev Distance: Let \R^2 be the real number plane. Let d_\infty: \R^2 \times \R^2 \to \R be the Chebyshev Distance on \R^2: : d_\infty \left({x, y}\right):= \max \left\{ {\left\vert{x_1 - y_1}\right\vert, \left\vert{x_2 - y_2}\right\vert}\right\} where x = \left({x_1, x_2}\right), y = \left({y_1, y_2}\right) \in \R^2. Then B_\epsilon \left({a}\right) is the interior of the square centered at a and whose sides are of length 2 \epsilon parallel to the coordinate axes.

Open Ball in Standard Discrete Metric Space: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a metric space. Let d be the standard discrete metric on M. Let a \in A. Let \map {B_\epsilon} {a; d} be an open \epsilon-ball of a in M. Then: :\map {B_\epsilon} {a; d} = \begin{cases} \set a & : \epsilon \le 1 \\ A & : \epsilon > 1 \end{cases}

Distance from Point to Subset is Continuous Function: Let M = \struct {X, d} be a metric space. Let A \subseteq X be a non-empty subset of X. Let f: X \to \R be the function defined as: :\forall x \in X: \map f x = \map d {x, A} where \map d {x, A} denotes the distance from x to A. Then f is continuous.

Neighbourhood of Point Contains Point of Subset iff Distance is Zero: Let M = \struct {X, d} be a metric space. Let A \subseteq X be a non-empty subset of X. Let x \in X. Then every neighborhood of x contains a point of A {{iff: :\map d {x, A} = 0 where \map d {x, A} denotes the distance from x to A.

Let d_\infty: \AA \times \AA \to \R be the Chebyshev distance on \AA: : \map {d_\infty} {x, y} = \max \set {\map {d'} {x_1, y_1}, \map {d'} {x_2, y_2} } where x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in \AA. Then the mapping: :d': \struct {A \times A, d_\infty} \to \struct {\R, d} where d is the usual metric, is continuous.
