Alternating Even-Odd Digit Palindromic Prime: Let the notation \left({abc}\right)_n be interpreted to mean n consecutive repetitions of a string of digits abc concatenated in the decimal representation of an integer. The integer: :\left({10987654321234567890}\right)_{42} 1 has the following properties: : it is a palindromic prime with 841 digits : its digits are alternately odd and even.

Smallest Titanic Palindromic Prime: The smallest titanic prime that is also palindromic is: :10^{1000} + 81 \, 918 \times 10^{498} + 1 which can be written as: :1 \underbrace {000 \ldots 000}_{497} 81918 \underbrace {000 \ldots 000}_{497} 1

Yoneda Embedding Theorem: Let C be a locally small category. Let \mathbf{Set} be the category of sets. Let [C^{\operatorname{op, \mathbf{Set}] be the contravariant functor category. Then the Yoneda embedding h_- : C \to [C^{\operatorname{op, \mathbf{Set}] is a fully faithful embedding.

Yoneda Lemma for Contravariant Functors: Let C be a locally small category. Let \mathbf{Set} be the category of sets. === Bijection === {{:Bijection in Yoneda Lemma for Contravariant Functors === Naturality === {{:Naturality of Yoneda Lemma for Contravariant Functors

Period of Reciprocal of Repunit 1031 is 1031: The decimal expansion of the reciprocal of the repunit prime R_{1031} has a period of 1031. :\dfrac 1 {R_{1031 = 0 \cdotp \underbrace{\dot 000 \ldots 000}_{1030} \dot 9 This is the only prime number to have a period of exactly 1031.

Titanic Prime whose Digits are all Prime: The integer defined as: :7532 \times \dfrac {10^{1104} - 1} {10^4 - 1} + 1 is a titanic prime all of whose digits are themselves prime. That is: :\underbrace{7532}_{275} 7533

Titanic Prime whose Digits are all 0 or 1: The integer defined as: :10^{641} \times \dfrac{10^{640} - 1} 9 + 1 is a titanic prime all of whose digits are either 0 or 1. That is: :\left({1}\right)_{640} \left({0}\right)_{640} 1 where \left({a}\right)_b means b instances of a in a string.

Titanic Prime whose Digits are all 9 except for one 1: The integer defined as: :2 \times 10^{3020} - 1 is a titanic prime all of whose digits are 9 except one, which is 1. That is: :1 \left({9}\right)_{3020} where \left({a}\right)_b means b instances of a in a string.

Titanic Prime consisting of Blocks of 111 of each Digit plus Zeroes: The integer defined as: :\left({1}\right)_{111} \left({2}\right)_{111} \left({3}\right)_{111} \left({4}\right)_{111} \left({5}\right)_{111} \left({6}\right)_{111} \left({7}\right)_{111} \left({8}\right)_{111} \left({9}\right)_{111} \left({0}\right)_{2284} 1 where \left({a}\right)_b means b instances of a in a string, is a titanic prime.

Titanic Prime whose Digits are all Odd: The integer defined as: :1358 \times 10^{3821} - 1 is a titanic prime all of whose digits are odd. That is: :1357 \paren 9_{3821} where \paren a_b means b instances of a in a string.

Pair of Titanic Twin Primes: The integers defined as: :190 \, 116 \times 3003 \times 10^{5120} \pm 1 are a pair of titanic twin primes. That is: :570 \, 918 \, 347 \paren 9_{5820} and: :570 \, 918 \, 348 \paren 0_{5819} 1 where \paren a_b means b instances of a in a string.

Gigantic Palindromic Prime: The integer defined as: :10^{11 \, 810} + 1 \, 465 \, 641 \times 10^{5902} + 1 is a gigantic prime which is also palindromic. That is: :1(0)_{5901}1465641(0)_{5901}1 where \left({a}\right)_b means b instances of a in a string.

Indexed Iterated Operation does not Change under Permutation: Let G be a commutative semigroup. Let a, b \in\Z be integers. Let \closedint a b be the integer interval between a and b. Let f: \closedint a b \to G be a mapping. Let \sigma: \closedint a b \to \closedint a b be a permutation.

Summation over Cartesian Product as Double Summation: Let \mathbb A be one of the standard number systems \N, \Z, \Q, \R, \C. Let S, T be finite sets. Let S \times T be their cartesian product. Then we have an equality of summations over finite sets: : \sum_{s \mathop \in S} \sum_{t \mathop \in T} \map f {s, t} = \sum_{\paren {s, t} \mathop \in S \times T} \map f {s, t}
Zeroth Hyperoperation is Successor Function: The zeroth hyperoperation is the successor function: :H_0 \left({x, y}\right) = y + 1
First Hyperoperation is Addition Operation: The 1st hyperoperation is the addition operation restricted to the positive integers: :\forall x, y \in \Z_{\ge 0}: H_1 \left({x, y}\right) = x + y

Second Hyperoperation is Multiplication Operation: The 2nd hyperoperation is the multiplication operation restricted to the positive integers: :\forall x, y \in \Z_{\ge 0}: H_2 \left({x, y}\right) = x \times y
Third Hyperoperation is Integer Power Operation: The 3rd hyperoperation is the integer power operation restricted to the positive integers: :\forall x, y \in \Z_{\ge 0}: H_3 \left({x, y}\right) = x^y

Fourth Hyperoperation is Tetration Operation: The 4th hyperoperation is the tetration operation restricted to the positive integers: :\forall x, y \in \Z_{\ge 0}: H_4 \left({x, y}\right) = x \uparrow \uparrow y where \uparrow \uparrow denotes tetration: :x \uparrow \uparrow n := \begin{cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ x \uparrow \left({x \uparrow \uparrow \left({n - 1}\right)}\right) & : n > 0 \\ \end{cases} In this context, x \uparrow y is the Knuth notation for powers: :x \uparrow y := x^y

Largest Integer Expressible by 3 Digits: The largest integer that can be represented using no more than 3 digits, with no additional symbols, is: :9^{9^9} = 9^{387 \, 420 \, 489} and (at 369 \, 693 \, 100 digits, is too large to be calculated on a conventional calculator. Note that this does not include the notation for tetration: {}^9 9.
Largest Integer Expressible by 3 Digits/Logarithm Base 10: \map {\log_{10} } {9^{9^9} } \approx 369 \, 693 \,099 \cdotp 63157 \, 03685 \, 87876 \, 1
Largest Integer Expressible by 3 Digits/Number of Digits: 9^{9^9} has 369 \, 693 \, 100 digits when expressed in decimal notation.

Number of Primes up to n Approximates to Eulerian Logarithmic Integral: The prime-counting function approximates to the Eulerian logarithmic integral: :\map \pi n \approx \int_2^n \frac {\d x} {\ln x}

Sign of Difference between Prime-Counting Function and Eulerian Logarithmic Integral Changes Infinitely Often: The sign of \map \pi n - \int_2^n \frac {\d x} {\ln x} changes infinitely often as n increases indefinitely.

Point at which Prime-Counting Function becomes less than Eulerian Logarithmic Integral/Using Riemann Hypothesis: Suppose the Riemann Hypothesis holds. Then: :\exists n < 10 \uparrow \paren {10 \uparrow \paren {10 \uparrow 34} }: \map \pi n - \int_2^n \frac {\d x} {\ln x} < 0

Point at which Prime-Counting Function becomes less than Eulerian Logarithmic Integral/Not using Riemann Hypothesis: Suppose the Riemann Hypothesis does not hold. Then: :\exists n < 10 \uparrow \left({10 \uparrow \left({10 \uparrow 964}\right)}\right): \pi \left({n}\right) - \int_2^n \frac {\mathrm d x} {\ln x} < 0
Point at which Prime-Counting Function becomes less than Eulerian Logarithmic Integral: Let \map \pi n denote the prime-counting function. Let a \uparrow b be interpreted as Knuth notation for a^b.
Compact Subset of Compact Space is not necessarily Closed: A compact subset of a compact space not necessarily closed.
Separability is not Weakly Hereditary: The property of separability is not weakly hereditary.

Filter is Finer iff Sets of Basis are Subsets: Let S be a set. Let \powerset S denote the power set of S. Let \FF, \FF' \subset \powerset S be two filters on S. Let \FF have a basis \BB. Let \FF' have a basis \BB'. \FF is finer than \FF' {{iff for every set of \BB', there is a set of \BB subset to it.
Existence of Topological Space which satisfies no Separation Axioms: There exists at least one example of a topological space for which none of the Tychonoff separation axioms are satisfied.

Existence of Topological Space which satisfies no Separation Axioms but T0: There exists at least one example of a topological space for which none of the Tychonoff separation axioms are satisfied except for the T_0 (Kolmogorov) axiom.

Existence of Topological Space which satisfies no Separation Axioms but T0 and T1: There exists at least one example of a topological space for which none of the Tychonoff separation axioms are satisfied except for the T_0 (Kolmogorov) axiom and T_1 (Fréchet) axiom.
Equivalence of Definitions of Unital Associative Commutative Algebra: Let A be a commutative ring with unity.

Existence of Hausdorff Space which is not T3, T4 or T5: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a T_2 (Hausdorff) space (and hence also T_0 (Kolmogorov) and T_1 (Fréchet), but is not a T_3 space, a T_4 space or a T_5 space.

Existence of Topological Space which satisfies no Separation Axioms but T3: There exists at least one example of a topological space for which none of the Tychonoff separation axioms are satisfied except for the T_3 axiom.

Existence of Topological Space which satisfies no Separation Axioms but T4: There exists at least one example of a topological space for which none of the Tychonoff separation axioms are satisfied except for the T_4 axiom.
Existence of Compact Hausdorff Space which is not T5: There exists at least one example of a compact T_2 (Hausdorff) space which is not a T_5 space.
Existence of Regular Space which is not Tychonoff: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a regular space, but is not also a Tychonoff space.
Existence of Tychonoff Space which is not Normal: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a Tychonoff space, but is not also a normal space.
Existence of T4 Space which is not T3 1/2: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a T_4 space, but is not also a T_{3 \frac 1 2} space.
Existence of Normal Space which is not Completely Normal: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a normal space, but is not also a completely normal space.
Existence of Completely Hausdorff Space which is not Regular: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a completely Hausdorff space, but is not also a regular space.

Existence of Hausdorff Space which is not Completely Hausdorff: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is a T_2 (Hausdorff) space, but is not also a completely Hausdorff space.

Separation Properties Not Preserved by Expansion: These separation properties are not generally preserved under expansion: :T_3 Space :Regular Space :T_4 Space :Completely Regular Space :T_5 Space :Normal Space :Completely Normal Space

Existence of Completely Normal Space whose Product Space is Not Normal: There exists at least one example of a completely normal topological space T such that the product space T \times T is not a normal topological space.

Separation Properties Preserved in Subspace/Corollary: If T has one of the following properties then T_H has the same property: :Regular Property :Tychonoff (Completely Regular) Property :Completely Normal Property That is, the above properties are all hereditary.
Existence of Completely Normal Space which is not Perfectly Normal: There exists at least one example of a completely normal topological space which is not perfectly normal.
Existence of Semiregular Topological Space which is not T3: There exists at least one example of a semiregular topological space which is not a T_3 space.
Existence of Semiregular Topological Space which is not Completely Hausdorff: There exists at least one example of a semiregular topological space which is not a completely Hausdorff space.
Existence of Semiregular Topological Space which is not Urysohn Space: There exists at least one example of a semiregular topological space which is not a Urysohn space.
Existence of Sigma-Compact Space which is not Compact: There exists at least one example of a \sigma-compact topological space which is not also a compact space.
Existence of Lindelöf Space which is not Sigma-Compact: There exists at least one example of a \sigma-compact topological space which is not also a compact space.
Existence of Compact Space which is not Sequentially Compact: There exists at least one example of a compact topological space which is not also a sequentially compact space.
Existence of Countably Compact Space which is not Sequentially Compact: There exists at least one example of a countably compact topological space which is not also a sequentially compact space.

Existence of Weakly Countably Compact Space which is not Countably Compact: There exists at least one example of a weakly countably compact topological space which is not also a countably compact space.
Existence of Pseudocompact Space which is not Countably Compact: There exists at least one example of a pseudocompact topological space which is not also a countably compact space.

Existence of Weakly Locally Compact Space which is not Strongly Locally Compact: There exists at least one example of a weakly locally compact topological space which is not also a strongly locally compact space.

Vectorization of Product of Three Matrices: Let R be a ring. Let A, B, C be matrices over R such that the matrix product ABC is defined. Then \map {\operatorname {vec} }{ABC} = \paren {C^\intercal \otimes A} \cdot \map {\operatorname {vec} } B where: :\operatorname {vec} denotes vectorization :C^\intercal is the transpose of C :\otimes denotes Kronecker product :\cdot denotes matrix product

Existence of Strongly Locally Compact Space which is not Weakly Sigma-Locally Compact: There exists at least one example of a strongly locally compact topological space which is not also a weakly \sigma-locally compact space.

Existence of Weakly Sigma-Locally Compact Space which is not Strongly Locally Compact: There exists at least one example of a weakly \sigma-locally compact topological space which is not also a strongly locally compact space.
Existence of First-Countable Space which is not Second-Countable: There exists at least one example of a first-countable topological space which is not also a second-countable space.
Existence of Lindelöf Space which is not Second-Countable: There exists at least one example of a Lindelöf space which is not also a second-countable space.
Existence of Separable Space which is not Second-Countable: There exists at least one example of a separable topological space which is not also a second-countable space.

Existence of Topological Space satisfying Countable Chain Condition which is not Separable: There exists at least one example of a topological space which satisfies the countable chain condition which is not also a separable space.
Equivalence of Definitions of Strongly Locally Compact Space: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space. {{TFAE|def = Strongly Locally Compact Space

Uniqueness of Representing Objects: Let C be a locally small category. Let \mathbf{Set} be the category of sets. Let F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set} be a covariant functor. Let (A, \eta) and (B, \xi) be representations of F. Then there exists a unique isomorphism f : A \to B such that \eta \circ h^f = \xi, where: :h^f is the precomposition natural transformation :\circ denotes vertical composition of natural transformations
Existence and Uniqueness of Reduced Form of Group Word: Let X be a set. Let w be a group word on X. Then w has a unique reduced form.

Abelianization of Free Group is Free Abelian Group: Let X be a set. Let \struct {F_X, \iota} be a free group on X. Let F_X^{\mathrm {ab} } be its abelianization. Let \pi : F_X \to F_X^{\mathrm {ab} } be the quotient group epimorphism. Then \struct {F_X^{\mathrm {ab} }, \pi \circ \iota} is a free abelian group on X.
Existence of Paracompact Space which is not Compact: There exists at least one example of a paracompact topological space which is not also a compact topological space.
Existence of Metacompact Space which is not Paracompact: There exists at least one example of a metacompact topological space which is not also a paracompact space.
Paracompact Countably Compact Space is Compact: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a countably compact space which is also paracompact. Then T is compact.

Existence of Minimal Hausdorff Space which is not Compact: Let S be a set. Let \tau be the minimal subset of the power set \powerset S such that \struct {S, \tau} is a Hausdorff space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is compact.

Existence of Maximal Compact Topological Space which is not Hausdorff: Let S be a set. Let \tau be the minimal subset of the power set \powerset S such that \struct {S, \tau} is a compact topological space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is a Hausdorff space.
Gauss's Lemma (Polynomial Theory): Gauss's lemma on polynomials may refer to any of the following statements.

Infinite Product of Sigma-Compact Spaces is not always Sigma-Compact: Let I be an indexing set with infinite cardinality. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be \sigma-compact. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also \sigma-compact.

Uncountable Product of Sequentially Compact Spaces is not always Sequentially Compact: Let I be an indexing set with uncountable cardinality. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be sequentially compact. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also sequentially compact.

Product of Countably Compact Spaces is not always Countably Compact: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be countably compact. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also countably compact.

Infinite Product of Weakly Locally Compact Spaces is not always Weakly Locally Compact: Let I be an indexing set with infinite cardinality. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be weakly locally compact-compact. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also weakly locally compact.

Product of Lindelöf Spaces is not always Lindelöf: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be a Lindelöf space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also Lindelöf space.

Uncountable Product of First-Countable Spaces is not always First-Countable: Let I be an indexing set with uncountable cardinality. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be a first-countable space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also a first-countable space.

Uncountable Product of Second-Countable Spaces is not always Second-Countable: Let I be an indexing set with uncountable cardinality. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be a second-countable space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also a second-countable space.

Uncountable Product of Separable Spaces is not always Separable: Let I be an indexing set with uncountable cardinality. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be a separable space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also a separable space.

Product of Paracompact Spaces is not always Paracompact: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be a paracompact space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also paracompact space.

Product of Metacompact Spaces is not always Metacompact: Let I be an indexing set. Let \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I} be a family of topological spaces indexed by I. Let \struct {S, \tau} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be the product space of \family {\struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} }_{\alpha \mathop \in I}. Let each of \struct {S_\alpha, \tau_\alpha} be a metacompact space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {S, \tau} is also metacompact space.

Paracompactness is not always Preserved under Open Continuous Mapping: Let T_A = \struct {X_A, \tau_A} be a topological space which is paracompact. Let T_B = \struct {X_B, \tau_B} be another topological space. Let \phi: T_A \to T_B be a mapping which is both continuous and open. Then it is not necessarily the case that T_B is also paracompact.

Correspondence Theorem for Ring Epimorphisms: Let A and B be commutative rings with unity. Let \pi : A \to B be a ring epimorphism. Let I be the set of ideals of A containing the kernel \operatorname{ker} \pi. Let J be the set of ideals of B.

Union of Closure with Closure of Complement is Whole Space: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space. Let H \subseteq S be a subset of S. Let H^- denote the closure of H in T. Let S \setminus H denote the complement of H relative to S. Then: :H^- \cup \left({S \setminus H}\right)^- = S

Equivalent Characterisations of Irrational Periodic Continued Fraction: Let x \in \R \setminus \Q be an irrational number. Let (a_n)_{n\geq 0} be its continued fraction. Let N \geq 0 be a natural number. {{TFAE :(1):\quad The sequence of partial quotients (a_n)_{n\geq 0} is periodic for n \geq N. :(2):\quad The sequence of complete quotients (x_n)_{n\geq 0} is periodic for n \geq N. :(3):\quad There exists M > N such that x_M = x_N.

Component of Point is not always Intersection of its Clopen Sets: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let x \in S. Let \map {\operatorname {Comp}_x} T denote the component of x in T. Let K_x = \bigcap_{x \mathop \in K} K clopen in T. Then it is not always the case that \map {\operatorname {Comp}_x} T = K_x

Complement of Clopen Set is Clopen: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let H \subseteq S be a clopen set of T. Let \relcomp S H denote the complement of H relative to S. Then \relcomp S H is also a clopen set of T.

Clopen Set and Complement form Separation: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let H \subseteq S be a clopen set of T. Let \relcomp S H be the complement of H relative to S. Then H and \relcomp S H form a separation of T.

Path Component is not necessarily Arc Component: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let P be a path component of T. Then it is not necessarily the case that P is also an arc component of T.
Component is not necessarily Path Component: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let C be a component of T. Then it is not necessarily the case that C is also an path component of T.
Quasicomponent is not necessarily Component: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let Q be a quasicomponent of T. Then it is not necessarily the case that C is also a component of T.

Simple Infinite Continued Fraction is Uniquely Determined by Limit: Let (a_n)_{n\geq 0} and (b_n)_{n\geq 0} be simple infinite continued fractions in \R. Let (a_n)_{n\geq 0} and (b_n)_{n\geq 0} have the same limit. Then they are equal.
Continued Fraction Expansion of Irrational Number Converges to Number Itself: Let x be an irrational number. Then the continued fraction expansion of x converges to x.

Continued Fraction Expansion of Limit of Simple Infinite Continued Fraction equals Expansion Itself: Let Let (a_n)_{n\geq 0} be a simple infinite continued fractions in \R. Then (a_n)_{n\geq 0} converges to an irrational number, whose continued fraction expansion is (a_n)_{n\geq 0}.

Correspondence between Irrational Numbers and Simple Infinite Continued Fractions: Let \R \setminus \Q be the set of irrational numbers. Let S be the set of all simple infinite continued fractions in \R. The mappings: :\R \setminus \Q \to S that sends an irrational number to its continued fraction expansion :S \to \R \setminus \Q that sends a simple infinite continued fractions to its value are inverses of each other.
Ultraconnected Space is Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is ultraconnected. Then T is connected.
Irreducible Space is not necessarily Path-Connected: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space which is irreducible. Then T is not necessarily path-connected.
Ultraconnected Space is not necessarily Arc-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is ultraconnected. Then T is not necessarily arc-connected.

Correspondence between Rational Numbers and Simple Finite Continued Fractions: Let \Q be the set of rational numbers. Let S be the set of all simple finite continued fractions in \Q, whose last partial quotient is not 1. The mappings: :\Q \to S that sends an rational number to its continued fraction expansion :S \to \Q that sends a simple finite continued fractions to its value are inverses of each other.

Existence of Non-Locally Connected Space where Components and Quasicomponents are Equal: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is not locally connected, but whose components and quasicomponents are equal.
Finite Irreducible Space is Path-Connected: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a finite irreducible topological space. Then T is path-connected.

Locally Connected Space is not necessarily Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is locally connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also a connected space.

Connected Space is not necessarily Locally Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also a locally connected space.
Irreducible Space with Finitely Many Open Sets is Path-Connected: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a irreducible topological space. Let its topology \tau be finite. Then T is path-connected.
Topological Space with Generic Point is Path-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let T have a generic point g \in S. Then T is path-connected.

Floor of Simple Finite Continued Fraction: Let \sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \ge 0} be a simple finite continued fraction of length n \ge 0. Let x = [a_0, \ldots, a_n] be its value. Then the floor of x is the partial denominator a_0: :\floor x = a_0 unless n = 1 and a_1 = 1, in which case x = \floor x = a_0 + 1.

Value of Finite Continued Fraction of Strictly Positive Real Numbers is Strictly Positive: Let (a_0, \ldots, a_n) be a finite continued fraction in \R of length n \geq 0. Let all partial quotients a_k>0 be strictly positive. Let x = [a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n] be its value. Then x>0.

Value of Finite Continued Fraction of Real Numbers is at Least First Term: Let (a_0, \ldots, a_n) be a finite continued fraction in \R of length n \geq 0. Let the partial quotients a_k>0 be strictly positive for k>0. Let x = [a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n] be its value. Then x \geq a_0, and x>a_0 if the length n\geq 1.

Finite Simple Continued Fraction has Rational Value: Let n \ge 0 be a natural number. Let \paren {a_0, \ldots, a_n} be a simple finite continued fraction of length n. Then its value \sqbrk {a_0, \ldots, a_n} is a rational number.

Accuracy of Convergents of Convergent Simple Infinite Continued Fraction: Let C = (a_0, a_1, \ldots) be an infinite simple continued fraction in \R. Let C converge to x \in \R. For n\geq0, let C_n = p_n/q_n be the nth convergent of C, where p_n and q_n are the nth numerator and denominator. Then for all n\geq 0: :\left\vert x - \dfrac {p_n}{q_n}\right\vert < \dfrac 1{q_nq_{n+1.

Equivalence of Definitions of Convergent of Continued Fraction: Let F be a field, such as the field of real numbers. Let n \in \N \cup \set \infty be an extended natural number. Let C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \dotsc} be a continued fraction in F of length n. Let k \le n be a natural number. {{TFAE|def = Convergent of Continued Fraction

Locally Path-Connected Space is not necessarily Locally Arc-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is locally path-connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also a locally arc-connected space.

Locally Connected Space is not necessarily Locally Path-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is locally connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also an locally patj-connected space.

Path-Connected Space is not necessarily Locally Path-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is path-connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also locally path-connected.

Lower Bounds for Denominators of Simple Continued Fraction: Let n \in \N \cup \{\infty\} be an extended natural number. Let \left[{a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}\right] be a simple continued fraction in \R of length N. Let q_0, q_1, q_2, \ldots be its denominators.

Equality of Rational Numbers: Let a, b, c, d be integers, with b and d nonzero. {{TFAE :(1): \quad The rational numbers \dfrac a b and \dfrac c d are equal. :(2): \quad The integers a d and b c are equal.

Locally Path-Connected Space is not necessarily Path-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is locally path-connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also path-connected.

Arc-Connected Space is not necessarily Locally Arc-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is arc-connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also locally arc-connected.

Locally Arc-Connected Space is not necessarily Arc-Connected: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is locally arc-connected. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is also arc-connected.
Odd Convergents of Simple Continued Fraction are Strictly Decreasing: The odd convergents satisfy C_1 > C_3 > C_5 > \cdots
Even Convergents of Simple Continued Fraction are Strictly Increasing: The even convergents satisfy C_0 < C_2 < C_4 \cdots.

Denominators of Simple Continued Fraction are Strictly Positive: Let n \in \N \cup \{\infty\} be an extended natural number. Let (a_0, a_1, \ldots) be a simple continued fraction in \R of length n. Let q_0, q_1, q_2, \ldots be its denominators. Then for 0 \leq k \leq n we have q_k > 0.

Simple Finite Continued Fraction is Almost Determined by Value: Let n,m \geq 0 be natural number. Let (a_k)_{0 \leq k \leq m} and (b_k)_{0 \leq k \leq n} be simple finite continued fractions in \R. Let (a_k)_{0 \leq k \leq m} and (b_k)_{0 \leq k \leq n} have the same value. Then either: *n = m, and the sequences are equal. *n = m + 1, a_k = b_k for k \leq m, a_m = b_m-1 and b_{m+1} = 1 *m = n + 1, a_k = b_k for k \leq n, b_n = a_n-1 and a_{n+1} = 1
Subgroup Generated by One Element is Set of Powers: Let G be a group. Let a \in G. Then the subgroup generated by a is the set of powers: :\gen a = \set {a^n : n \in \Z}

Finite Product Space is Connected iff Factors are Connected: Let T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}, T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}, \dotsc, T_n = \struct {S_n, \tau_n} be topological spaces. Let T = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n T_i be the product space of T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n. Then T is connected {{iff each of T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n are connected.

Equivalence of Definitions of Limit of Vector-Valued Function: Let D \subseteq \mathbb R be a subset and f: D \to \mathbb R^n, f(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_n(x)) a vector valued function. Let x_0 \in \mathbb R be a limit point of D and L = (L_1,\ldots,L_n) \in \mathbb R^n. Then \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = L if and only if \lim_{x \to x_0} f_j(x) = L_j In particular the limit of f exists if and only if the limit of each component exists.

Continuous Mapping from Compact Space to Hausdorff Space Preserves Local Connectedness: Let T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1} be a compact topological space. Let T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2} be a T_2 (Hausdorff) space. Let f: T_1 \to T_2 be a continuous mapping. Let T_1 be locally connected. Then T_2 is also locally connected.
Minimum Degree Bound for Simple Planar Graph: Let G be a simple connected planar graph. Then: :\map \delta G \le 5 where \map \delta G denotes the minimum degree of vertices of G.
Linear Bound Lemma: For a simple connected planar graph G_n, where n \geq 3 is a number of vertices: :m \leq 3 n − 6, where m is a number of edges.
Existence of Connected Space which is Totally Pathwise Disconnected: There exists at least one example of a topological space which is both connected and totally pathwise disconnected.
Zero Dimensional Space is not necessarily T0: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a zero dimensional topological space. Then T is not necessarily a T_0 (Kolmogorov) space.
Scattered Space is not necessarily T1: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a scattered topological space. Then T is not necessarily a T_1 (Fréchet) space.
Existence of Connected Non-T1 Scattered Space: There exists at least one example of a connected topological space which is not a T_1 (Fréchet) space, which is also a scattered space.
Sorgenfrey Line is not Second-Countable: Let T = \struct {\mathbb R, \tau} be the Sorgenfrey line. Then T is not second-countable.
Existence of Biconnected Set without Dispersion Point: There exists at least one example of a biconnected set which does not have a dispersion point.
Existence of Connected Punctiform Space: There exists at least one example of a connected topological space which is also punctiform.
Metric Space is Completely Normal: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a metric space. Then M is a completely normal space.
Metric Space is Perfectly Normal: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a metric space. Then M is a perfectly normal space.
Bounded Metric Space is not necessarily Totally Bounded: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a bounded metric space. Then it is not necessarily the case that M is totally bounded.

Total Boundedness is not Preserved under Homeomorphism: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a totally bounded metric space. Let M' = \struct {A', d'} be a metric space. Let M be homeomorphic to M'. Then it is not necessarily the case that M' is totally bounded.

Topological Completeness is not Hereditary: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is topologically complete. Let H \subseteq S be a subset of S. Let \struct {H, \tau_H} be the topological subspace of T induced by H. Then it is not necessarily the case that \struct {H, \tau_H} is also topologically complete. That is, topological completeness is not hereditary.
Completion Theorem (Metric Space)/Lemma 4: \tilde M = \struct {\tilde A, \tilde d} is unique up to isometry.

Sorgenfrey Line is First-Countable: Let \R be the set of real numbers. Let \BB = \set {\hointr a b: a, b \in \R}. Let \tau be the topology generated by \BB, that is, the Sorgenfrey line. Then \tau is first-countable.
Metrizable Space is not necessarily Second-Countable: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is metrizable. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is second-countable.
Regular Paracompact Space is not necessarily Metrizable: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space which is regular and paracompact. Then it is not necessarily the case that T is metrizable.

Uniform Space whose Topology is Metrizable is not necessarily Metrizable: Let \UU be a uniformity on a set S. Let \struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau} be the uniform space generated from \UU. Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be the uniformizable space yielded by \struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}. Let T be a metrizable space. Then it is not necessarily the case that \UU is itself a metrizable uniformity.
Open Sets in Indiscrete Topology: H is an open set of T {{iff either H = S or H = \O.
Closed Sets in Indiscrete Topology: H is a closed set of T {{iff either H = S or H = \O.
F-Sigma Sets in Indiscrete Topology: H is an F_\sigma (F-sigma) set of T {{iff either H = S or H = \O.
G-Delta Sets in Indiscrete Topology: H is a G_\delta (G-delta) set of T {{iff either H = S or H = \O.
Subset of Indiscrete Space is Sequentially Compact: H is sequentially compact in T.

Limit Points of Sequence in Indiscrete Space on Uncountable Set: Let S be an uncountable set. Let T = \struct {S, \set {\O, S} } be the indiscrete topological space on S. Let \sequence {s_n} be a sequence in T. Then every sequence in T has an uncountable number of limit points.

Partition Topology is not Completely Hausdorff: Let S be a set and let \PP be a partition on S which is not the (trivial) partition of singletons. Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be the partition space whose basis is \PP. Then T is not a T_{2 \frac 1 2} (completely Hausdorff) space.

Partition Topology is not Hausdorff: Let S be a set and let \PP be a partition on S which is not the (trivial) partition of singletons. Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be the partition space whose basis is \PP. Then T is not a T_2 (Hausdorff) space.

Partition Topology is not T1: Let S be a set and let \PP be a partition on S which is not the (trivial) partition of singletons. Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be the partition space whose basis is \PP. Then T is not a T_1 (Fréchet) space.

Particular Point Space less Particular Point is Discrete: Let T = \left({S, \tau_p}\right) be a particular point space, whose particular point is p. Let H = S \setminus \left\{ {p}\right\} where \setminus denotes set difference. Then the topological subspace T_H = \left({H, \tau_H}\right) induced on H by \tau_p is a discrete space.

Zero is Accumulation Point of Sequence in Sierpiński Space: Let T = \struct {\set {0, 1}, \tau_0} be a Sierpiński space. The sequence in T: :\sigma = \sequence {0, 1, 0, 1, \ldots} has 0 as an accumulation point.
1 is Limit Point of Sequence in Sierpiński Space: Let T = \struct {\set {0, 1}, \tau_0} be a Sierpiński space. The sequence in T: :\sigma = \sequence {0, 1, 0, 1, \ldots} has 1 as a limit point.
Infinite Particular Point Space is not Metacompact: Let T = \left({S, \tau_p}\right) be an infinite particular point space. Then T is not metacompact.
Infinite Particular Point Space is not Countably Paracompact: Let T = \left({S, \tau_p}\right) be an infinite particular point space. Then T is not countably paracompact.

Closed Extension Topology is not Hausdorff: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let T^*_p = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_p} be the closed extension space of T. Then T^*_p is not a T_2 (Hausdorf) space.
Closed Extension Topology is not T3: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let T^*_p = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_p} be the closed extension space of T. Then T^*_p is not a T_3 space.

Condition for Closed Extension Space to be T4 Space: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let T^*_p = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_p} be the closed extension space of T. Then: :T^*_p is a T_4 space {{iff T is a T_4 space vacuously and T^*_p in this case is also a T_4 space vacuously.

Condition for Closed Extension Space to be T5 Space: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. Let T^*_p = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_p} be the closed extension space of T. Then: :T^*_p is a T_5 space {{iff T is a T_5 space vacuously and T^*_p in this case is also a T_5 space vacuously.
Either-Or Topology is T4: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be the either-or space. Then T is a T_4 space.
Limit Points in Fort Space: Let T = \struct {S, \tau_p} be a Fort space. Let x \in S such that x \ne p. Then p is the only limit point of x.
Real Number Line is First-Countable: Let \struct {\R, \tau_d} be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Then \struct {\R, \tau_d} is first-countable.

Rational Numbers in Real Euclidean Plus Space are Open Set: Let \R be the set of real numbers. Let d: \R \times \R \to \R be the Euclidean plus metric: :\map d {x, y} := \size {x - y} + \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty 2^{-i} \map \inf {1, \size {\max_{j \mathop \le i} \frac 1 {\size {x - r_j} } - \max_{j \mathop \le i} \frac 1 {\size {y - r_j} } } } Let \Q be the set of rational numbers. Then \Q is an open set of \struct {\R, d}.

Alexandroff Extension is Compact: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a non-empty topological space. Let p be a new element not in S. Let S^* := S \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {S^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on S. Then T^* is a compact topological space.

Condition for Alexandroff Extension to be T1 Space: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a non-empty topological space. Let p be a new element not in S. Let S^* := S \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {S^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on S. Then T^* is a T_1 (Fréchet) space {{iff T is a T_1 (Fréchet) space.

Condition for Alexandroff Extension to be T2 Space: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a non-empty topological space. Let p be a new element not in S. Let S^* := S \cup \set p. Let T^* =\struct {S^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on S. Then T^* is a T_2 (Hausdorff) space {{iff T is a locally compact Hausdorff space.

Alexandroff Extension which is T2 Space is also T4 Space: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a non-empty topological space. Let p be a new element not in S. Let S^* := S \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {S^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on S. Let T^* be a T_2 (Hausdorff) space. Then T^* is a T_4 space.

Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is not Hausdorff: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \struct {\Q, \tau_d}. Then T^* is not a T_2 (Hausdorff) space.

Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is T1 Space: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \struct {\Q, \tau_d}. Then T^* is a T_1 (Fréchet) space.

Separation Properties of Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \struct {\Q, \tau_d}. Then T^* satisfies no Tychonoff separation axioms higher than a T_1 (Fréchet) space.

Particular Point of Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Dispersion Point: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \left({\Q, \tau_d}\right). Then p is a dispersion point of T^*.

Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Connected: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \struct {\Q, \tau_d}. Then T^* is a connected space.

Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Biconnected: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \struct {\Q, \tau_d}. Then T^* is a biconnected space.

Alexandroff Extension of Rational Number Space is Sequentially Compact: Let \struct {\Q, \tau_d} be the rational number space under the Euclidean topology \tau_d. Let p be a new element not in \Q. Let \Q^* := \Q \cup \set p. Let T^* = \struct {\Q^*, \tau^*} be the Alexandroff extension on \struct {\Q, \tau_d}. Then T^* is a sequentially compact space.

Hilbert Sequence Space is Complete Metric Space: Let A be the set of all real sequences \left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is a complete metric space.

Hilbert Sequence Space is Separable: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is a separable space.
Hilbert Sequence Space is Second-Countable: Let \ell^2 be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is a second-countable space.
Hilbert Sequence Space is Lindelöf: Let \ell^2 be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is a Lindelöf space.

Hilbert Sequence Space is not Locally Compact Hausdorff Space: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is not a locally compact Hausdorff space.

Compact Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space is Closed: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Let H be a compact subset of \ell^2 Then H is closed in \ell^2.

Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space with Non-Empty Interior is not Compact: Let A be the set of all real sequences \left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Let H be a subset of \ell^2 whose interior is non-empty. Then H is not compact in \ell^2.

Point in Hilbert Sequence Space has no Compact Neighborhood: Let A be the set of all real sequences \left\langle{x_i}\right\rangle such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then no point of \ell^2 has a compact neighborhood.

Compact Subset of Hilbert Sequence Space is Nowhere Dense: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Let H be a compact subset of \ell^2. Then H is nowhere dense in \ell^2.

Hilbert Sequence Space is not Sigma-Compact: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is not \sigma-compact.

Hilbert Sequence Space is Arc-Connected: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Then \ell^2 is arc-connected.

Hilbert Sequence Space is Homeomorphic to Countable Infinite Product of Real Number Spaces: Let A be the set of all real sequences \sequence {x_i} such that the series \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2 is convergent. Let \ell^2 = \struct {A, d_2} be the Hilbert sequence space on \R. Let \struct {\R, \tau_d} denote the real number line under the Euclidean topology. Let \R^\omega = \prod_{i \mathop \in \N} \struct {\R, \tau_d} denote the countable-dimensional real Cartesian space under the Tychonoff topology. Then \ell^2 is homeomorphic to \R^\omega.
Fréchet Space (Functional Analysis) is Metric Space: Let \struct {\R^\omega, d} be the Fréchet space on \R^\omega. Then \struct {\R^\omega, d} is a metric space.

Countable Infinite Product of Real Number Spaces is Homeomorphic to Fréchet Metric Space: Let \struct {\R, \tau_d} denote the real number line under the Euclidean topology. Let T = \struct {\R^\omega, \tau} = \prod_{i \mathop \in \N} \struct {\R, \tau_d} denote the countable-dimensional real Cartesian space under the product topology \tau. Let \struct {\R^\omega, d} be the Fréchet space on \R^\omega, where: :\map d {x, y} = \sum_{i \mathop \in \N} \dfrac {2^{-i} \size {x_i - y_i} } {1 + \size {x_i - y_i} } Then the topology induced by d is exactly the Tychonoff topology \tau.
Fréchet Space (Functional Analysis) is Complete Metric Space: Let \struct {\R^\omega, d} be the Fréchet space on \R^\omega. Then \struct {\R^\omega, d} is a complete metric space.

Separable Metric Space is Homeomorphic to Subspace of Fréchet Metric Space: Let M = \struct {A, d} be a metric space whose induced topology is separable. Then M is homeomorphic to a subspace of the Fréchet space \struct {\R^\omega, d} on the countable-dimensional real Cartesian space \R^\omega.
Hilbert Cube is Metric Space: Let M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube. Then M is a metric space.

Hilbert Cube is Homeomorphic to Countable Infinite Product of Real Number Unit Intervals: Let M_1 = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube: :M_1 = \prod_{k \mathop \in \N} \closedint 0 {\dfrac 1 k} under the same metric as that of the Hilbert sequence space: : \forall x = \sequence {x_i}, y = \sequence {y_i} \in I^\omega: \map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{k \mathop \ge 0} \paren {x_k - y_k}^2}^{\frac 1 2} Let M_2 be the metric space defined as: :M_2 = \prod_{k \mathop \in \N} \closedint 0 1 under the Tychonoff topology. Then M_1 and M_2 are homeomorphic.
Hilbert Cube is Completely Normal: Let M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube. Then M is a completely normal space.
Hilbert Cube is Separable: Let M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube. Then M is a separable space.
Hilbert Cube is Second-Countable: Let M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube. Then M is a second-countable space.
Hilbert Cube is Compact: Let M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube. Then M is a compact space.
Hilbert Cube is Arc-Connected: Let M = \struct {I^\omega, d_2} be the Hilbert cube. Then M is an arc-connected space.
Interval of Totally Ordered Set is Convex: Let \struct {S, \preccurlyeq} be a totally ordered set. Let I \subseteq S be an interval in S. Then I is convex.
Convex Set of Ordered Set is not necessarily Interval: Let \struct {S, \preccurlyeq} be an ordered set. Let C be a convex set of S. Then it is not necessarily the case that C is an interval of S.

Union of Non-Disjoint Convex Sets is Convex Set: Let \struct {S, \preccurlyeq} be an ordered set. Let \CC be a set of convex sets of S such that their intersection is non-empty: : \bigcap \CC \ne \O Then the union \bigcup \CC is also convex.

Subset of Convex Set can be Uniquely Expressed as Partition of Maximal Convex Sets: Let \struct {S, \preccurlyeq} be an ordered set. Then S can be uniquely expressed as the partition whose components are maximally convex sets.

Separated Subsets of Linearly Ordered Space under Order Topology: Let T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau} be a linearly ordered space. Let A and B be separated sets of T. Let A^* and B^* be defined as: :A^* := \bigcup \set {\closedint a b: a, b \in A, \closedint a b \cap B^- = \O} :B^* := \bigcup \set {\closedint a b: a, b \in B, \closedint a b \cap A^- = \O} where A^- and B^- denote the closure of A and B in T. Then A^* and B^* are themselves separated sets of T.

Generators of Special Linear Group of Order 2 over Integers: Let: : S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and: :T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} Then S and T are generators for the special linear group of order 2 over \Z.
Linearly Ordered Space is T5: Let T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau} be a linearly ordered space. Then T is a T_5 space.
Linearly Ordered Space is T1: Let T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau} be a linearly ordered space. Then T is a T_1 (Fréchet) space.
Linearly Ordered Space is Completely Normal: Let T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau} be a linearly ordered space. Then T is a completely normal space.
Linearly Ordered Space is Compact iff Complete: Let T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau} be a linearly ordered space. Then T is a compact space {{iff it is complete.

Every Point except Endpoint in Connected Linearly Ordered Space is Cut Point: Let T = \struct {S, \preceq, \tau} be a linearly ordered space. Let A \subseteq S be a connected space. Let p \in A be a point of A which is not an endpoint of A. Then p is a cut point of A.

Basis for Open Ordinal Topology: Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal. Let \hointr 0 \Gamma denote the open ordinal space on \Gamma. Consider the set \BB of subsets of \hointr 0 \Gamma of the form: :\openint \alpha {\beta + 1} = \hointl \alpha \beta = \set {x \in \hointr 0 \Gamma: \alpha < x < \beta + 1} for \alpha, \beta \in \hointr 0 \Gamma. {{explain|It's unclear from the source work used whether this is the basis for the Open Ordinal Topology or Closed Ordinal Topology. Then \BB forms a basis for \hointr 0 \Gamma.

Omega is Closed in Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space but not G-Delta Set: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Omega denote the closed ordinal space on \Omega. Then \set \Omega is a closed set of \closedint 0 \Omega but not a G_\delta set.

Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not First-Countable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Omega denote the closed ordinal space on \Omega. Then \closedint 0 \Omega is not a first-countable space.

Omega as Limit Point of Intervals of Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Omega denote the closed ordinal space on \Omega. Then \Omega is a limit point of the set \openint a \Omega, but not the limit point of any sequence of points in \openint a \Omega.

Uncountable Open Ordinal Space is not Separable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \hointr 0 \Omega denote the open ordinal space on \Omega. Then \hointr 0 \Omega is not a separable space.

Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not Separable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Omega denote the closed ordinal space on \Omega. Then \closedint 0 \Omega is not a separable space.

Uncountable Open Ordinal Space is First-Countable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \hointr 0 \Omega denote the open ordinal space on \Omega. Then \hointr 0 \Omega is a first-countable space.

Ordinal Space is Completely Normal: Let \Gamma denote a limit ordinal. Let \hointr 0 \Gamma denote the open ordinal space on \Gamma. Let \closedint 0 \Gamma denote the closed ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \hointr 0 \Gamma and \closedint 0 \Gamma are both completely normal.

Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not Perfectly Normal: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Omega denote the closed ordinal space on \Omega. Then \closedint 0 \Omega is not a perfectly normal space.

Uncountable Closed Ordinal Space is not Second-Countable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Omega denote the closed ordinal space on \Omega. Then \closedint 0 \Omega is not a second-countable space.

Uncountable Open Ordinal Space is not Second-Countable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \hointr 0 \Omega denote the open ordinal space on \Omega. Then \hointr 0 \Omega is not a second-countable space.

Ring Element is Unit iff Unit in Integral Extension: let A be a commutative ring with unity. Let a \in A. Let B be an integral ring extension of A. {{TFAE :(1): \quad a is a unit of A :(2): \quad a is a unit of B
Separable Elements Form Field: Let E/F be an algebraic field extension. Then the subset of separable elements of E form a intermediate field, called the relative separable closure.

Decomposition of Field Extension as Separable Extension followed by Purely Inseparable: Let E/F be an algebraic field extension. Then the relative separable closure K=F^{sep} in E is the unique intermediate field with the following properties: * K/F is separable. * E/K is purely inseparable.
Subextensions of Separable Field Extension are Separable: Let E/K/F be a tower of fields. Let E/F be separable. Then E/K and K/F are separable.

Finite Orbit under Group of Automorphisms of Field implies Separable over Fixed Field: Let E be a field. Let G \le \Aut E be a subgroup of its automorphism group. Let F = \map {\operatorname {Fix}_E} G be its fixed field. Let \alpha \in E have a finite orbit under G. Then \alpha is separable over F.

Countable Closed Ordinal Space is Second-Countable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes \Omega. Let \closedint 0 \Gamma denote the closed ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \closedint 0 \Gamma is a second-countable space.

Countable Open Ordinal Space is Second-Countable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes \Omega. Let \hointr 0 \Gamma denote the open ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \hointr 0 \Gamma is a second-countable space.

Minimal Polynomial of Element with Finite Orbit under Group of Automorphisms over Fixed Field in terms of Orbit: Let E be a field. Let G \le \Aut E be a subgroup of its automorphism group. Let F = \map {\operatorname {Fix_E} } G be its fixed field. Let \alpha \in E have a finite orbit under G. Then \alpha is algebraic over F and the product of polynomials :\map p x = \prod_{\beta \mathop \in \Lambda} \paren {x - \beta} is the minimal polynomial of \alpha over F.

Countable Closed Ordinal Space is Metrizable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes \Omega. Let \closedint 0 \Gamma denote the closed ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \closedint 0 \Gamma is a metrizable space.

Countable Open Ordinal Space is Metrizable: Let \Omega denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal which strictly precedes \Omega. Let \hointr 0 \Gamma denote the open ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \hointr 0 \Gamma is a metrizable space.
Closed Ordinal Space is Complete Order Space: Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Gamma denote the closed ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \closedint 0 \Gamma is a complete order space.
Closed Ordinal Space is Compact: Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal. Let \closedint 0 \Gamma denote the closed ordinal space on \Gamma. Then \closedint 0 \Gamma is a compact space.
Ordinal Space is Strongly Locally Compact: Let T denote an ordinal space on a limit ordinal \Gamma. Then T is a strongly locally compact space.

Open Ordinal Space is not Compact in Closed Ordinal Space: Let \Gamma be a limit ordinal. Let \hointr 0 \Gamma denote the open ordinal space on \Gamma. Consider the compact subspace \hointr 0 \Gamma. Then \hointr 0 \Gamma is not compact in \closedint 0 \Gamma.

Integral Transform is Mapping: Let \map F p be an integral transform: :\map F p = \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x Let T be the integral operator associated with \map F p. Then T is a mapping from the domain of T to its image. That is, for every \map f x there exists a unique \map F p.

Integral Operator is Linear: Let T be an integral operator. Let f and g be integrable real functions on a domain appropriate to T. Then T is a linear operator: :\forall \alpha, \beta \in \R: \map T {\alpha f + \beta g} = \alpha \map T f + \beta \map T g
Integral Operator is Linear/Corollary 1: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R: \map T {f + g} = \map T f + \map T g
Integral Operator is Linear/Corollary 2: \forall \alpha \in \R: \map T {\alpha f} = \alpha \map T f

Inverse Integral Operator is Linear if Unique: Let T be an integral operator. Let f be an integrable real function on a domain appropriate to T. Let F = \map T f and G = \map T g. Let T have a unique inverse T^{-1}. Then T^{-1} is a linear operator: :\forall p, q \in \R: \map {T^{-1} } {p F + q G} = p \map {T^{-1} } F + q \map {T^{-1} } G

Trigonometric Series is Convergent if Sum of Absolute Values of Coefficients is Convergent: Let \map S x be a trigonometric series: :\map S x = \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n x + b_n \sin n x} Let the series: : \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {\size {a_n} + \size {b_n} } be convergent. Then S is a convergent series.

Convergent Trigonometric Series is Periodic: Let \map S x be a trigonometric series: :\map S x = \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n x + b_n \sin n x} Let S be convergent. Then S is periodic: :\forall r \in \Z: \map S {x + 2 r \pi} = \map S x

Sum of Infinite Series of Product of Power and Sine: Let r \in \R such that \size r < 1. Let x \in \R such that x \ne 2 m \pi for any m \in \Z. Then: {{begin-eqn \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty r^k \sin k x r \sin x + r^2 \sin 2 x + r^3 \sin 3 x + \cdots ; r = \dfrac {r \sin x} {1 - 2 r \cos x + r^2} ; {{end-eqn

Integral over 2 pi of Sine of m x by Sine of n x: Let m, n \in \Z be integers. Let \alpha \in \R be a real number. Then: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \sin m x \sin n x \rd x = \begin{cases} 0 & : m \ne n \\ \pi & : m = n \end{cases} That is: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \sin m x \sin n x \rd x = \pi \delta_{m n} where \delta_{m n} is the Kronecker delta.

Integral over 2 pi of Cosine of m x by Cosine of n x: Let m, n \in \Z be integers. Let \alpha \in \R be a real number. Then: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \cos m x \cos n x \rd x = \begin {cases} 0 & : m \ne n \\ \pi & : m = n \end {cases} That is: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \cos m x \cos n x \rd x = \pi \delta_{m n} where \delta_{m n} is the Kronecker delta.
Integral over 2 pi of Sine of m x by Cosine of n x: Let m, n \in \Z be integers. Let \alpha \in \R be a real number. Then: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \sin m x \cos n x \rd x = 0
Integral over 2 pi of Sine of n x: Let m \in \Z be an integer. Then: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \sin m x \rd x = 0
Integral over 2 pi of Cosine of n x: Let m \in \Z be an integer. Then: : \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \cos m x \rd x = \begin {cases} 0 & : m \ne 0 \\ 2 \pi & : m = 0 \end {cases}

Coefficients of Cosine Terms in Convergent Trigonometric Series: Let \map S x be a trigonometric series which converges to \map f x on the interval \openint \alpha {\alpha + 2 \pi}: :\map f x = \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_m \cos m x + b_m \sin m x} Then: :\forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: a_n = \dfrac 1 \pi \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \map f x \cos n x \rd x

Coefficients of Sine Terms in Convergent Trigonometric Series: Let \map S x be a trigonometric series which converges to \map f x on the interval \openint \alpha {\alpha + 2 \pi}: :\map f x = \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^\infty \left({a_m \cos m x + b_m \sin m x}\right) Then: :\forall n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: b_n = \dfrac 1 \pi \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \map f x \sin n x \rd x
Sine of Angle plus Full Angle/Corollary: Let n \in \Z be an integer. Then: :\map \sin {x + 2 n \pi} = \sin x
Cosine of Angle plus Full Angle/Corollary: Let n \in \Z be an integer. Then: : \cos \left({x + 2 n \pi}\right) = \cos x

Step Function satisfies Dirichlet Conditions: Let \alpha, \beta \in \R be a real numbers such that \alpha < \beta. Let \map f x be a step function defined on the interval \openint \alpha \beta. Then f satisfies the Dirichlet conditions.

Parseval's Theorem/Formulation 2: Let f be a real function which is square-integrable over the interval \openint {-\pi} \pi. Let f be expressed by the Fourier series: :\map f x = \sum_{n \mathop = -\infty}^\infty c_n e^{i n x} where: :c_n = \frac 1 {2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \map f t e^{-i n t} \rd t Then: : \frac 1 {2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \size {\map f x}^2 \rd x = \sum_{n \mathop = -\infty}^\infty \size {c_n}^2

Parseval's Theorem/Formulation 1: Let f be a real function which is square-integrable over the interval \openint {-\pi} \pi. Let f be expressed by the Fourier series: :\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n x + b_n \sin n x} Then: : \frac 1 \pi \int_{-\pi}^\pi \size {\map {f^2} x} \rd x = \frac { {a_0}^2} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren { {a_n}^2 + {b_n}^2}

Dilogarithm of Square: \operatorname {Li_2} \left({z}\right) + \operatorname {Li_2} \left({-z}\right) = \frac 1 2 \operatorname {Li_2} \left({z^2}\right) where \operatorname {Li_2} denotes Spence's Function.

Power Series Expansion for Spence's Function: Spence's function has a power series expansion: : \operatorname {Li}_2 \left({z}\right) = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {z^n} {n^2} This converges for \left|{z}\right| \le 1. {{explain|The domain needs to be clarified. Odd Function of Zero is Zero: Let f: \R \to \R be an odd function. Let f be defined at the point x = 0. Then: :\map f 0 = 0

Fourier Cosine Coefficients for Even Function over Symmetric Range: Let \map f x be an even real function defined on the interval \openint {-\lambda} \lambda. Let the Fourier series of \map f x be expressed as: :\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda} Then for all n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: :a_n = \dfrac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x

Fourier Sine Coefficients for Even Function over Symmetric Range: Let \map f x be an even real function defined on the interval \openint {-\lambda} \lambda. Let the Fourier series of \map f x be expressed as: : \map f x \sim \frac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda} Then for all n \in \Z_{> 0}: :b_n = 0

Fourier Series for Even Function over Symmetric Range: Let \map f x be an even real function defined on the interval \openint {-\lambda} \lambda. Then the Fourier series of \map f x can be expressed as: :\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda where for all n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: :a_n = \dfrac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x

Fourier Cosine Coefficients for Odd Function over Symmetric Range: Let \map f x be an odd real function defined on the interval \openint {-\lambda} \lambda. Let the Fourier series of \map f x be expressed as: :\map f x \sim \dfrac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda} Then for all n \in \Z_{\ge 0}: :a_n = 0

Fourier Sine Coefficients for Odd Function over Symmetric Range: Let \map f x be an odd real function defined on the interval \openint {-\lambda} \lambda. Let the Fourier series of \map f x be expressed as: : \map f x \sim \frac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda} Then for all n \in \Z_{> 0}: :b_n = \frac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x

Fourier Series for Odd Function over Symmetric Range: Let \map f x be an odd real function defined on the interval \openint {-\lambda} \lambda. Then the Fourier series of \map f x can be expressed as: :\map f x \sim \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda where for all n \in \Z_{> 0}: :b_n = \frac 2 \lambda \int_0^\lambda \map f x \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x
