Definition:Injection/Definition 1: A mapping f is an injection, or injective {{iff: :\forall x_1, x_2 \in \Dom f: \map f {x_1} = \map f {x_2} \implies x_1 = x_2 That is, an injection is a mapping such that the output uniquely determines its input.
Definition:Injection/Definition 2: An injection is a relation which is both one-to-one and left-total.

Definition:Injection/Definition 3: Let f be a mapping. Then f is an injection {{iff: :f^{-1} {\restriction_{\Img f} }: \Img f \to \Dom f is a mapping where f^{-1} {\restriction_{\Img f} } is the restriction of the inverse of f to the image set of f.

Definition:Injection/Definition 4: Let f be a mapping. f is an injection {{iff: :\forall y \in \Img f: \card {\map {f^{-1} } y} = \card {\set {f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y} } } = 1 where: :\Img f denotes the image set of f :\card {\, \cdot \,} denotes the cardinality of a set :\map {f^{-1} } y is the preimage of y :f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y} is the preimage of the subset \set y \subseteq \Img f.

Definition:Injection/Definition 5: Let f: S \to T be a mapping where S \ne \O. Then f is an injection {{iff: :\exists g: T \to S: g \circ f = I_S where g is a mapping. That is, {{iff f has a left inverse.

Then f is an injection {{iff f is left cancellable: :\forall X: \forall g_1, g_2: X \to S: f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2 \implies g_1 = g_2 where g_1 and g_2 are arbitrary mappings from an arbitrary set X to the domain S of f.

Definition:Associative Operation: Let S be a set. Let \circ : S \times S \to S be a binary operation. Then \circ is associative {{iff: :\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ y} \circ z = x \circ \paren {y \circ z}

Definition:Set/Uniqueness of Elements: A set is uniquely determined by its elements. This means that the only thing that defines what a set is is what it contains. So, how you choose to list or define the contents makes no difference to what the contents actually are.

Definition:Tally Marks: Tally marks are a system of recording (usually) small numbers. For each unit in a given natural number, a mark is made. Thus, for example, 13 could be recorded |||||||||||||. It is usual for tally marks to be arranged in groups of 5, by drawing every fifth line diagonally across the group of 4 before it. Thus 13 would then be recorded: :File:Tally5.pngFile:Tally5.pngFile:Tally3.png
Definition:Ancient Tally Bones: The ancient tally bones are archaeological relics purporting to demonstrate the earliest known indications of recorded numbers.

Definition:Wolf Bone: The (Czechoslovakian) wolf bone is a wolf bone dating from approximately 30 \ 000 years ago, bearing 57 marks which appear to have been made deliberately. It was discovered in 1937 in {{WP|Czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia at {{WP|Doln%C3%AD_V%C4%9Bstonice_(archaeology)|Dolní Věstonice in {{WP|Moravia|Moravia, by a team led by {{WP|Karel_Absolon|Karl Absolon. The markings are believed to be tally marks, and are arranged in 11 groups of 5, with 2 left over. The untestable hypothesis has been made that the number corresponds to a double lunar period.

Definition:Ordered Tuple/Definition 1: An ordered tuple (of length n) is a finite sequence whose domain is \N^*_n.

Definition:Ordered Tuple/Also known as: Some sources refer to an ordered tuple as a tuple. The term ordered n-tuple can sometimes be seen, particularly for specific instances of n. Instead of writing 2-tuple, 3-tuple and 4-tuple, the terms couple, triple and quadruple are usually used. In the context of abstract algebra, the concept is encountered as (associative) word.

Definition:Ordered Tuple/Definition 2: Let \family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in \N_n} be a family of sets indexed by \N_n. Let \prod_{i \mathop \in \N_n} S_i be the Cartesian product of \family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in \N_n}. An ordered tuple of length n of \family {S_i} is an element of \prod_{i \mathop \in \N_n} S_i.

Definition:Direct Image Mapping/Mapping: Let f \subseteq S \times T be a mapping from S to T. The direct image mapping of f is the mapping f^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T that sends a subset X \subseteq S to its image under f: :\forall X \in \powerset S: \map {f^\to} X = \begin {cases} \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \map f s = t} & : X \ne \O \\ \O & : X = \O \end {cases}

Definition:Direct Image Mapping/Relation: Let \RR \subseteq S \times T be a relation on S \times T. The direct image mapping of \RR is the mapping \RR^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T that sends a subset X \subseteq T to its image under \RR: :\forall X \in \powerset S: \map {\RR^\to} X = \begin {cases} \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR} & : X \ne \O \\ \O & : X = \O \end {cases}

Examples are: :x \mathrel \RR y :x \equiv \map y \RR :x \equiv y \pmod \RR and so on. Specialised equivalence relations generally have their own symbols, which can be defined as they are needed. Such symbols include: :\cong, \equiv, \sim, \simeq, \approx

Definition:Equivalence Relation/Definition 1: Let \RR be: :(1): \quad reflexive :(2): \quad symmetric :(3): \quad transitive Then \RR is an equivalence relation on S.

Definition:Minimal/Ordered Set/Definition 1: An element x \in T is a minimal element of T {{iff: :\forall y \in T: y \preceq x \implies x = y That is, the only element of T that x succeeds or is equal to is itself.

Definition:Minimal/Ordered Set/Definition 2: An element x \in T is a minimal element of T {{iff: :\neg \exists y \in T: y \prec x where y \prec x denotes that y \preceq x \land y \ne x. That is, {{iff x has no strict predecessor.
Definition:Maximal/Ordered Set/Definition 1: An element x \in T is a maximal element of T {{iff: :x \preceq y \implies x = y That is, the only element of S that x precedes or is equal to is itself.

Definition:Bessel Function/First Kind: A Bessel function of the first kind of order n is a Bessel function which is non-singular at the origin It is usually denoted \map {J_n} x, where x is the dependent variable of the instance of Bessel's equation to which \map {J_n} x forms a solution.

Definition:Bessel Function/Second Kind: A Bessel function of the second kind of order n is a Bessel function which is singular at the origin. It is usually denoted \map {Y_n} x, where x is the dependent variable of the instance of Bessel's equation to which \map {Y_n} x forms a solution.
Definition:Markov Chain/State Space: The set S is called the state space of the Markov chain.
Definition:Markov Chain/Homogeneous: \sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0} is homogeneous {{iff \map \Pr {X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i} does not depend on the value of n for all i, j \in S.
Definition:Tool: A tool is a physical device used as an aid to a process.
Definition:Straightedge: A straightedge is an ideal tool for constructing straight lines. A straightedge is of unlimited length, but has no markings on it, so it cannot be used for measurement.

Definition:Compass: A compass is an ideal tool for drawing circles. Hence it can be used according to Euclid's third postulate to construct a circle using any two given points: :(1): \quad the center and: :(2): \quad an arbitrary point on the circumference.

Definition:Compass and Straightedge Construction: A compass and straightedge construction is a technique of drawing geometric figures using only a straightedge and a compass. The operations available are: :using the straightedge to draw a straight line determined by two given points :using the compass to draw a circle whose center is at a given point and whose radius is the distance between two given points :finding the points of intersection between straight lines and circles.

Definition:Pólya's Urn: Pólya's urn is an implementation of an urn such that, when a ball of a particular colour is taken out and examined, that ball is replaced and another of the same colour is added. {{NamedforDef|George Pólya|cat = Pólya Category:Definitions/Probability Theory ncbllm09u1lm8ewv2p4t2zx98p91h4n
Definition:Trisection: To trisect a finite geometrical object is to cut it into 3 equal parts.
Definition:Neusis Ruler: A neusis ruler is a straightedge on which two points have been marked with a specific fixed length between them.
Definition:Neusis Construction: A neusis construction is a technique of drawing geometric figures using only a neusis ruler and a compass.
Definition:Neusis Ruler/Diastema: On a neusis ruler, the diastema is the specific fixed length between the two marked points.
Definition:Line/Curve/Plane: A plane curve is a curve which can be embedded in the plane.

Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone: 600px Let C be a double napped right circular cone whose base is B. Let \theta be half the opening angle of C. That is, let \theta be the angle between the axis of C and a generatrix of C. Let a plane D intersect C. Let \phi be the inclination of D to the axis of C. Let K be the set of points which forms the intersection of C with D. Then K is a conic section, whose nature depends on \phi.

Definition:Parabola/Focus-Directrix: 300px Let D be a straight line. Let F be a point. Let K be the locus of points P such that the distance p from P to D equals the distance q from P to F: :p = q Then K is a parabola.

Definition:Hyperbola/Focus-Directrix: 300px Let D be a straight line. Let F_1 be a point. Let \epsilon \in \R: \epsilon > 1. Let K be the locus of points P such that the distance p from P to D and the distance q from P to F_1 are related by the condition: :\epsilon \, p = q Then K is a hyperbola.
Definition:Conic Section/Directrix: The line D is known as the directrix of the conic section.
Definition:Conic Section/Focus: The point F is known as the focus of the conic section.
Definition:Conic Section/Eccentricity: The constant \epsilon is known as the eccentricity of the conic section.
Definition:Ellipse/Focus: The point F is known as the focus of the ellipse.
Definition:Ellipse/Directrix: The line D is known as the directrix of the ellipse.
Definition:Ellipse/Eccentricity: The constant \epsilon is known as the eccentricity of the ellipse.
Definition:Hyperbola/Focus: The point F_1 is known as a focus of the hyperbola. The symmetrically-positioned point F_2 is also a focus of the hyperbola.
Definition:Hyperbola/Directrix: The line D is known as the directrix of the hyperbola.
Definition:Hyperbola/Eccentricity: The constant \epsilon is known as the eccentricity of the hyperbola.
Definition:Parabola/Focus: The point F is known as the focus of the parabola.
Definition:Parabola/Directrix: The line D is known as the directrix of the parabola.
Definition:Greek Numerals: === Attic System === {{:Definition:Greek Numerals/Attic System === Classical Period === {{:Definition:Greek Numerals/Classical Period
Definition:Rational Number/Fraction/Denominator: The term b is known as the denominator of \dfrac a b.
Definition:Rational Number/Fraction/Numerator: The term a is known as the numerator of \dfrac a b.
Definition:Babylonian Clay Tablets: The Babylonian clay tablets are the written remains of the {{WP|First_Babylonian_Dynasty|Old Babylonian empire.

Definition:Mnemonic: A mnemonic is a learning technique whose purpose is to make it easier to remember a fact. It works by making an association with an easily-remembered or commonly-known fact, and translating that fact into that which needs to be learned.
Definition:Trigonometry: Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics which studies the relationships between the lengths of sides and angles of triangles.
Definition:Spherical Geometry: Spherical geometry is the branch of mathematics which concerns spatial relationships on the surface of a sphere.
Definition:Spherical Trigonometry: Spherical trigonometry is the branch of mathematics which concerns the measurement of spherical triangles and related figures on the surface of a sphere.

Definition:Prosthaphaeresis: Prosthaphaeresis is the process whereby multiplication and division are performed by: :(1): \quad converting the numbers into a form where they can be added or subtracted :(2): \quad performing the addition or subtraction :(3): \quad converting the result back again, using the inverse process to step (1).

Definition:Prosthaphaeresis/Trigonometry: The trigonometric technique of prosthaphaeresis is based on the Prosthaphaeresis Formula for Sine plus Sine: :\dfrac {\sin \alpha + \sin \beta} 2 = \map \sin {\dfrac {\alpha + \beta} 2} \, \map \cos {\dfrac {\alpha - \beta} 2}

Definition:Napierian Logarithm: The Napierian logarithms are a system of logarithms where: :\log_{\text {Nap} } 10 \, 000 \, 000 = 0 :\log_{\text {Nap} } 9 \, 999 \, 999 = 1 Thus: :\log_{\text {Nap} } 10^7 x y = \log_{\text {Nap} } x + \log_{\text{Nap} } y

Definition:Prosthaphaeresis/Logarithms: The logarithmic technique of prosthaphaeresis is based on the rule of the Sum of Logarithms: :\log_b x y = \log_b x + \log_b y Any base b can be used. The original tecnhique used Napierian logarithms where the base was 0.9999999 In due course the common (base 10) logarithm was used, as developed by {{AuthorRef|Henry Briggs, called Briggsian logarithms.

Definition:Epicycle: An epicycle is the path described by an object moving in a uniform circular motion around a point which is itself moving in a uniform circular motion around another point. :400px That point may itself also be moving in a uniform circular motion around yet another point.
Definition:Oblique Axes: Oblique axes are a pair of coordinate axes which are not at right angles to each other. :400px

Definition:Equation of Geometric Figure: Let there be a coordinate system. Let the variables \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots be used to identify points within that coordinate system. Let the variables be related to each other by means of an equation. Then the equations define the set of points which form a geometric figure. This equation is known as the equation of the geometric figure.
Definition:Folium of Descartes: === Cartesian Form === {{:Definition:Folium of Descartes/Cartesian Form === Parametric Form === {{:Definition:Folium of Descartes/Parametric Form :500px
Definition:Archimedean Spiral: The Archimedean spiral is the locus of the equation expressed in Polar coordinates as: :r = a \theta :600px
Definition:Number Theory: Number theory is the branch of mathematics which studies the properties of the natural numbers.

Definition:Algebraic Number Theory: Algebraic number theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies structures in which the usual number fields are embedded. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.

Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch): Topology is a geometry of transformations in which the only invariant is continuity. Some sources suggest that it can indeed be described simply as the study of continuity. As such, it is closely interwoven with the branch of analysis.
Definition:Plane Geometry: Plane geometry is the study of geometric figures in two dimensions.

Definition:Computer Science: Computer science is the branch of mathematics studying questions arising from the operation of [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer digital computers]. As such it can be considered as an offshoot of both mathematical logic and discrete mathematics.
Definition:Computability Theory: Computability theory is a branch of mathematical logic which concerns itself with the algorithmic implementation of mathematical proofs.
Definition:Functional Analysis: Functional analysis is a branch of analysis, which studies vector spaces endowed a structure such as inner product, norm or topology.

Definition:Analysis: Analysis is a branch of mathematics that studies continuous change. It subsumes the fields of calculus, differential equations, the calculus of variations, power series, Fourier series, real analysis and complex analysis. It is one of the main branches of mathematics, alongside geometry, number theory and algebra.
Definition:Analysis/Real: Real analysis is a branch of mathematics that studies real functions.
Definition:Analysis/Complex: Complex analysis is a branch of mathematics that studies complex functions.
Definition:Ring Theory: Ring Theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies rings and other related algebraic structures.
Definition:Analytic Number Theory: Analytic number theory is a branch of number theory which uses tools from analysis to solve problems about the integers.
Definition:Calculus/Differential: Differential calculus is a subfield of calculus which is concerned with the study of the rates at which quantities change.

Definition:Calculus/Integral: Integral calculus is a subfield of calculus which is concerned with the study of the rates at which quantities accumulate. Equivalently, given the rate of change of a quantity integral calculus provides techniques of providing the quantity itself. The equivalence of the two uses are demonstrated in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The technique is also frequently used for the purpose of calculating areas and volumes of curved geometric figures.
Definition:Calculus: Calculus is the branch of mathematics which studies change.
Definition:Mathematical Physics: Mathematical physics is the branch of mathematics concerned with the development of mathematical methods for application to problems in physics.

Definition:Physics: Physics is the branch of science which studies basic concepts including motion, energy, force, and the fundamental nature of spacetime. The study of physics is generally based in mathematical concepts, especially those of calculus.
Definition:Knot Theory: Knot theory is the branch of topology which studies the embedding of knots in 3-dimensional space.

Definition:Calculus of Variations: Calculus of variations is the subfield of analysis concerned maximizing or minimizing real functionals, which are mappings from a set of functions to the real numbers.
Definition:Matrix Algebra: Matrix algebra is the subfield of algebra whose subjects of manipulation are matrices.

Definition:Graph Theory: Graph theory is the branch of mathematics concerned with the structure and properties of graphs. As a (graph-theoretical) graph has the same conceptual definition as a relation, it follows that there is considerable overlap between the fields of graph theory and relation theory.

Definition:Relation Theory: Relation theory is the subfield of set theory concerned with the properties of relations and relational structures. As a relation has the same conceptual definition as a (graph-theoretical) graph, it follows that there is considerable overlap between the fields of relation theory and graph theory.
Definition:Mapping Theory: Mapping theory is the subfield of set theory concerned with the properties of mappings.
Definition:Measure Theory: Measure theory is the subfield of analysis concerned with the properties of measures, particularly the Lebesgue measure.
Definition:Linear Algebra: Linear algebra is the branch of algebra which studies vector spaces and linear transformations between them.
Definition:Commutative Algebra (Mathematical Branch): Commutative algebra is the branch of abstract algebra concerned with commutative and unitary rings.
Definition:Hamiltonian Mechanics: Hamiltonian mechanics was a reformulation of classical mechanics using a more abstract mathematical framework. It laid the groundwork for quantum mechanics.
Definition:Classical Mechanics: Classical mechanics is the study of the physical laws describing the motion of and forces on bodies under the action of a system of forces.
Definition:Galois Theory: Galois theory is a subfield of abstract algebra which provides a connection between field theory and group theory.
Definition:Field Theory: Field Theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies fields and other related algebraic structures.
Definition:Lattice Theory: Lattice theory is the branch of abstract algebra concerned with the structure and properties of lattices.
Definition:Geometrical Mechanics: Geometrical mechanics is the branch of mathematics which uses techniques from geometry to solve problems in mechanics.
Definition:Mechanics: Mechanics is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the motion of and forces on bodies.

Definition:Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional analysis is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the relationships between physical quantities by identifying their fundamental dimensions and units of measurement. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.
Definition:Applied Mathematics: Applied mathematics is the branch of mathematics which concerns the solution of real world applications by the construction of mathematical models.

Definition:Astronomy: Astronomy is the branch of physics which studies the features which can be seen in the sky that are outside the atmosphere of Earth. Certain of its mathematical aspects can be considered a subfield of solid geometry.

Definition:Modulo Arithmetic: Modulo arithmetic is the branch of abstract algebra which studies the residue class of integers under a modulus. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.
Definition:Homological Algebra: Homological algebra is the branch of algebra and topology which studies homology.
Definition:Umbral Calculus: Umbral calculus is a branch of analysis which studies polynomial spaces by means of linear functionals. The modern approach concerns the study of Sheffer sequences
Definition:Order Theory: Order theory is the branch of relation theory which studies orderings.
Definition:Category Theory: Category theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies categories. It can be described as the theory of functors.

Definition:Laws of Conservation: The laws of conservation are laws of physics that states that certain particular measurable properties of isolated physical systems do not change as the system evolves over time.

Definition:Multiplication/Natural Numbers/Addition: Let + denote addition. The binary operation \times is recursively defined on \N as follows: :\forall m, n \in \N: \begin{cases} m \times 0 & = 0 \\ m \times \left({n + 1}\right) & = m \times n + m \end{cases} This operation is called multiplication. Equivalently, multiplication can be defined as: :\forall m, n \in \N: m \times n := +^n m where +^n m denotes the nth power of m under +.
Definition:Ideal Theory: Ideal Theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies ideals of rings.
Definition:Algebraic Topology: Algebraic Topology is a branch of topology which uses tools from abstract algebra to study topological spaces.
Definition:Fractional Calculus: Fractional calculus is the branch of calculus which considers the concept of derivatives of fractional order.

Definition:Approximation Theory: Approximation theory is a branch of numerical analysis and applied mathematics concerned with the approximation of a function over an interval can be approximated by a simpler function (usually polynomial).
Definition:Module Theory: Module Theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies modules.
Definition:Polynomial Theory: Polynomial Theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies polynomials.
Definition:Vector Algebra: Vector Algebra is the branch of mathematics which studies the algebra of vector spaces.
Definition:Discrete Mathematics: Discrete mathematics is the branch of mathematics which studies mathematical structures that are discrete rather than continuous.
Definition:Discrete (Word): Discrete is a word used to define an object which is not continuous.
Definition:Quantum Mechanics: Quantum mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the behaviour of matter at the smallest scale accessible to observation.
Definition:Ergodic Theory: Ergodic Theory is the study of dynamical systems with an invariant measure.
Definition:Economics: Economics is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the movement of money.
Definition:Mathematical Programming: Mathematical programming is the branch of applied mathematics which applies techniques from computer science to solve problems in economics.

Definition:Game Theory: Game theory is the branch of discrete mathematics which studies mathematical models of conflict and cooperation between intelligent rational decision-makers. Problems in game theory are a special case of those of linear programming.
Definition:Numerical Analysis: Numerical analysis is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the processes by which certain kinds of numerical solutions to problems in (mainly) physics.

Definition:Perturbation Theory: Perturbation Theory is a branch of applied mathematics which studies systems by investigating their behaviour when certain parameters are changed slghtly. That is, it is the study of the effects of small disturbances.
Definition:Model Theory: Model theory is a sub-branch of mathematical logic which studies mathematical structures by means of formal languages.
Definition:Cybernetics: Cybernetics is the branch of science which studies the man-machine interface.
Definition:Fourier Analysis: Fourier analysis is a branch of analysis which seeks to express functions (usually periodic) by means of series of sines and cosines.
Definition:Operator Theory: Operator theory is the study of linear operators on function spaces, beginning with differential operators and integral operators.
Definition:Non-Euclidean Geometry: Non-Euclidean geometry is branch of geometry in which {{AuthorRef|Euclid's fifth postulate does not hold.
Definition:Ordered Geometry: Ordered geometry is a sub-branch of geometry which featured the concept of betweenness but, like projective geometry, omitting the basic notion of distance.
Definition:Hyperbolic Geometry: Hyperbolic geometry is a branch of non-Euclidean geometry in which there more than one straight line can pass through a point parallel to another straight line.

Definition:Algebraic Geometry: Algebraic geometry is the branch of geometry which studies objects in multi-dimensional space using the techniques of abstract algebra. In particular, techniques from commutative algebra are mainly used.
Definition:Brill-Noether Theory: Brill-Noether Theory is the branch of algebraic geometry which studies special divisors.
Definition:Tarski-Grothendieck Set Theory: Tarski-Grothendieck set theory is an implementation of axiomatic set theory which allows for the existence of a universe.
Definition:Kummer Theory: Kummer Theory is a branch of abstract algebra and number theory which investigates certain types of field extensions.
Definition:Tensor Theory: Tensor theory is the branch of linear algebra which studies tensors.
Definition:Vector Analysis: Vector analysis is the branch of linear algebra concerned with differentiation and integration of vector spaces, primarily in Euclidean space of 3-dimensional space.
Definition:Fluid Mechanics: Fluid mechanics is the branch of mechanics concerned with the behaviour of fluids.
Definition:Electromagnetism: Electromagnetism is the branch of physics concerned with the study of the combined phenomena of electricity and magnetism, and their interconnected nature.
Definition:Partition Theory: Partition theory is the subfield of combinatorics which studies integer partitions.
Definition:Proof Theory: Proof theory is the subfield of mathematical logic which studies proofs as mathematical objects, thus allowing them to be analysed mathematically.
Definition:Fluid Dynamics: Fluid dynamics is the branch of fluid mechanics concerned with the behaviour of fluids in motion.
Definition:Class Theory: Class theory is an extension of set theory which allows the creation of collections that are not sets by classes.
Definition:Descriptive Set Theory: Descriptive set theory is a branch of set theory which studies certain classes subsets of the real number line and other Polish spaces.
Definition:Recursion Theory: Recursion theory is a branch of computability theory which concerns itself with recursive structures.
Definition:Inner Model Theory: Inner model theory is a branch of set theory and model theory which studies certain models of ZFC.

Definition:Cantor-Bendixson Derivative: Let \struct {X, \tau} be a topological space. Let S \subseteq X. Then for all ordinals \beta, the \betath Cantor-Bendixson derivative of S is defined by Transfinite Recursion thus: :S^{\paren \beta} = \begin {cases} S & : \beta = 0 \\ \paren {S^{\paren \alpha} }' & : \beta = \alpha^+ \\ \bigcap_{\alpha \mathop < \lambda} S^{\paren \alpha} & : \beta = \lambda \end{cases} where: :\paren {S^{\paren \alpha} }' is the derived set of S^{\paren \alpha} :\lambda is a limit ordinal. {{NamedforDef|Georg Cantor|name2 = Ivar Otto Bendixson|cat = Cantor|cat2 = Bendixson
Definition:Directed Hamilton Cycle Problem/Function Version: Given a directed graph G with n vertices, to find a Hamilton cycle in G.

Definition:Directed Hamilton Cycle Problem: There are two versions of the Directed Hamilton Cycle Problem. === Function Version === {{:Definition:Directed Hamilton Cycle Problem/Function Version === Decision Version === {{:Definition:Directed Hamilton Cycle Problem/Decision Version
Definition:Finite Subset: Let S be a set. Let T be a subset of S which is a finite set. Then T is a finite subset of S. Category:Definitions/Subsets 18w2vinwyqq86kfnhdobc63kpxnfvps

Definition:Quotient Module: Let M be an R-module and M^\ast be the underlying group. Let N be a submodule of M and N^\ast be the underlying subgroup. Let a + N denote the coset of the quotient group M^\ast / N^\ast. Define the R-action on M^\ast / N^\ast as: :\forall r \in R, \forall a \in M / N: r \left({a + N^\ast}\right) := r a + N^\ast Then (M^\ast / N^\ast,\circ) is a quotient R-module.
Definition:Tensor Algebra: Tensor algebra is the branch of module theory which studies tensor products.
Definition:Module Direct Product: === Finite Case === {{:Definition:Module Direct Product/Finite Case === General Case === {{:Definition:Module Direct Product/General Case
Definition:Ramsey Theory: Ramsey theory is a branch of combinatorics that studies the conditions under which order must appear.

Definition:Angle Inscribed in Circle: 300px Let AB and BC be two chords of a circle which meet at B. The angle \angle ABC is the angle inscribed at B (with respect to A and C). Category:Definitions/Circles 62ne3b5n8dhn4vvvb4wya45hixd45f4
Definition:Path (Topology)/Endpoint: The initial point and final point of \gamma can be referred to as the endpoints of \gamma
Definition:Infinite Path: An infinite path is a path of infinite length Category:Definitions/Graph Theory 9zbjdb17ulh1ua4rmn8i5zy8hutbh33
Definition:Supremum/Also defined as: Some sources refer to the supremum as being the upper bound. Using this convention, any element greater than this is not considered to be an upper bound.

Definition:Infimum/Also known as: Particularly in the field of analysis, the infimum of a set T is often referred to as the greatest lower bound of T and denoted \map {\mathrm {glb} } T or \map {\mathrm {g.l.b.} } T. Some sources refer to the infimum of a set as the infimum on a set. Some sources introduce the notation \inf_{y \mathop \in S} y, which may improve clarity in some circumstances. Some older sources, applying the concept to a (strictly) decreasing real sequence, refer to a infimum as a lower limit.
Definition:Infimum/Also defined as: Some sources refer to the infimum as being the lower bound. Using this convention, any element less than this is not considered to be a lower bound.

Definition:Differential Equation/Solution: Let \Phi be a differential equation defined on a domain D. Let \phi be a function which satisfies \Phi on the whole of D. Then \phi is known as a solution of \Phi. Note that, in general, there may be more than one solution to a given differential equation. On the other hand, there may be none at all. === General Solution === {{:Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/General Solution === Particular Solution === {{:Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/Particular Solution
Definition:Differential Equation/Solution/General Solution: The general solution of \Phi is the set of all functions \phi that satisfy \Phi.

Definition:Linear Representation/Group: Let \left({\mathbb k, +, \circ}\right) be a field. Let V be a vector space over \mathbb k of finite dimension. Let \operatorname {GL} \left({V}\right) be the general linear group of V. Let \left({G, \cdot}\right) be a finite group. A linear representation of G on V is a group homomorphism \rho: G \to \operatorname {GL} \left({V}\right).

Definition:Linear Representation/Algebra: Let K be a field. Let A be an associative unitary algebra over K. Then a (linear) representation of A is a vector space V over K equipped with a homomorphism of algebras: :\rho: A \to \map {\operatorname {End} } V where \map {\operatorname {End} } V is the endomorphism ring of V.
Definition:Singleton Graph: The singleton graph N_1 is the simple graph with one vertex: :60px

Definition:Complete Distributive Lattice: Let \left({S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}\right) be a lattice. Then S is a complete distributive lattice {{iff :(1): \quad S is a complete lattice :(2): \quad S is a distributive lattice. Category:Definitions/Lattice Theory 19ry08xqa1fj2agz8s5bokuc36ohn0t

Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Complex Numbers: Let \sequence {z_n} be a sequence in \C. Then \sequence {z_n} is a Cauchy sequence {{iff: : \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \size {z_n - z_m} < \epsilon where \size {z_n - z_m} denotes the complex modulus of z_n - z_m.
Definition:Accumulation Point/Set: Let x \in S. Then x is an accumulation point of A {{iff: :x \in \cl {A \setminus \set x} where \operatorname{cl} denotes the (topological) closure of a set.

Definition:Set Derivative: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space. Let A \subseteq S. The derivative of A in T is the set of all accumulation points of A. It is usually denoted on {{ProofWiki as A'.

Definition:Pythagoras's Constant: Pythagoras's constant is sometimes used to mean \sqrt 2, the square root of 2. === Decimal Expansion === {{:Square Root of 2 {{NamedforDef|Pythagoras of Samos|cat = Pythagoras Category:Number Theory m3ug0rekc6r54r0n4b62jnacyopnvvr

Definition:Existential Quantifier/Exact: The symbol \exists_n denotes the existence of an exact number of objects fulfilling a particular condition. :\exists_n x: \map P x means: :There exist exactly n objects x such that \map P x holds.

Definition:Set Union/General Definition: Let S be a collection, which could be either a set or a class. The union of S is: : \bigcup S := \set {x: \exists X \in S: x \in X} That is, the set of all elements of all elements of S which are themselves sets.

Definition:Ordered Pair/Informal Definition: An ordered pair is a two-element set together with an ordering. In other words, one of the elements is distinguished above the other - it comes first. Such a structure is written: :\tuple {a, b} and it means: : first a, then b.

Definition:Ordered Pair/Kuratowski Formalization: The concept of an ordered pair can be formalized by the definition: :\tuple {a, b} := \set {\set a, \set {a, b} } This formalization justifies the existence of ordered pairs in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

Definition:Inverse Mapping/Also defined as: Let S and T be sets. Let f: S \to T be an injection. Then its inverse mapping is the mapping g such that: :its domain \Dom g equals the image \Img f of f :\forall y \in \Img f: \map f {\map g y} = y Thus f is seen to be a surjection by tacit use of Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection.

Definition:Weight of Topological Space: Let T be a topological space. Let \mathbb B be the set of all bases of T. === Definition 1 === {{:Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 1 === Definition 2 === {{:Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 2

Definition:Operation Compatible with Equivalence: Let F be a (unary) operation which can be applied to sets. Then F is compatible with set equivalence {{iff: :F \left({A}\right) = F \left({B}\right) \iff A \sim B where: :A and B are arbitrary sets :\sim denotes set equivalence.
Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 1: The weight of T is defined as: : \map w T := \bigcap_{\BB \mathop \in \mathbb B} \card \BB where \card \BB denotes the cardinality of \BB.
Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 2: The weight of T is the smallest cardinality of the elements of \mathbb B: :\map w T := \min \set {\card \BB: \BB \in \mathbb B}

Definition:Character of Point in Topological Space: Let T be a topological space. Let x be a point of T. Let \mathbb B \left({x}\right) be the set of all local bases at x. The character of (the point) x in T is the smallest cardinality of the elements of \mathbb B \left({x}\right): :\chi \left({x,T}\right) := \min \left\{ {\left\vert{\mathcal B}\right\vert: \mathcal B \in \mathbb B \left({x}\right)}\right\}

Definition:Character of Topological Space: Let T be a topological space. The character of (the topological space) T is the supremum of the set of characters of the points of T: :\chi \left({T}\right) := \sup \left\{ {\chi \left({x, T}\right): x \in T}\right\}

Definition:Bound Variable/Examples/Universal Statement: In the universal statement: :\forall x: \map P x the symbol x is a bound variable. Thus, the meaning of \forall x: \map P x does not change if x is replaced by another symbol. That is, \forall x: \map P x means the same thing as \forall y: \map P y or \forall \alpha: \map P \alpha. And so on.

Definition:Bound Variable/Examples/Existential Statement: In the existential statement: :\exists x: \map P x the symbol x is a bound variable. Thus, the meaning of \exists x: \map P x does not change if x is replaced by another symbol. That is, \exists x: \map P x means the same thing as \exists y: \map P y or \exists \alpha: \map P \alpha. And so on.

Definition:Existential Statement/Conditional: A conditionally existential statement is an existential statement which states the existence of an object fulfilling a certain propositional function dependent upon the existence of certain other objects.

Definition:Conditional/Formal Implication: Formal implication is a usage of an implication in which it is necessary for there to be a formal connection between the antecedent and the consequent in order for the implication to have any semantic meaning.

Definition:Stoic School: The stoic school was a school of Greek philosophy which emphasized the importance of goodness and peace of mind gained from living a life of Virtue in accordance with Nature. The writings of its philosophers reveal the first beginnings of the discipline of propositional logic.

Definition:Truth Table/Matrix Presentation: A two-element truth table can be presented in matrix form: :{{:Definition:Conditional/Truth Table/Matrix Form\qquad{{:Definition:Conjunction/Truth Table/Matrix Form\qquad{{:Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table/Matrix Form\qquad{{:Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table/Matrix Form that is, in the form of a Cayley table. This, however, can be used only when the operation being displayed has two elements.
Definition:Conjunction/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \land & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \F \\ \F & \F & \F \\ \end{array}
Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \lor & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \T \\ \F & \T & \F \\ \end{array}
Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \iff & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \F \\ \F & \F & \T \\ \end{array}
Definition:Conditional/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \implies & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \T & \F \\ \F & \T & \T \\ \end{array}

Definition:Fundamental Truth Table: The fundamental truth tables are the characteristic truth tables for: : Logical Not : Conjunction : Disjunction : Conditional : Biconditional as follows: === Logical Not === {{:Definition:Logical Not/Truth Table === Conjunction === {{:Definition:Conjunction/Truth Table === Disjunction === {{:Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table === Conditional === {{:Definition:Conditional/Truth Table === Biconditional === {{:Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table

Definition:Derivative Truth Table: A derivative truth table is a truth table for a statement form which is not mapped by one of the fundamental truth tables: : Logical Not : Conjunction : Disjunction : Conditional : Biconditional

Definition:Truth Table/Row: A row of a truth table is one of the horizontal lines that consists of instances of the symbols T and F. Each row contains the truth values of each of the boolean interpretations of the statement forms according to the propositional variables that comprise them. There are as many rows in a truth table as there are combinations of T and F for all the propositional variables that constitute the statement forms.

Definition:Truth Table/Column: A row of a truth table is one of the vertical lines headed by a statement form presenting all the truth values that the statement form takes. Each entry in the column corresponds to one specific combination of truth values taken by the propositional variables that the statement form comprises.

Definition:Conjugate Statements: Let p and q be statements. The conditional statement: :p \implies q its inverse: :\lnot p \implies \lnot q its converse: :q \implies p and its contrapositive: :\lnot q \implies \lnot p are all conjugate statements.

Definition:Rubik's Cube: Rubik's cube is a toy consisting of a plastic cube divided into 27 smaller cubes, interlocking at the center cube and allowing each face to rotate independently of the others. Each of the 6 faces of the main cube is colored with one of six contrasting colors. Rotating the faces of the cube causes these 6 faces to become mixed up. The object of the exercise is to restore the 6 faces to their original single colors.
Definition:Exclusive Or/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \oplus & \T & \F \\ \hline \T & \F & \T \\ \F & \T & \F \\ \end{array}

Definition:Cardinality/Finite: Let S be a finite set. The cardinality \card S of S is the number of elements in S. That is, if: :S \sim \N_{< n} where: :\sim denotes set equivalence :\N_{<n} is the set of all natural numbers less than n then we define: :\card S = n
Definition:Rubik's Cube/Basic Moves: The set of basic moves of the Rubik's cube can be denoted: :\set {U, D, L, R, F, B} where U, D, L, R, F, B are in Singmaster notation.
Definition:Rubik's Cube/Facet: Each of the 9 small squares into which the faces of Rubik's cube is subdivided is called a facet.
Definition:Symmetric Difference/Definition 5: S * T := \set {x: x \in S \oplus x \in T}
Definition:Rubik's Cube/Corner Facet: Of each of the 9 facets of each face of Rubik's cube, the 4 in the corners of the face are called the corner facets. The set of corner facets can be denoted S_C.
Definition:Rubik's Cube/Edge Facet: Of each of the 9 facets of each face of Rubik's cube, the 4 on the edges of the face are called the edge facets. The set of edge facets can be denoted S_E.

Definition:Rubik's Cube/Center Facet: Of each of the 9 facets of each face of Rubik's cube, the ones in the centers of the faces are called the center facets. The set of center facets can be denoted S_Z.
Definition:Trivial Partition/Singleton: The singleton partition on S is defined as: :\mathcal P = \left\{{S}\right\} That is, it is a partition with only one component.

Definition:Trivial Partition/Partition of Singletons: The partition of singletons on S is defined as: :\mathcal P = \set {\set x: x \in S} That is, it is a partition such that every component is a singleton.
Definition:Prime Number/Definition 5: A prime number p is an integer greater than 1 that has no (positive) divisors less than itself other than 1.

Definition:Prime-Counting Function/Examples/16: The value of the prime-counting (\pi) function for 16 is determined as follows. The prime numbers less than 16 are: :2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 Hence: :\map \pi {16} = 6
Definition:Mapping/Definition 1: A mapping from S to T is a binary relation on S \times T which associates each element of S with exactly one element of T.

Definition:Mapping/Definition 2: A mapping f from S to T, denoted f: S \to T, is a relation f = \struct {S, T, G}, where G \subseteq S \times T, such that: :\forall x \in S: \forall y_1, y_2 \in T: \tuple {x, y_1} \in G \land \tuple {x, y_2} \in G \implies y_1 = y_2 and :\forall x \in S: \exists y \in T: \tuple {x, y} \in G

Definition:Mapping/Definition 3: A mapping f from S to T, denoted f: S \to T, is a relation f = \struct {S, T, R}, where R \subseteq S \times T, such that: :\forall \tuple {x_1, y_1}, \tuple {x_2, y_2} \in f: y_1 \ne y_2 \implies x_1 \ne x_2 and :\forall x \in S: \exists y \in T: \tuple {x, y} \in f
Definition:Mapping/Definition 4: A mapping from S to T is a relation on S \times T which is: :(1): \quad Many-to-one :(2): \quad Left-total, that is, defined for all elements in S.

Definition:Countable Set/Also known as: When the terms denumerable and enumerable are encountered, they generally mean the same as countably infinite. Some modern pedagogues (for example {{AuthorRef|Vi Hart and {{AuthorRef|James Grime) use the term listable, but this has yet to catch on.
Definition:Countable Set/Countably Infinite/Cardinality: The cardinality of a countably infinite set is denoted by the symbol \aleph_0 (aleph null).
Definition:Countable Set/Countably Infinite/Definition 1: S is countably infinite {{iff there exists a bijection: :f: S \to \N where \N is the set of natural numbers.
Definition:Countable Set/Countably Infinite/Definition 2: S is countably infinite {{iff there exists a bijection: :f: S \to \Z where \Z is the set of integers.
Definition:Countable Set/Definition 3: S is countable {{iff there exists a bijection between S and a subset of \N.

Definition:Polish Notation/Formal Definition: Let \mathcal A be an alphabet. Let each s \in \mathcal A be assigned a natural number called its arity. The formal grammar for Polish notation is given by the single bottom-up rule: ::If s has arity n and \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n are well-formed formulas, then: :::s \phi_1 \cdots \phi_n ::is also a well-formed formula. Notably, in the case where s has arity 0, this is a vacuous truth, so any such s constitutes a well-formed formula.
Definition:Matrix Theory: Matrix theory is the field of mathematics which studies matrices.
Definition:Unit Matrix/Examples/3 x 3: The 3 \times 3 unit matrix is as follows: :\mathbf I_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}
Definition:Matrix/Lower Triangular Elements: Let \mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n} be a matrix. The elements a_{i j}: i > j are called the lower triangular elements.
Definition:Matrix/Upper Triangular Elements: Let \mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n} be a matrix. The elements a_{i j}: i < j are called the upper triangular elements.
Definition:Permutation Matrix: A permutation matrix (of order n) is an n \times n square matrix with: : exactly one instance of 1 in each row and column : 0 elsewhere.
Definition:Monomial Matrix: A monomial matrix (of order n) is an n \times n square matrix with: :exactly one element in each row and column which is not 0 :0 elsewhere.
Definition:(0, 1)-Matrix: A \tuple {0, 1}-matrix is a matrix whose elements consist only of instances of 0 and 1.
Definition:Determinant/Matrix/Order: The order of a determinant is defined as the order of the square matrix on which it is defined.

Definition:Minor of Determinant/Notation/Order n-1: Let a submatrix \mathbf B of \mathbf A be of order n - 1. Let: :j be the row of \mathbf A which is not included in \mathbf B :k be the column of \mathbf A which is not included in \mathbf B. Thus, let \mathbf B := \map {\mathbf A} {j; k}. Then \map \det {\mathbf B} can be denoted: :D_{i j} That is, D_{i j} is the minor of order n - 1 obtained from D by deleting all the elements of row i and column j.

Definition:Cofactor/Element: Let a_{r s} be an element of D. Let D_{r s} be the determinant of order n-1 obtained from D by deleting row r and column s. Then the cofactor A_{r s} of the element a_{r s} is defined as: :A_{r s} := \paren {-1}^{r + s} D_{r s}
Definition:Non-Invertible Matrix/Definition 1: Let \mathbf A have no inverse. Then \mathbf A is referred to as non-invertible.
Definition:Non-Invertible Matrix/Definition 2: Let the determinant of \mathbf A be equal to 0. Then \mathbf A is referred to as non-invertible.

Definition:Zero Vector/Euclidean Space: Let \struct {\R^n, +, \times}_\R be a real vector space. The zero vector in \struct {\R^n, +, \times}_\R is: :\mathbf 0_{n \times 1} := \begin {bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end {bmatrix} where 0 \in \R.

Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Integers/Remainder after Division: Congruence modulo m is defined as the relation \equiv \pmod m on the set of all a, b \in \Z: :a \equiv b \pmod m := \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m} That is, such that a and b have the same remainder when divided by m.

Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Remainder after Division: We define a relation \mathcal R_z on the set of all x, y \in \R: :\mathcal R_z := \left\{{\left({x, y}\right) \in \R \times \R: \exists k \in \Z: x = y + k z}\right\} This relation is called congruence modulo z, and the real number z is called the modulus. When \left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R_z, we write: :x \equiv y \pmod z and say: : x is congruent to y modulo z.

Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Historical Note: The concept of congruence modulo an integer was first explored by {{AuthorRef|Carl Friedrich Gauss. He originated the notation a \equiv b \pmod m in his work {{BookLink|Disquisitiones Arithmeticae|Carl Friedrich Gauss, published in 1801.
Definition:Equivalence Class/Representative: Let \eqclass x \RR be the equivalence class of x under \RR. Let y \in \eqclass x \RR. Then y is a representative of \eqclass x \RR.

Definition:Word (Natural Language): A word in natural language is intuitively understood as a sequence of sounds which expresses a concept. When written down, it appears as a sequence of letters, each one of which either is, or contributes to, a [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme phoneme].

Definition:Scope of Occurrence: Let \FF be a formal language with alphabet \AA. Let \mathbf A be a well-formed formula of \FF. Let a be a fixed occurrence of some element of \AA in \mathbf A. Then the scope of a is the smallest well-formed part of \mathbf A that contains a.

Definition:Universal Closure of Well-Formed Formula: Let \mathcal L_1 be the language of predicate logic. Let \mathbf A be a well-formed formula of \mathcal L_1. A universal closure of \mathbf A is a sentence \mathbf B of \mathcal L_1 of the form: :\forall x_1: \cdots \forall x_n: \mathbf A By definition of sentence, this means that at least the variables occurring freely in \mathbf A should be quantified over.
Definition:Logical NAND/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \uparrow & T & F \\ \hline T & F & T \\ F & T & T \\ \end{array}
Definition:Logical NOR/Truth Table/Matrix Form: \begin{array}{c|cc} \downarrow & T & F \\ \hline T & F & F \\ F & F & T \\ \end{array}
Definition:Conjunction/Truth Table/Number: The truth table number of the conjunction operator p \land q is as follows: Ascending order: :0001 or \F \F \F \T Descending order: :1000 or \T \F \F \F
Definition:Conditional/Truth Table/Number: The truth table number of the conjunction operator p \land q is as follows: Ascending order: :1101 or \T \T \F \T Descending order: :1011 or \T \F \T \T
Definition:Disjunction/Truth Table/Number: The truth table number of the conjunction operator p \lor q is as follows: Ascending order: :0111 or \F \T \T \T Descending order: :1110 or \T \T \T \F
Definition:Biconditional/Truth Table/Number: The truth table number of the biconditional operator p \iff q is as follows: Ascending and descending order: :1001 or \T \F \F \T
Definition:Exclusive Or/Truth Table/Number: The truth table number of the exclusive or operator p \oplus q is as follows: Ascending and descending order: :0110 or \F \T \T \F

Definition:Structure for Predicate Logic: Let \LL_1 be the language of predicate logic. A structure \AA for \LL_1 comprises: :(1): \quad A non-empty set A; :(2): \quad For each function symbol f of arity n, a mapping f_\AA: A^n \to A; :(3): \quad For each predicate symbol p of arity n, a mapping p_\AA: A^n \to \Bbb B where \Bbb B denotes the set of truth values. A is called the underlying set of \AA. f_\AA and p_\AA are called the interpretations of f and p in \AA, respectively.

Definition:Assignment for Structure/Formula: Let \mathbf A be a well-formed formula of \mathcal L_1. Denote with V \left({\mathbf A}\right) the variables which occur freely in \mathbf A. An assignment for \mathbf A in \mathcal A is a mapping \sigma with codomain A, whose domain is subject to the following condition: :V \left({\mathbf A}\right) \subseteq \operatorname{dom} \left({\sigma}\right) \subseteq \mathrm{VAR} That is, the domain of \sigma contains only variables, and at least those with a free occurrence in \mathbf A.

Definition:Assignment for Structure/Term: Let \tau be a term of \mathcal L_1. Denote with V \left({\tau}\right) the variables which occur in \tau. An assignment for \tau in \mathcal A is a mapping \sigma with codomain A, whose domain is subject to the following condition: :V \left({\tau}\right) \subseteq \operatorname{dom} \left({\sigma}\right) \subseteq \mathrm{VAR} That is, the domain of \sigma contains only variables, and at least those which occur in \tau.

Definition:Language of Predicate Logic/Formal Grammar/Term: The terms of \LL_1 are identified by the following bottom-up grammar: {{begin-axiom {{axiom \mathbf T \ \textrm {VAR} | t = Any variable of \LL_1 is a term; {{axiom \mathbf T \ \FF_n | t = Given an n-ary function symbol f \in \FF_n and terms \tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n: :\map f {\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_n} is also a term. {{end-axiom

Definition:Local Minimum in Set of Reals: Let X be a subset of \R, the set of all real numbers. Let x be a real number, x \in \R. x is local minimum in set X {{iff :x \in X \land \exists y \in \R: y < x \land \left({y \,.\,.\, x}\right) \cap X = \varnothing
Definition:Variable/Restricted: A restricted variable is a variable whose values are confined to some only of those of which it is capable.
Definition:Variable/Unrestricted: An unrestricted variable is a variable whose values are not confined in any way to some only of those of which it is capable.

Definition:Prime Number/Definition 6: Let p \in \N be an integer such that p \ne 0 and p \ne \pm 1. Then p is a prime number {{iff :\forall a, b \in \Z: p \divides a b \implies p \divides a or p \divides b where \divides means is a divisor of.
Definition:Twin Primes: Twin primes are pairs of prime numbers whose difference is 2.
Definition:Quadratic Residue/Non-Residue: If there is no such integer x such that x^2 \equiv a \pmod p, then a is a quadratic non-residue of p.
Definition:Quadratic Residue/Character: a is either a quadratic residue or a quadratic non-residue of p. Whether it is or not is known as the quadratic character of a modulo p.
Definition:Heptagon: A heptagon is a polygon with exactly 7 sides. :300px === Regular Heptagon === {{:Definition:Heptagon/Regular
Definition:Octagon: An octagon is a polygon with exactly 8 sides. :300px === Regular Octagon === {{:Definition:Octagon/Regular
Definition:Nonagon: A nonagon is a polygon with exactly 9 sides. :300px === Regular Nonagon === {{:Definition:Nonagon/Regular
Definition:Hendecagon: A hendecagon is a polygon with exactly 11 sides. :300px === Regular Hendecagon === {{:Definition:Hendecagon/Regular
Definition:Dodecagon: A dodecagon is a polygon with exactly 12 sides. :300px === Regular Dodecagon === {{:Definition:Dodecagon/Regular
Definition:Heptadecagon: A heptadecagon is a polygon with exactly 17 sides. :300px === Regular Heptadecagon === {{:Definition:Heptadecagon/Regular

Definition:Pentagon/Regular: A regular pentagon is a pentagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 5 sides. That is, a pentagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Hexagon/Regular: A regular hexagon is a hexagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 6 sides. That is, a hexagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Heptagon/Regular: A regular heptagon is a heptagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 7 sides. That is, a heptagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Octagon/Regular: A regular octagon is an octagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 8 sides. That is, an octagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Nonagon/Regular: A regular nonagon is a nonagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 9 sides. That is, a nonagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Decagon/Regular: A regular decagon is a decagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 10 sides. That is, a decagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Hendecagon/Regular: A regular hendecagon is a hendecagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 11 sides. That is, a hendecagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Heptadecagon/Regular: A regular heptadecagon is a heptadecagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 17 sides. That is, a heptadecagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px

Definition:Dodecagon/Regular: A regular dodecagon is a dodecagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with 12 sides. That is, a dodecagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px
Definition:Cryptography: Cryptography is the branch of mathematics which concerns the encoding of information for secrecy and security.

Definition:Real Function/Multivariable: Let f: S_1 \times S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n \to \R be a mapping where S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n \subseteq \R. Then f is defined as a (real) function of n (independent) variables. The expression: :y = \map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} means: :(The dependent variable) y is a function of (the independent variables) x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.

Definition:Derivative/Real Function/Derivative at Point/Definition 1: That is, suppose the limit \lim_{x \mathop \to \xi} \frac {f \left({x}\right) - f \left({\xi}\right)} {x - \xi} exists. Then this limit is called the derivative of f at the point \xi.

Definition:Derivative/Real Function/Derivative at Point/Definition 2: That is, suppose the limit \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map f {\xi + h} - \map f \xi} h exists. Then this limit is called the derivative of f at the point \xi.

Definition:Secant Line: Let f: \R \to \R be a real function. Let the graph of f be depicted on a Cartesian plane. :400px A secant to f is a straight line which intersects the graph of f in (at least) two points. In the above diagram, the secant is the line AB in \color {blue} {\text {blue} }.
Definition:Celestial Mechanics: Celestial mechanics is the branch of astronomy which studies the motion of celestial bodies such as planets, stars and comets.

Definition:Orbit (Physics): The orbit of body A around body B is the path taken by A as it travels around B under the influence of the force acting between A and B. === Period of Orbit === {{:Definition:Orbit (Physics)/Period
Definition:Orbit (Physics)/Period: The period of an orbit of body A around body B is the length of time it takes for A to travel once around B and return to its original position.
Definition:Astrophysics: Astrophysics is the branch of physics which studies the internal nature of celestial bodies as opposed to their positions and movements.
Definition:Celestial Body: A celestial body is a more-or-less internally coherent body of matter that exists outside the Earth's atmosphere.

Definition:Planet: A planet is a celestial body which orbits a star (or the remains of a star) that: :(1): \quad has enough mass so that its own gravitational field makes it approximately spherical :(2): \quad does not have enough mass to trigger thermonuclear fusion :(3): \quad has cleared its neighbouring region of planetesimals.
Definition:Star (Physics): A star is a celestial body that consists of a luminous sphere of plasma held together by its own gravitational field.
Definition:Sun: The Sun is the star around which Earth (and the other planets of the solar system) is in orbit.
Definition:Earth: Earth is the planet on which we live. It is the third planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Venus and Mars.
Definition:Solar System: The solar system is the system of celestial bodies which are under the direct influence of the gravitational field of the sun.
Definition:Mercury (Planet): Mercury is the innermost planet of the solar system. Its orbit lies within that of Venus. Category:Definitions/Solar System plp5e2aklqfluk6yspee40yd9qjgu7b
Definition:Venus: Venus is the second planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Mercury and Earth. Category:Definitions/Solar System 24j4o8crdk8571medw9pcgt6ngffo04
Definition:Mars: Mars is the fourth planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Earth and Jupiter.
Definition:Jupiter: Jupiter is the fifth planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Mars and Saturn.
Definition:Saturn: Saturn is the sixth planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Jupiter and Uranus. Category:Definitions/Solar System 158qpaeeuovkq9yz648dncuu4nzyb1r
Definition:Uranus: Uranus is the seventh planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Saturn and Neptune. Category:Definitions/Solar System mavyjtjplsijg8xj0d8uvoilw3g6ur3

Definition:Neptune: Neptune is the eighth planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies mainly between those of Uranus and Pluto, although the latter comes closer to the sun than Neptune on part of its orbit.
Definition:Pluto: Pluto is a dwarf planet of the solar system. Its orbit lies mostly outside that of Neptune. Category:Definitions/Solar System jljizc0dsjw0y2cdo2fyfxxb9rbpteb

Definition:Dwarf Planet: A dwarf planet is a celestial body which orbits a star (or the remains of a star) that: :(1): \quad has enough mass so that its own gravitational field makes it approximately spherical :(2): \quad does not have enough mass to trigger thermonuclear fusion :(3): \quad has not cleared its neighbouring region of planetesimals.

Definition:Planetesimal: A planetesimal is a celestial body consisting of solid matter such that: :(1): \quad it is held together by its own gravitational field :(2): \quad it is not large enough for its gravitational field to significantly affect other celestial bodies nearby.

Definition:Time/Dimension: Time is one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is assigned the symbol T or \mathbf T. It is a scalar quantity which can be mapped directly to the real number line.

Definition:Time/Unit Time: The usual units of time are seconds, and compound units consisting of multiples of seconds. However, when discussing a general physical process it is convenient to discuss the general situation, in which case the term unit time is used. Thus the specific units are not mentioned.

Definition:Time/Length: A quantity of time is usually referred to in natural language in the same terms as linear measure. Thus it is usual to refer to a length of time of an elapsed quantity of time.
Definition:Derived Unit: Derived units are units of measurement created by taking specific multiples or fractions of fundamental units.
Definition:System of Measurement: A system of measurement is a set of fundamental units of measurement with which one can measure any measurable physical property.
Definition:Time/Unit/Minute: The minute is a derived unit of time. :1 minute = 60 seconds.
Definition:Time/Unit/Second/Symbol: The symbol for the second is \mathrm s.
Definition:Time/Unit/Minute/Symbol: The symbol for the minute is \mathrm {min}.
Definition:Time/Unit/Hour/Symbol: The symbol for the hour is \mathrm {hr}.
Definition:Time/Unit/Hour: {{begin-eqn o = 1 ; hour r = 60 ; minutes r = 60 \times 60 = 3600 ; seconds {{end-eqn
Definition:Time/Unit/Day: {{begin-eqn o = 1 ; day r = 24 ; hours r = 60 \times 24 = 1440 ; minutes r = 60 \times 60 \times 24 = 86\, 400 ; seconds {{end-eqn
Definition:Time/Unit/Day/Symbol: The symbol for the day is \mathrm {day} or \mathrm d.

Definition:Sidereal Day: A sidereal day is (approximately) the length of time it takes for Earth to rotate once on its axis relative to the stars. The mean duration of a sidereal day is: : 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4.0916 seconds : 23.9344699 hours : 0.99726958 (solar) days. The duration of any given sidereal day is not constant because of various astronomical effects.

Definition:Algorithm/Input: An algorithm has zero or more inputs. These are values supplied either: : before the algorithm starts : as the algorithm runs. These inputs are taken from specified sets of objects.
Definition:Algorithm/Output: An algorithm has one or more outputs. These are values which are specifically determined by the inputs.
Definition:Computational Problem: A computational problem is a mathematical object which represents a collection of questions that are to be solved by algorithmic techniques.
Definition:Algorithm/Finiteness: An algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps.
Definition:Algorithm/Definiteness: Each step of an algorithm must be precisely defined.

Definition:Algorithm/Effectiveness: An algorithm is supposed to be effective. That is, its operations must be basic enough to be able to be done exactly and in a finite length of time by, for example, somebody using pencil and paper.

Definition:Algorithm/Analysis: There are two primary methods for analyzing algorithms formally: === Correctness === {{:Definition:Algorithm/Analysis/Correctness === Complexity === {{:Definition:Algorithm/Analysis/Complexity

Definition:Algorithm/Analysis/Complexity: An algorithm may be analysed in the context of its complexity. This is typically via measures of run-times using big-O, or big-omega, or big-theta notation. Complexity can be through 3 main types of analysis: # Average-Case Analysis, using a distribution of cases to find an average case of the algorithm run-time for analysis # Best-Case Analysis, using the best possible problem instance of the algorithm for analysis # Worst-Case Analysis,using the worst possible problem instance of the algorithm for analysis
Definition:Stationary: A body is stationary if its velocity (in a given frame of reference) is zero.

Definition:Infinitesimal: An infinitesimal is a mathematical object \delta resembling a (real) number such that: :(1): \quad \delta > 0 :(2): \quad \forall x \in \R_{>0}: \delta < x That is, an infinitesimal is a (strictly) positive real number which is smaller than every other (strictly) positive real number.

Definition:Solid of Revolution: Let F be a plane figure. Let L be a straight line in the same plane as F. Let F be rotated one full turn about L in 3-dimensional space. The solid of revolution generated by F around L is the solid figure whose boundaries are the paths taken by the sides of F as they go round L.
Definition:Differential Equation/Order: The order of a differential equation is defined as being the order of the highest order derivative that is present in the equation.

Definition:Differential Equation/Ordinary: An ordinary differential equation (abbreviated O.D.E. or ODE) is a differential equation which has exactly one independent variable. All the derivatives occurring in it are therefore ordinary. The general ODE of order n is: :\map f {x, y, \dfrac {\d x} {\d y}, \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d y^2}, \ldots, \dfrac {\d^n x} {\d y^n} } = 0 or, using the prime notation: :\map f {x, y, y', y, \ldots, y^{\paren n} } = 0

Definition:Differential Equation/Partial: A partial differential equation (abbreviated P.D.E. or PDE) is a differential equation which has: :one dependent variable :more than one independent variable. The derivatives occurring in it are therefore partial.

Definition:Differential Equation/Linear: A linear differential equation is a differential equation where all dependent variables and their derivatives appear to the first power. Neither are products of dependent variables allowed.
Definition:Differential Equation/Non-Linear: A non-linear differential equation is a differential equation which is not linear.

Definition:Differential Equation/System: A system of differential equations is a set of simultaneous differential equations. The solutions for each of the differential equations are in general expected to be consistent.
Definition:Differential Equation/System/Autonomous: A system of differential equations is autonomous if all of the differential equations which it comprises are themselves autonomous.

Definition:Differential Equation/Explicit: A differential equation is called explicit if it can be written in the form: :y^{\left({n}\right)} = f \left({x, y, y', y, \dots, y^{\left({n-1}\right)\right)

Definition:Differential Equation/Autonomous: A differential equation is autonomous if none of the derivatives depend on the independent variable. The nth order autonomous differential equation takes the form: :y^{\paren n} = \map f {y, y', y, \dots, y^{\paren {n - 1} } }
Definition:Legendre's Differential Equation: \paren {1 - x^2} \frac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} - 2 x \frac {\d y} {\d x} + p \paren {p + 1} y = 0

Definition:Parameter of Differential Equation: Let f be a differential equation with general solution F. A parameter of F is an arbitrary constant arising from the solving of a primitive during the course of obtaining the solution of f.
Definition:Substance: A substance is a particular kind of matter with properties specific to it.

Definition:First-Order Reaction: Suppose a body has a tendency to decompose spontaneously into smaller bodies at a rate independent of the presence of other bodies. Then the number of bodies that decompose in a single unit of time is proportional to the total number present. Such a reaction is called a first-order reaction.

Definition:Matter: Matter is the stuff of which the physical universe is composed. At a certain level, can be considered as a form of energy. Matter is (to a first degree of approximation) composed of atoms.

Definition:Chemical Element: A chemical element is a substance which is composed of atoms of one type. A chemical element is characterised uniquely by the number of protons it has in the nucleus of its atoms.

Definition:Atom (Physics): An atom (in the context of physics and chemistry) is the smallest piece of matter that can exist of a particular type of substance. Atoms can be subdivided into smaller particles, but then it ceases to be that substance.
Definition:Radioactive Decay: Radioactive decay is a first-order reaction in which the atoms of a substance may spontaneously break apart, thereby turning into atoms of a different substance.

Definition:Radioactive Decay/Half-Life: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for exactly half of an arbitrary quantity of that isotope to undergo radioactive decay. Thus it is the time it takes for exactly half of an arbitrary quantity of that isotope to remain.
Definition:Radioactive Decay/Radioactive Element: A chemical element whose isotopes are all subject to radioactive decay is known as a radioactive element.

Definition:First-Order Reaction/Rate Constant: Let S be a substance which decomposes spontaneously in a first-order reaction. By First-Order Reaction, this is governed by the equation: :x = x_0 e^{-k t} where: :x is the quantity of S at time t :x_0 is the quantity of S at time t = 0 :k is a positive number. The number k is called the rate constant. k is constant for a particular substance, and different substances, in general, have different rate constants.

Definition:Chemical Element/Isotope: Isotopes are instances of chemical elements which have the same number of protons in the nuclei of their atoms, but different numbers of neutrons. Thus it is usual to discuss an isotope of a particular element.

Definition:Atom (Physics)/Nucleus: The nucleus of an atom is the relatively dense core at its center. It consists (to a first degree of approximation) of a number of protons and a similar number of neutrons.

Definition:Elementary Particle: An elementary particle is one of the basic building blocks of matter. To a first degree of approximation, those building blocks can be considered to be protons, neutrons and electrons. Modern research in particle physics suggests the existence of smaller constituents of protons and neutrons, but at time of writing, electrons are believe to be truly, fundamentally indivisible. Category:Definitions/Particle Physics 2yejk9j01j4hb0trbc4tynec4cuny6z
Definition:Particle Physics: Particle physics is the branch of physics which studies the structure and interactions of the elementary particles of matter.
Definition:Radioactive Decay/Radioactive Isotope: An isotope of a chemical element which is subject to radioactive decay is known as a radioactive isotope.

Definition:Time/Unit/Year: {{begin-eqn o = 1 ; year o = \approx 365 \cdotp 24219 \, 878 ; days o = \approx 365 \cdotp 24219 \, 878 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 ; seconds {{end-eqn That is: {{begin-eqn o = 1 ; year o = \approx 365 ; days, o = 5 ; hours, o = 48 ; minutes, and o = 45 \cdotp 9747 ; seconds {{end-eqn It is defined to be equal to the orbital period of Earth round the sun.
Definition:Time/Unit/Year/Symbol: The symbol for the year is \mathrm {yr} or \mathrm y. In some scientific contexts \mathrm a (for annus, Latin for year) is used.

Definition:Time/Unit/Year/Calendar: A calendar year is the number of days between dates with the same designation in adjacent years. As a year is not an integral number of days, it is necessarily an approximation to the actual year. {{begin-eqn o = 1 ; calendar year r = 12 ; months usually, depending on the calendar used r = 365 \text{ or } 366 ; days, usually, but it depends on the calendar used {{end-eqn
Definition:Radioactive Decay/Stable: An isotope of a chemical element which is not subject to radioactive decay is described as stable.

Definition:Density of Topological Space: Let T be a topological space. The density of T is the smallest cardinality of dense subset of T: :d \left({T}\right) := \min \left\{{\left\vert{A}\right\vert: A \subseteq T \land A}\right. is dense\left.{}\right\}
Definition:Chemical Compound: A (chemical) compound is a (chemical) substance that consists of molecules composed of more than one type of chemical element.

Definition:Molecule: A molecule is an arrangement of atoms, possibly of different elements, which are held together in a configuration which requires the application of external energy to break apart. The molecule is the basic unit of a chemical compound.

Definition:Chemical Reaction: A chemical reaction is a physical process in which the atoms composing the molecules of the chemical substances involved change their configurations into different molecules. Category:Definitions/Chemistry Category:Definitions/Physics qoic8xfj9qwghpvwl74fqa2ik9qbkue

Definition:Second-Order Reaction: Let \AA and \BB be two chemical substances in solution which react together to form a compound \CC. Let the reaction occur by means of the molecules of \AA and \BB colliding and interacting as a result. Then the rate of formation of \CC is proportional to the number of collisions in unit time. This in turn is jointly proportional to the quantities of \AA and \BB which have not yet transformed. Such a chemical reaction is called a second-order reaction.
Definition:Thermodynamics: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics which studies the behaviour of heat.

Definition:Heat: Heat is a form of energy which is held within a body in the form of the physical motion of the molecules or atoms of which that body is composed. Category:Definitions/Physics Category:Definitions/Thermodynamics dij5rrbowaoa9k8gdp108dyza63xjcl
Definition:Energy: Energy is a property of physical bodies which can be defined as the ability to do work. Like time, it is difficult to define exactly what energy actually is.

Definition:Linear Measure/Thickness: Thickness, like breadth, is used as a term for linear measure in a dimension perpendicular to both length and depth. However, whereas breadth has connotations of across, thickness is used for distances through the solid figure.
Definition:Kinetic Energy: Let B be a body. The kinetic energy of B is defined as the energy appertaining to B due to its motion. It is a scalar quantity.

Definition:Potential Energy: Let B be a body. The potential energy of B is the energy appertaining to B as a result of its position in a force field or because of the internal configuration of its components.

Definition:Force Field: A force field is a field in which the physical quantity associated with every point is a force which applies to a body placed at that point. Category:Definitions/Physics lg50nsn2tmwne5pkz9xntjsy0t777br
Definition:Constant (Physics): A physical quantity is defined as being constant if it does not change with the passage of time.

Definition:Pendulum/Ideals: The ideals of a pendulum are as follows: :The rod is of zero thickness, infinite stiffness and zero mass. :The pivot is immovable and has zero friction. :The bob is of zero volume. :The gravitation field is (usually) taken to be constant and uniform. :The medium in which the pendulum moves offers no resistive force, unless otherwise specifically stated.
Definition:Pendulum/Bob: The point mass at the free end of the rod of a pendulum is called the (pendulum) bob.
Definition:Pendulum: A pendulum is an ideal body consisting of two parts: :(1): \quad a rod attached at one end to a pivot :(2): \quad a point mass at the other end of the rod.
Definition:Rod: A rod is a rigid straight body whose width and mass are approximated to zero.

Definition:Escape Velocity: Let a body be propelled vertically upwards from the surface of a planet Let the body keep travelling away from the planet indefinitely. Let resistance from the atmosphere of the planet be considered as negligible. The smallest initial speed at which this is possible is known as the escape velocity of the planet.

Definition:Terminal Velocity: Let a body travelling under a constant force through a medium which resists its progress. The terminal velocity of the body is the limiting speed through that medium for the given force.

Definition:Speed/Also known as: Some authors erroneously or carelessly refer to the speed of a body as its velocity. But this is technically wrong if the author does not specify its direction as well as its magnitude.
Definition:Sine/Real Function/Arch: Each section of the sine function between adjacent zeroes is called an arch of the sine function
Definition:Lemniscate of Bernoulli/Lobe: Each of the two loops that constitute the lemniscate can be referred to as a lobe of the lemniscate.
