Definition:Elliptic Integral of the First Kind/Incomplete/Amplitude: The parameter \phi = \operatorname{am} u of u = F \left({k, \phi}\right) is called the amplitude of u.

Definition:Brachistochrone: Let a point A be joined by a wire to a lower point B. Let the wire be allowed to be bent into whatever shape is required. Let a bead be released at A to slide down without friction to B. The shape of the wire so that the bead takes least time to descend from A to B is called the brachistochrone.
Definition:Wire: A wire is a rigid body modelled by a specific curve whose width and mass are approximated to zero.
Definition:Cycloid/Generating Circle: The circle which rolls along the straight line is called the generating circle of the cycloid.
Definition:Confocal Conics: Let F be a set of conic sections. Then F is a set of confocal conics {{iff they all share the same foci.

Definition:Self-Orthogonal Trajectories: Let \map f {x, y, c} define a one-parameter family of curves F. Let the family of orthogonal trajectories of F be F itself. Then \map f {x, y, c} is self-orthogonal.
Definition:One-Parameter Family of Curves/Parameter: The value c is the parameter of F.
Definition:T1/2 Space: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space. Then T is a T_{\frac 1 2} space {{iff: :\forall A \subseteq S: A' is closed where A' denotes the derivative of A.
Definition:Confocal Ellipses: Let F be a set of ellipses. Then F is a set of confocal ellipses {{iff they all share the same foci. Category:Definitions/Conic Sections l20rp6jtvnamympx7ddmlkq7prci5is

Definition:Confocal Hyperbolas: Let F be a set of hyperbolas. Then F is a set of confocal hyperbolas {{iff they all share the same foci. Category:Definitions/Conic Sections r8883h0y4x4pw2nxv9c8eyajujtws6h

Definition:Asymptote: 500px|right|thumb|Asymptotes to y = x + \dfrac 1 x (blue): [[Definition:Y-Axis|y-axis, and the line x = y (red)]] Let C be a curve in the plane. Let L be a straight (infinite) line such that the distance between C and L approaches zero as they tend to infinity. Then L is an asymptote to (or of) C.

Definition:Conic Section/Center: The center of a section is the point midway between the foci. === Center of Circle === The circle is usually treated differently. From Circle has Two Coincident Foci, the foci and the center are all the same point. :300px {{:Definition:Circle/Center === Center of Ellipse === Let K be an ellipse. :500px {{:Definition:Ellipse/Center === Center of Hyperbola === Let K be a hyperbola. :500px {{:Definition:Hyperbola/Center === Center of Parabola === {{:Definition:Parabola/Center

Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form: Let K be a conic section. Let K be embedded in a cartesian plane such that: :(1) the center is at the origin :(2) the foci are at \left({\pm c, 0}\right) for some c \in \R_{\ge 0}. This can be interpreted in the contexts of the specific classes of conic section as follows: === Reduced Form of Ellipse === {{:Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Ellipse === Reduced Form of Hyperbola === {{:Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Hyperbola === Reduced Form of Circle === {{:Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Circle === Reduced Form of Parabola === {{:Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Parabola

Definition:Parabola/Center: The parabola has no center. From Parabola has One Focus, the definition of the center as being the point midway between the foci, it follows that for a parabola the definition is inapplicable.

Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Ellipse: Let K be an ellipse embedded in a cartesian plane. K is in reduced form {{iff: :(1) its major axis is aligned with the x-axis :(2) its minor axis is aligned with the y-axis. :500px

Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Hyperbola: Let K be a hyperbola embedded in a cartesian plane. K is in reduced form {{iff: :(1) its major axis is aligned with the x-axis :(2) its minor axis is aligned with the y-axis. :500px
Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Circle: Let K be a circle embedded in a cartesian plane. K is in reduced form {{iff its center is located at the origin. :500px

Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Parabola: Let K be a parabola embedded in a cartesian plane. As a Parabola has no Center, it is not possible to define the reduced form of a parabola in the same way as for the other classes of conic section. Instead, K is in reduced form {{iff: :(1) its focus is at the point \tuple {c, 0} :(2) its directrix is aligned with the line x = -c for some c \in \R_{> 0}. :400px

Definition:Hyperbola/Equidistance:   :400px Let F_1 and F_2 be two points in the plane. Let d be a length less than the distance between F_1 and F_2. Let K be the locus of points P which are subject to the condition: :\size {d_1 - d_2} = d where: :d_1 is the distance from P to F_1 :d_2 is the distance from P to F_2 :\size {d_1 - d_2} denotes the absolute value of d_1 - d_2. Then K is a hyperbola.

Definition:Set of Condensation Points: Let T = \left({S, \tau}\right) be a topological space. Let A be a subset of S. The set of condensation points of A is the set of all condensation points of A, :A^0 = \left\{{x \in S:x}\right. is condensation point of \left.{A}\right\}
Definition:Homogeneous Function/Real Space/Degree: The integer n is known as the degree of f.

Definition:Homogeneous Function/Real Space: Let f: \R^2 \to \R be a real-valued function of two variables. f \left({x, y}\right) is a homogeneous function of degree zero {{iff: :\exists n \in \Z: \forall t \in \R: f \left({t x, t y}\right) = t^n f \left({x, y}\right)
Definition:Homogeneous Function/Degree: The element n \in \N is the degree of f.

Definition:Homogeneous Function/Real Space/Zero Degree: f \left({x, y}\right) is a homogeneous function of degree zero or of zero degree {{iff: :\forall t \in \R: f \left({t x, t y}\right) = t^0 f \left({x, y}\right) = f \left({x, y}\right)
Definition:Homogeneous Function/Zero Degree: f is a homogeneous function of degree zero {{iff: :f \left({\alpha \mathbf v}\right) = \alpha^0 f \left({\mathbf v}\right) = f \left({\mathbf v}\right)

Definition:Linear Ordinary Differential Equation: A linear ordinary differential equation is an ordinary differential equation where all dependent variables and their derivatives appear to the first power. Neither are products of dependent variables allowed.

Definition:Linear Second Order Ordinary Differential Equation: A linear second order ordinary differential equation is a differential equation which is in (or can be manipulated into) the form: :\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \map P x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map Q x y = \map R x where, as is indicated by the notation, \map P x, \map Q x and \map R x are functions of x alone (or constants).

Definition:Neighborhood System: Let T = \struct {S, \tau} be a topological space. A neighborhood system is a family \family {\NN_x}_{x \mathop \in S} indexed by points of S, such that \NN_x is a local basis at x for x \in S.

Definition:Tractrix: Let S be a cord situated as a (straight) line segment whose endpoints are P and T. Let T be dragged in a direction perpendicular to the straight line in which S is aligned. The curve along which P travels is known as a tractrix. :400px
Definition:Tractrix/Linguistic Note: The word tractrix derives from the Latin traho (trahere, traxi, tractum) meaning to pull or to drag. The plural is tractrices.
Definition:Pursuit Curve: A pursuit curve is a curve constructed to model pursuers and pursuees. The pursuit curve is the curve traced by the pursuers. The pursuee is always on the pursuer's tangent.

Definition:Rate of Change: The rate of change of a physical quantity is its (first) derivative with respect to time. Loosely speaking, it means how fast something changes, with a wider scope than change in physical displacement. === Dimension === {{:Definition:Rate of Change/Dimension
Definition:Steady-State: === First Order ODE === {{:Definition:Steady-State/First Order ODE === Second Order ODE === {{:Definition:Steady-State/Second Order ODE

Definition:Steady-State/Electronics: The electric current I in K is given by the equation: :I = \dfrac {E_0} R + \left({I_0 - \dfrac {E_0} R}\right) e^{-R t / L} The term \dfrac {E_0} R is known as the steady-state part of (1).

Definition:Transient/Electronics: The electric current I in K is given by the equation: :I = \dfrac {E_0} R + \left({I_0 - \dfrac {E_0} R}\right) e^{-R t / L} The term: :\left({I_0 - \dfrac {E_0} R}\right) e^{-R t / L} which dies away to zero over time, is known as the transient part.

Definition:Transient: Consider the Decay Equation: :\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = k \paren {y_a - y} where: :k \in \R: k > 0 :y = y_0 at x = 0 which has the particular solution: :(1): \quad y = y_a + \paren {y_0 - y_a} e^{-k x} The term: :\paren {y_0 - y_a} e^{-k x} which tends to zero with increasing x, is known as the transient part. === Electronics === The term is often seen in the context of the current in an LR electric circuit K: {{:Definition:Transient/Electronics
Definition:Electronics: Electronics is the branch of electromagnetism which studies how to control electricity.

Definition:Barrier: A complex function \varphi \in \map \C {\overline \Omega} is a barrier for \Omega at z \in \partial \Omega {{iff: :\varphi is subharmonic :\map \varphi z = 0 :\varphi < 0 on \partial \Omega \setminus \set z {{explain|Define \map \C {\overline \Omega} {{explain|Define \Omega {{explain|Define \partial \Omega {{explain|What is the domain and range of \varphi? {{explain|If \varphi is a complex function, its range is also complex, and so cannot be ordered, so the meaning of \varphi < 0 needs to be explained carefully

Definition:Surface of Revolution: Let F be a plane figure. Let L be a straight line in the same plane as F. Let F be rotated one full turn about L in 3-dimensional space. The surface of revolution generated by F around L is the surface of the solid of revolution generated by F around L.
Definition:Riccati Equation: The Riccati equation is the first order ordinary differential equation: :y' = p \left({x}\right) + q \left({x}\right) y + r \left({x}\right) y^2
Definition:Special Riccati Equation: The special Riccati equation is the first order ordinary differential equation: :y' + b y^2 = c x^m {{NamedforDef|Jacopo Francesco Riccati|cat = Riccati

Definition:Burnout Velocity: Let R be a rocket which is propelled by backwards expulsion of the exhaust products of the burning of its internal fuel supply. Let R be fired straight up from the surface of a planet. The burnout velocity of R is the velocity attained by R at the instant when its fuel has become exhausted.
Definition:Dynamics: Dynamics is the branch of the mechanics describing the motion of bodies under the influence of forces.

Definition:Burnout Height: Let R be a rocket which is propelled by backwards expulsion of the exhaust products of the burning of its internal fuel supply. Let R be fired straight up from the surface of a planet. The burnout height of R is the height attained by R at the instant when its fuel has become exhausted.

Definition:Homogeneous Linear Second Order ODE: A homogeneous linear second order ODE is a differential equation which is in (or can be manipulated into) the form: :\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \map P x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map Q x y = 0 where, as is indicated by the notation, \map P x and \map Q x are functions of x alone (or constants).

Definition:Nonhomogeneous Linear Second Order ODE: A nonhomogeneous linear second order ODE is a differential equation which is in (or can be manipulated into) the form: :\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \map P x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map Q x y = \map R x where: :\map P x, \map Q x and \map R x are functions of x alone (or constants) :\map R x is not the zero constant function. That is, a nonhomogeneous linear second order ODE is a linear second order ODE which is not homogeneous.

Definition:Linear Combination of Solutions to Homogeneous Linear 2nd Order ODE: Let C_1 and C_2 be real numbers. Let \map {y_1} x and \map {y_2} x be particular solutions to the homogeneous linear second order ODE: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \map P x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map Q x y = 0 Then: :C_1 \, \map {y_1} x + C_2 \, \map {y_2} x is known as a linear combination of particular solutions to (1).

Definition:Linearly Dependent Real Functions: Let f \left({x}\right) and g \left({x}\right) be real functions defined on a closed interval \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]. Let f and g be constant multiples of each other: :\exists c \in \R: \forall x \in \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]: f \left({x}\right) = c g \left({x}\right) or: :\exists c \in \R: \forall x \in \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]: g \left({x}\right) = c f \left({x}\right) Then f and g are linearly dependent.

Definition:Linearly Independent Real Functions: Let f \left({x}\right) and g \left({x}\right) be real functions defined on a closed interval \left[{a \,.\,.\, b}\right]. Let f and g be such that they are not linearly dependent. Then f and g are linearly independent.

Definition:Wronskian: Let \map f x and \map g x be real functions defined on a closed interval \closedint a b. Let f and g be differentiable on \closedint a b. The Wronskian of f and g is defined as: :\map W {f, g} = \begin {vmatrix} \map f x & \map g x \\ \map {f'} x & \map {g'} x \\ \end {vmatrix} = \map f x \, \map {g'} x - \map g x \, \map {f'} x === General Definition === {{:Definition:Wronskian/General Definition

Definition:Homogeneous Linear Second Order ODE with Constant Coefficients: A homogeneous linear second order ODE with constant coefficients is a second order ODE which can be manipulated into the form: :y + p y' + q y = 0 where p and q are real constants. Thus it is a homogeneous linear second order ODE: :y + \map P x y' + \map Q x y = 0 where \map P x and \map Q x are constant functions.

Definition:Auxiliary Equation: Let: :(1): \quad y + p y' + q y = 0 be a constant coefficient homogeneous linear second order ODE. The auxiliary equation of (1) is the quadratic equation: :m^2 + p m + q = 0
Definition:Cauchy-Euler Equation: The linear second order ordinary differential equation: :x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + p x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + q y = 0 is the Cauchy-Euler equation.

Definition:Cauchy-Euler Equation/General Form: Let n \in \Z_{>0} be a strictly positive integer. The linear ordinary differential equation: :a_n x^n \, \map {y^{\paren n} } x + \dotsb + a_1 x \, \map {y'} x + a_0 \, \map y x = 0 is the nth order Cauchy-Euler equation.

Definition:Directed Subset: Let \struct {S, \precsim} be a preordered set. Let H be a non-empty subset of S. Then H is a directed subset of S {{iff: :\forall x, y \in H: \exists z \in H: x \precsim z and y \precsim z

Definition:Filtered Subset: Let \left({S, \precsim}\right) be a preordered set. Let H be a non-empty subset of S. Then H is a filtered subset of S {{iff: :\forall x, y \in H: \exists z \in H: z \precsim x and z \precsim y

Definition:Spring/Ideal: An ideal spring obeys Hooke's Law: :\mathbf F = -k \mathbf x where: : \mathbf F is the force caused by a displacement \mathbf x : k is the constant of proportion. The negative sign indicates that the force pulls in the opposite direction to that of the displacement imposed.

Definition:Spring/Force Constant: The constant of proportion: :k \in \R_{>0} is known as the (spring) force contant. Its value depends on the particular spring under investigation. The SI unit of the force constant is newtons per metre: \mathrm N \ \mathrm m^{-1}.
Definition:Wall: A wall is an immovable vertical plane in space to which other physical objects may be attached.

Definition:Cart: A cart is a body with a given mass which is free to move with zero friction in a single dimension, that is, back and forth. It is usually imagined as having wheels on which it can roll.
Definition:Immovable: An immovable body is one whose position cannot be changed by applying a force to it. It can be considered as having an infinite mass and zero momentum.

Definition:Spring/Equilibrium Position: The equilibrium position of a body B attached to a spring S is the position it occupies when S is exerting no force upon B. For an ideal spring obeying Hooke's Law \mathbf F = -k \mathbf x, the equilibrium position is set to be the point \mathbf x = \bszero.
Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Amplitude: The parameter A is known as the amplitude of the motion.

Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion: Consider a physical system S whose motion can be expressed in the form of the following equation: :x = A \map \sin {\omega t + \phi} where A and \phi are constants. Then S is in a state of simple harmonic motion. === Amplitude === {{:Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Amplitude === Period === {{:Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Period === Frequency === {{:Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Frequency
Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Period: The period T of the motion of S is the time required for one complete cycle: :T = \dfrac {2 \pi} \omega
Definition:Simple Harmonic Motion/Frequency: The frequency \nu of the motion of S is the number of complete cycles per unit time: :\nu = \dfrac 1 T = \dfrac \omega {2 \pi}
Definition:Periodic Function/Frequency: The frequency \nu of f is the reciprocal of the period L of f: :\nu = \dfrac 1 L

Definition:Fluid: A fluid is a substance which has no defined shape, but which is free to flow according to external forces. === Ideal Fluid === {{:Definition:Fluid/Ideal Category:Definitions/Fluid Mechanics Category:Definitions/Ideals in Physics 36by7c8128e3a1nfmb1k1rs3pv2ei7t
Definition:Medium: A medium is a fluid F through which a body B can pass. Category:Definitions/Mechanics 49mnpwqf8fu8ddljeprdc05kuq7kusi

Definition:Damping Force: Consider a physical system consisting of a body B passing through a medium M. In order for B to move, it needs to push M out of the way to make room for it. Hence M exerts a force upon B which opposes the motion of B. This force opposing the motion of B is referred to as a damping force.

Definition:Viscosity: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of how large a damping force it exerts upon a body moving through it. {{stub|Establish its formal definition: how great the damping force against how large a body at what velocity. Fluid mechanics has not really been started on this site yet. I have a degree semester to infodump.
Definition:Fluid/Ideal: An ideal fluid is a fluid which delivers a damping force whose magnitude is proportional to the velocity of a body passing through it.

Definition:Overdamped: Consider a physical system S whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0 for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b > a, so that the solution of (1) is in the form: :x = C_1 e^{m_1 t} + C_2 e^{m_1 t} for m_1, m_2 < 0. Then S is described as being overdamped. :500px

Definition:Critically Damped: Consider a physical system S whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0 for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b = a, so that the solution of (1) is in the form: :x = C_1 e^{-a t} + C_2 t e^{-a t} Then S is described as being critically damped. :500px

Definition:Underdamped: Consider a physical system S whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0 for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b < a, so that the solution of (1) is in the form: :x = e^{-b t} \paren {C_1 \cos \alpha t + C_2 \sin \alpha t} where \alpha = \sqrt {a^2 - b^2}. Then S is described as being underdamped. :600px

Definition:Natural Frequency: Consider a physical system S whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\mathrm d^2 x} {\mathrm d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\mathrm d x} {\mathrm d t} + a^2 x = 0 for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b < a, so as to make S underdamped. :600px The natural frequency \nu of S is defined as: :\nu = \dfrac 1 T where T is the period of the oscillation of S.

Definition:Free Vibration: Consider a physical system S whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\d^2 x} {\d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\d x} {\d t} + a^2 x = 0 for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b < a, so as to make S underdamped. Then the motion of S is referred to as free vibration of S. :600px

Definition:Steady-State/First Order ODE: Consider the Decay Equation: :\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = k \paren {y_a - y} where: :k \in \R: k > 0 :y = y_0 at x = 0 which has the particular solution: :(1): \quad y = y_a + \paren {y_0 - y_a} e^{-k x} The term y_a is known as the steady-state component of (1).

Definition:Forced Vibration: Consider a physical system S whose behaviour can be described with the second order ODE in the form: :(1): \quad \dfrac {\mathrm d^2 x} {\mathrm d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\mathrm d x} {\mathrm d t} + a^2 x = K \cos \omega x for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b < a, so as to make S underdamped. Then the steady-state motion of S is referred to as forced vibration of S. === Forcing Frequency === {{:Definition:Forced Vibration/Forcing Frequency
Definition:Forced Vibration/Forcing Frequency: The frequency: :\dfrac \omega {2 \pi} is known as the forcing frequency of S.

Definition:Resonance Frequency: Consider a second order ODE in the form: :\dfrac {\mathrm d^2 x} {\mathrm d t^2} + 2 b \dfrac {\mathrm d x} {\mathrm d t} + a^2 x = K \cos \omega x for a, b \in \R_{>0}. Let b < a, so as to make S underdamped. Let the forcing frequency \omega be such that S is in resonance. Then \omega is known as the resonance frequency.

Definition:Polish Space: A Polish space is a topological space which is separable and metrizable, with a metric that makes it a complete metric space. Category:Definitions/Descriptive Set Theory Category:Definitions/Topology Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces gdlarwvzk7c4gy9pd4q2wo64zxxup1s

Definition:Tetractys: The tetractys is a central concept in the mystical beliefs of the Pythagoreans. It consists of 10 points arranged in a triangle: :300px based on the notions that: :1 represents the point :2 represents the line :3 represents the surface :4 represents the solid :1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 and therefore: :10 represents the universe.

Definition:Numerology/Historical Note: The concept of numerology seems to have begun with {{AuthorRef|Pythagoras of Samos|Pythagoras and the Pythagorean school, continuing with the neo-Pythagoreans. {{AuthorRef|Plato adopted the ideas, and from there they were passed on through the emerging Christian tradition into the heart of the philosophy of Western civilization, where it still exerts a powerful influence.

Definition:Platonic Realism: At the heart of {{AuthorRef|Plato's philosophy is the concept of Ideas, or Ideals, or Forms. It is supposed that for every object there exists an ideal form of that object which is that object in perfect form. In modern language, these would be referred to as mathematical abstractions. Platonic realism is the idea that these abstractions actually exist in some place outside of space and time. {{NamedforDef|Plato|cat = Plato
Definition:Plato's Academy: Plato's Academy was the second university in the Western world, after the Pythagorean school. It placed great emphasis on the study of mathematics.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum: Let \left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right), \left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right) be ordered sets. Let f: S_1 \to S_2 be a mapping.

Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Subset: Let F be a subset of S_1. f preserves supremum of F {{iff :F admits a supremum in \left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right) implies :: f^\to \left({F}\right) admits a supremum in \left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right) and \sup \left({f^\to\left({F}\right)}\right) = f \left({\sup F}\right)
Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/All: f preserves all suprema {{iff :for every subset F of S_1, f preserves the supremum of F.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Join: f preserves join {{iff :for every pair of elements x, y of S_1, f preserves the supremum of \left\{ {x, y}\right\}.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Finite: f preserves finite suprema {{iff :for every finite subset F of S_1, f preserves the supremum of F.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Supremum/Directed: f preserves directed suprema {{iff :for every directed subset F of S_1, f preserves the supremum of F.

Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Subset: Let F be a subset of S_1. f preserves infimum of F {{iff :F admits a infimum in \left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right) implies :: f^\to \left({F}\right) admits an infimum in \left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right) and \inf \left({f^\to \left({F}\right)}\right) = f \left({\inf F}\right)
Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/All: f preserves all infima {{iff :for every subset F of S_1, f preserves the infimum of F.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Meet: f preserves meet {{iff :for every pair of elements x, y of S_1, f preserves the infimum of \left\{ {x, y}\right\}.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Finite: f preserves finite infima {{iff :for every finite subset F of S_1, f preserves the infimum of F.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum: Let \left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right), \left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right) be ordered sets. Let f: S_1 \to S_2 be a mapping.
Definition:Mapping Preserves Infimum/Filtered: f preserves filtered infima {{iff :for every filtered subset F of S_1, f preserves the infimum of F.

Definition:Conic Section/Focus-Directrix Property/Historical Note: The focus-directrix definition of a conic section was first documented by {{AuthorRef|Pappus of Alexandria. It appears in his {{BookLink|Collection|Pappus of Alexandria. As he was scrupulous in documenting his sources, and he gives none for this construction, it can be supposed that it originated with him.
Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Tilting Angle: The inclination \phi of the slicing plane with the axis of C is known as the tilting angle of D for K.
Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Slicing Plane: The plane D is known as the slicing plane of C for K.
Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 1: A line is vertical {{iff it is aligned perpendicular to the horizon.
Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 2: A line is vertical {{iff it is parallel to the path taken by a body released from rest in a constant gravitational field.
Definition:Vertical: === Vertical Line === {{:Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 2 Hence the adjective vertically, meaning in a vertical line. === Vertical Plane === {{:Definition:Vertical Plane
Definition:Vertical Plane: A plane is vertical {{iff it contains a vertical line.

Definition:Horizontal: === Horizontal Line === {{:Definition:Horizontal Line/Definition 2 Hence the adjective horizontally, meaning in a horizontal line. === Horizontal Plane === {{:Definition:Horizontal Plane
Definition:Horizontal Line/Definition 2: A line is horizontal {{iff it is aligned parallel to the horizon
Definition:Horizontal Line/Definition 1: A line is horizontal {{iff it is perpendicular to a given vertical line.
Definition:Horizontal Line/Definition 3: A line is horizontal {{iff it can be embedded within a horizontal plane.
Definition:Horizontal Plane: A plane is horizontal {{iff it is perpendicular to a given vertical line.

Definition:Conic Section/Focus-Directrix Property/Circle: 400px It is not possible to define the circle using the focus-directrix property. This is because as the eccentricity e tends to 0, the distance p from P to D tends to infinity. Thus a circle can in a sense be considered to be a degenerate ellipse whose foci are at the same point, that is, the center of the circle.

Definition:Circle/Focus: As a circle cannot be specified using the focus-directrix property, the focus cannot be defined using that technique. Consider an ellipse K with eccentricity e. Let e tend to zero. Then as e becomes smaller, the foci of K become closer together. In the limit, the foci coincide. Thus the focus of the circle can be understood as being its center.

Definition:Académie Parisienne: The Académie Parisienne was an informal academic society established in 1635 by the Franciscan friar {{AuthorRef|Marin Mersenne, sponsored and encouraged by {{WP|Cardinal_Richelieu|Cardinal Richelieu. It consisted of some 140 correspondents from around Europe, and formed a hub of mathematical interaction through which the leading minds of the time could communicate with each other. {{AuthorRef|Marin Mersenne|Mersenne's copious correspondence held it all together. It was to form the nucleus of the later more formal {{WP|French_Academy_of_Sciences|Académie des Sciences, which was chartered in 1666.
Definition:Acoustics: Acoustics is the branch of physics which studies the properties of sound.
Definition:Optics: Optics is the branch of physics which studies the properties of light.

Definition:Light: Light is electromagnetic radiation whose wavelength is between approximately 700 \, \text{nm} and 390 \, \text{nm}. It is characterised by its ability to stimulate the visual senses of humans. Category:Definitions/Optics Category:Definitions/Physics 4rebzuewkr183shrxfw4160ir9ltfv2

Definition:Sound (Physics): Sound is the vibration of an elastic medium whose frequency ranges between approximately 20 \, \text {Hz} and 20 \, \text {kHz}. It is characterised by the ability of humans to detect it with their aural sensory systems.
Definition:Filter in Ordered Set: Let \left({S, \preceq}\right) be a preordered set. Let F be a subset of S. F is filter in \left({S, \preceq}\right) {{iff :F is non-empty filtered and upper.
Definition:Ideal in Ordered Set: Let \left({S, \preceq}\right) be a preordered set. Let I be a subset of S. I is ideal in \left({S, \preceq}\right) {{iff: :I is non-empty directed and lower.
Definition:Logarithmic Spiral: The logarithmic spiral is the locus of the equation expressed in Polar coordinates as: :r = a e^{b \theta} :600px

Definition:Spiral: A spiral is a plane curve, or part of a plane curve, which can be expressed in polar coordinates in the form: :r = \map f \theta where f is either (strictly) increasing or (strictly) decreasing. Hence a spiral is a plane curve which emanates from a central point, getting progressively farther away (or closer in) as it revolves around that point.
Definition:Gabriel's Horn: Gabriel's Horn is the name given to the solid of revolution formed by rotating about the x-axis the curve: :y = \dfrac 1 x :400px
Definition:Hydrostatics: Hydrostatics is the branch of physics concerned with the study of forces on fluids at rest.

Definition:Tautochrone: Let A and B be points in space that are neither on the same horizontal line nor on the same vertical line. A tautochrone is the curve into which a wire is to be shaped so that a bead sliding down it (without friction) takes the same time to reach the lowest point independently of where on that wire it is released from rest.
Definition:Evolute: Consider a curve C embedded in a plane. The evolute of C is the locus of the centers of curvature of each point on C.
Definition:Involute: Consider a curve C embedded in a plane. Imagine an ideal (zero thickness) cord K wound round C. The involute of C is the locus of the end of K as it is unwound from C.
Definition:Abscissa: Consider the graph y = \map f x of a real function f embedded in a Cartesian plane. :500px The x coordinate of a point P = \tuple {x, y} on f is known as the abscissa of P.
Definition:Ordinate: Consider the graph y = \map f x of a real function f embedded in a Cartesian plane. :500px The y coordinate of a point P = \tuple {x, y} on f is known as the ordinate of P.

Definition:Lemniscate of Bernoulli/Linguistic Note: The word lemniscate comes from the Latin word lemniscus, which means pendant ribbon. The word may ultimately derive from the Latin lēmniscātus, which means decorated with ribbons. This may in turn come from the ancient Greek island of Lemnos where ribbons were worn as decorations.
Definition:Integer Partition/Part: In a partition of a (strictly) positive integer, one of the summands in that partition is referred to as a part.
Definition:Integer Partition: A partition of a (strictly) positive integer n is a way of writing n as a sum of (strictly) positive integers.

Definition:Integer Partition/Partition Function: The partition function p: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0} is defined as: :\forall n \in \Z_{>0}: \map p n = the number of partitions of the (strictly) positive integer n.

Definition:Genus of Surface: Let S be a surface. Let G = \left({V, E}\right) be a graph which is embedded in S. Let G be such that each of its faces is a simple closed curve. Let \chi \left({G}\right) = v - e + f = 2 - 2 p be the Euler characteristic of G where: : v = \left|{V}\right| is the number of vertices : e = \left|{E}\right| is the number of edges : f is the number of faces. Then p is known as the genus of S.
Definition:Plane Geometry/Historical Note: The first definitive work on Plane Geometry was {{ElementsLink.

Definition:Hydrodynamics: Hydrodynamics is the branch of physics concerned with the study of fluids in motion.

Definition:Analytical Mechanics: Analytical mechanics is a subfield of mathematical physics which uses techniques of analysis, in particular the calculus of variations, to solve problems in mechanics. Hence, instead of solving equations in vector quantities, it involves solutions of differential equations of scalar quantities.
Definition:Metric System: The metric system is the colloquial term for the system of measurement based on the metre. Its main characteristic is that its units are constructed on a decimal system.
Definition:Decimal System: A decimal system is a system of measurement in which the standard multiples and fractions of the units of measurement are powers of 10.

Definition:Up-Complete: Let \left({S, \precsim}\right) be a preordered set. Then \left({S, \precsim}\right) is up-complete {{iff: :every directed subset of S admits a supremum in \left({S, \precsim}\right).
Definition:Definite Integral/Integrand: In the expression for the definite integral: : \int_a^b f \left({x}\right) \, \mathrm d x the function f is called the integrand.

Definition:Gaussian Distribution: Let X be a continuous random variable on a probability space \struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}. Then X has a Gaussian distribution {{iff the probability density function of X is: :\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\sigma \sqrt {2 \pi} } \map \exp {-\dfrac {\paren {x - \mu}^2} {2 \sigma^2} } for \mu \in \R, \sigma \in \R_{> 0}. This is written: :X \sim \Gaussian \mu {\sigma^2}
Definition:Stirling Numbers/Karamata Notation: The notation {n \brack k} and {n \brace k} for Stirling numbers is known as Karamata notation.

Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Notation: The notation {n \brack k} for the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind is that proposed by {{AuthorRef|Jovan Karamata and publicised by {{AuthorRef|Donald Ervin Knuth|Donald E. Knuth. The notation \map s {n, k} for the signed Stirling numbers of the first kind is similar to variants of that sometimes given for the unsigned. Usage is inconsistent in the literature.
Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Unsigned: {{:Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Unsigned/Definition 1
Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Signed: {{:Definition:Stirling Numbers of the First Kind/Signed/Definition 1

Definition:Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind/Notation: The notation {n \brace k} for Stirling numbers of the second kind is that proposed by {{AuthorRef|Jovan Karamata and publicised by {{AuthorRef|Donald Ervin Knuth|Donald E. Knuth. Other notations exist. Usage is inconsistent in the literature.
Definition:Integer Sequence: An integer sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of integers \Z.
Definition:Geodesy: Geodesy is the branch of geometry which studies the shape of the surface of the Earth.
Definition:Gaussian Curvature: The Gaussian curvature \Kappa of a surface at a point is the product of the principal curvatures, \kappa_1 and \kappa_2, at the given point: :\Kappa = \kappa_1 \kappa_2

Definition:Geodesic Curve: Let A and B be points on a surface S. A geodesic curve between A and B is the line between A and B completely embedded in S whose length is the smallest of all lines between A and B.

Definition:Integral Curvature: Let ABC be a geodesic triangle on a surface S. The integral curvature of ABC is given by: : \int_{ABC} \Kappa \, \mathrm d a where \Kappa is the Gaussian curvature at each point on ABC.

Definition:Geodesic Triangle: Let A, B and C be points on a surface S. Let AB, BC and CA be geodesic curves between A and B, B and C, and C and A respectively. The figure enclosed by AB, BC and CA is known as a geodesic triangle, and can be denoted ABC.

Definition:Biquadratic Residue: Let p be an odd prime. Let a \in \Z be an integer such that a \not \equiv 0 \pmod p. Then a is a biquadratic residue of p {{iff x^4 \equiv a \pmod p has a solution. That is, {{iff: : \exists x \in \Z: x^4 \equiv a \pmod p
Definition:Gaussian Prime: A Gaussian prime is a Gaussian integer which has exactly 4 divisors which are themselves Gaussian integers.

Definition:Harmonic Function: A harmonic function is a is a twice continuously differentiable function f: U \to \R (where U is an open set of \R^n) which satisfies Laplace's equation: :\dfrac {\partial^2 f} {\partial {x_1}^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 f} {\partial {x_2}^2} + \cdots + \dfrac {\partial^2 f} {\partial {x_n}^2} = 0 everywhere on U. This is usually written as: :\nabla^2 f = 0 or: :\Delta f = 0

Definition:Galois Connection: Let \struct {S, \preceq} and \struct {T, \precsim} be ordered sets. Let g: S \to T, d: T \to S be mappings. Then \struct {g, d} is a Galois connection {{iff: :g and d are increasing mappings and ::\forall s \in S, t \in T: t \precsim \map g s \iff \map d t \preceq s g is upper adjoint and d is lower adjoint of a Galois connection. {{definition wanted|monotone, antitone, closure operator, closed {{NamedforDef|Évariste Galois|cat = Galois

Definition:Taylor Series/Remainder/Lagrange Form: The Lagrange form of the remainder R_n is given by: :R_n = \dfrac {\map {f^{\paren {n + 1} } } {x^*} } {\paren {n + 1}!} \paren {x - \xi}^{n + 1} where x^* \in \openint \xi x.

Definition:Taylor Series/Remainder/Cauchy Form: The Cauchy form of the remainder R_n is given by: :R_n = \dfrac {\paren {x - \eta}^n} {n!} \paren {x - \xi} \map {f^{\paren {n + 1} } } \eta where \eta \in \closedint \xi x.
Definition:Pentagonal Number/Examples: The first few pentagonal numbers are as follows: :700px === Sequence of Pentagonal Numbers === {{:Definition:Pentagonal Number/Sequence

Definition:Polygonal Number/Degenerate Case: Consider the polygonal number P \left({2, n}\right) when k = 2. In this case, the polygon degenerates into a straight line, and the recurrence formula becomes: :P \left({2, n}\right) = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ P \left({2, n-1}\right) + 0 \times \left({n-1}\right) + 1 & : n > 0 \end{cases} Hence: :P \left({2, n}\right) = P \left({2, n-1}\right) + 1 and the sequence goes: :0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots which is of course the natural numbers.
Definition:Triangular Number/Definition 2: T_n = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n i = 1 + 2 + \cdots + \left({n-1}\right) + n
Definition:Triangular Number/Definition 1: T_n = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ n + T_{n-1} & : n > 0 \end{cases}

Definition:Triangular Number/Definition 3: \forall n \in \N: T_n = P \left({3, n}\right) = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ P \left({3, n - 1}\right) + \left({n - 1}\right) + 1 & : n > 0 \end{cases} where P \left({k, n}\right) denotes the k-gonal numbers.
Definition:Pentagonal Number/Definition 1: P_n = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ P_{n-1} + 3 n - 2 & : n > 0 \end{cases}
Definition:Pentagonal Number/Definition 2: P_n = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \left({3 i - 2}\right) = 1 + 4 + \cdots + \left({3 \left({n - 1}\right) - 2}\right) + \left({3 n - 2}\right)

Definition:Pentagonal Number/Definition 3: \forall n \in \N: P_n = \map P {5, n} = \begin {cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ \map P {5, n - 1} + 3 \paren {n - 1} + 1 & : n > 0 \end {cases} where \map P {k, n} denotes the k-gonal numbers.
Definition:Hexagonal Number/Definition 1: H_n = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ H_{n-1} + 4 \left({n-1}\right) + 1 & : n > 0 \end{cases}

Definition:Hexagonal Number/Definition 2: H_n = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \left({4 \left({i - 1}\right) + 1}\right) = 1 + 5 + \cdots + \left({4 \left({n-2}\right) + 1}\right) + \left({4 \left({n - 1}\right) + 1}\right)

Definition:Hexagonal Number/Definition 3: \forall n \in \N: H_n = P \left({6, n}\right) = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ P \left({6, n - 1}\right) + 4 \left({n - 1}\right) + 1 & : n > 0 \end{cases} where P \left({k, n}\right) denotes the k-gonal numbers.
Definition:Square Number/Definition 2: S_n = \begin {cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ S_{n - 1} + 2 n - 1 & : n > 0 \end {cases}

Definition:Square Number/Definition 1: An integer n is classified as a square number {{iff: :\exists m \in \Z: n = m^2 where m^2 denotes the integer square function. ==== Euclid's Definition ==== {{EuclidSaid :{{:Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book VII/18 - Square Number {{EuclidDefRefNocat|VII|18|Square Number
Definition:Square Number/Definition 3: S_n = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {2 i - 1} = 1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + \paren {2 n - 1}

Definition:Square Number/Definition 4: \forall n \in \N: S_n = \map P {4, n} = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ \map P {4, n - 1} + 2 \paren {n - 1} + 1 & : n > 0 \end{cases} where \map P {k, n} denotes the k-gonal numbers.
Definition:Triangular Number/Sequence: The sequence of triangular numbers, for n \in \Z_{\ge 0}, begins: :0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66, \ldots
Definition:Pentagonal Number/Sequence: The sequence of pentagonal numbers, for n \in \Z_{\ge 0}, begins: :0, 1, 5, 12, 22, 35, 51, 70, 92, 117, 145, 176, \ldots
Definition:Hexagonal Number/Sequence: The sequence of hexagonal numbers, for n \in \Z_{\ge 0}, begins: :0, 1, 6, 15, 28, 45, 66, 91, 120, 153, 190, 231, \ldots
Definition:Odd Integer/Definition 1: An integer n \in \Z is odd {{iff it is not divisible by 2. That is, {{iff it is not even.
Definition:Odd Integer/Definition 2: An integer n \in \Z is odd {{iff: :\exists m \in \Z: n = 2 m + 1
Definition:Convex Polyhedron: Let P be a polyhedron. P is a convex polyhedron {{iff: :For all points A and B located inside P, the line AB is also inside P.

Definition:Center of Gravity: Let B be a body. The center of gravity of B is that point through which the resultant of the system of parallel forces formed by the weights of all the particles constituting B passes for all positions of B.

Definition:Archimedean Spiral/Archimedes' Definition: If a straight line of which one extremity remains fixed be made to revolve at a uniform rate in a plane until it returns to the position from which it started, and if, at the same time as the straight line revolves, a point moves at a uniform rate along the straight line, starting from the fixed extremity, the point will describe a spiral in the plane.
Definition:Information Theory: Information theory is that branch of mathematics concerned with the flow of information.

Definition:Special Function: Special functions are particular functions which have more or less established names and notations due to their importance in, for example, analysis, functional analysis or physics. There is no general formal definition, but the list of mathematical functions contains functions which are commonly accepted as special.
Definition:Stochastic Process: A stochastic process is a collection of random variables representing the evolution of some real-world system over time.
Definition:Non-Linear System: A non-linear system is a system of differential equations which are non-linear.

Definition:Catastrophe Theory: Catastrophe theory is a branch of bifurcation theory in the study of dynamical systems. It is also a particular special case of more general singularity theory in geometry.
Definition:Chaos Theory: Chaos theory is the branch of non-linear systems that studies the behavior and condition of dynamical systems that are highly sensitive to initial conditions.
Definition:Atomic Physics: Atomic physics is the branch of physics concerned with the structure and behaviour of the atom.
Definition:Wave Mechanics: Wave mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the physical behaviour of waves.

Definition:Point of Inflection: Let f be a real function which is differentiable on an interval \Bbb I \subseteq \R. Let \xi \in \Bbb I. === Definition 1 === {{:Definition:Point of Inflection/Definition 1 === Definition 2 === {{:Definition:Point of Inflection/Definition 2
Definition:Point of Inflection/Definition 1: f has a point of inflection at \xi {{iff \xi is a point on f at which f changes from being concave to convex, or vice versa.
Definition:Point of Inflection/Definition 2: f has a point of inflection at \xi {{iff the derivative f' of f has either a local maximum or a local minimum at \xi.

Definition:Ordering on Mappings: Let S be a set. Let \left({T, \preceq}\right) be an ordered set. Let f, g: S \to T be mappings. Then ordering on mappings f and g denoted f \preceq g is defined by :\forall s \in S: f\left({s}\right) \preceq g\left({s}\right)

Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point/Infimum: Let \mathcal N_x be the set of open subset neighborhoods of x. The oscillation of f at x is defined as: : \omega_f \left({x}\right) := \inf_{U \mathop \in \mathcal N_x} \omega_f \left({U \cap X}\right) where \omega_f \left({U \cap X}\right) denotes the oscillation of f on U \cap X.

Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point/Limit: The oscillation of f at x is defined as: : \omega_f \left({x}\right) := \lim_{h \to 0^+} \omega_f \left({\left({x - h \,.\,.\, x + h}\right) \cap X}\right) where \omega_f \left({\left({x - h \,.\,.\, x + h}\right) \cap X}\right) denotes the oscillation of f on \left({x - h \,.\,.\, x + h}\right) \cap X.

Definition:Language of Predicate Logic: In order to define \LL_1, it is necessary to specify: * An alphabet \AA * A collation system with the unique readability property for \AA * A formal grammar (which determines the WFFs of \LL_1)
Definition:Abelian Function: An Abelian function is an inverse function of an Abelian integral. {{NamedforDef|Niels Henrik Abel|cat = Abel

Definition:Dirichlet Function: A Dirichlet function D: \R \to \R is a real function defined as: :\forall x \in \R: \map D x = \begin {cases} c & : x \in \Q \\ d & : x \notin \Q \end {cases} for c, d \in \R such that c \ne d. The canonical example of this has c = 1 and d = 0. {{NamedforDef|Johann Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|cat = Dirichlet

Definition:Liouville's Constant: Liouville's constant is the real number defined as: {{begin-eqn \sum_{n \mathop \ge 1} \dfrac 1 {10^{n!} } \frac 1 {10^1} + \frac 1 {10^2} + \frac 1 {10^6} + \frac 1 {10^{24} } + \cdots ; r = 0 \cdotp 11000 \, 10000 \, 00000 \, 00000 \, 00010 \, 00 \ldots ; {{end-eqn {{OEIS|A012245
Definition:Riemann Surface/Elliptic/Definition 2: A Riemann surface is elliptic {{iff it admits a metric of constant positive curvature.
Definition:Riemannian Geometry (Mathematical Branch): Riemannian geometry is the branch of differential geometry that studies Riemannian manifolds.

Definition:Riemannian Geometry: A Riemannian geometry is a Riemannian manifold \mathcal M together with the Riemannian metric that has been applied to M.

Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Critical Line: Let s = \sigma + i t. The line defined by the equation \sigma = \dfrac 1 2 is known as the critical line. Hence the popular form of the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis: :All the nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line.
Definition:Weierstrass Function: A Weierstrass function is a real function defined on a closed real interval I which is: :(1):\quad continuous on I :(2):\quad nowhere differentiable on I.
Definition:Entire Function/Transcendental: Let f be an entire function that has an essential singularity at \infty. Then f is a transcendental entire function.

Definition:Dedekind Cut/Definition 1: A Dedekind cut of \struct {S, \preceq} is a non-empty proper subset L \subsetneq S such that: :(1): \quad \forall x \in L: \forall y \in S: y \prec x \implies y \in L (L is a lower set in S) :(2): \quad \forall x \in L: \exists y \in L: x \prec y

Definition:Dedekind Cut/Definition 2: A Dedekind cut of \struct {S, \preceq} is an ordered pair \tuple {L, R} such that: :(1): \quad \set {L, R} is a partition of S. :(2): \quad L does not have a greatest element. :(3): \quad \forall x \in L: \forall y \in R: x \prec y.
Definition:Peano Curve: A Peano curve is a fractal curve which can be written as a Lindenmayer system. :800px {{stub {{NamedforDef|Giuseppe Peano|cat = Peano

Definition:Cartesian Product of Ordered Sets: Let \left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right), \left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right) be ordered sets. Cartesian product of (ordered sets) \left({S_1, \preceq_1}\right) and \left({S_2, \preceq_2}\right) is a pair \left({S_1 \times S_2, \preceq}\right) where :{\preceq} \subseteq \left({S_1 \times S_2}\right) \times \left({S_1 \times S_2}\right) such that :\forall s_1, t_1 \in S_1, s_2, t_2 \in S_2: \left({s_1,s_2}\right) \preceq \left({t_1,t_2}\right) \iff s_1 \preceq_1 t_1 \land s_2 \preceq_2 t_2
Definition:Prime Number/Definition 7: A prime number p is an integer greater than 1 which cannot be written in the form: :p = a b where a and b are both positive integers less than p.
Definition:Perfect Number/Definition 1: A perfect number is a (strictly) positive integer equal to its aliquot sum.
Definition:Perfect Number/Definition 2: A perfect number n is a (strictly) positive integer such that: : \sigma \left({n}\right) = 2 n where \sigma: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0} is the sigma function.
Definition:Momentum: === Linear Momentum === {{:Definition:Linear Momentum === Angular Momentum === {{:Definition:Angular Momentum

Definition:Thrust: The thrust of a rocket is defined as the product of the exhaust velocity and the rate at which its fuel is being consumed: :\mathbf t = \mathbf b \paren {\dfrac {\d m} {\d t} } where: :\mathbf b is the exhaust velocity :m is the mass of the rocket as a function of time t.

Definition:Meet-Continuous Lattice: Let \left({S, \preceq}\right) be a meet semilattice. Then \left({S, \preceq}\right) is meet-continuous {{iff :\left({S, \preceq}\right) is up-complete and ::(MC): for every an element x \in S and a directed subset D of S: x \wedge \sup D = \sup \left\{ {x \wedge d: d \in D}\right\}
Definition:Twin Primes/Sequence: The sequence of twin primes begins: :3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 29, 31, 41, 43, 59, 61, 71, 73, 101, 103, 107, 109, \ldots
Definition:Rational Point in Plane: Consider the Cartesian plane \R^2. The points \tuple {x, y} \in \R^2 such that x, y \in \Q are called the rational points (of \R^2).
Definition:Linear Polynomial: A linear polynomial is a polynomial whose degree is 1. Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory 8ffuktvxhlxm4sq1yfifr3z2ugp5i91

Definition:Algebraic Number/Degree: Let \alpha be an algebraic number. By definition, \alpha is the root of at least one polynomial P_n with rational coefficients. The degree of \alpha is the degree of the minimal polynomial P_n whose coefficients are all in \Q.

Definition:Gelfond-Schneider Constant: The Gelfond-Schneider constant is defined as 2 raised to the power of the square root of 2: :2^{\sqrt 2} Its decimal expansion begins: :2^{\sqrt 2} \approx 2 \cdotp 66514 \, 4 {{OEIS|A007507 {{NamedforDef|Alexander Osipovich Gelfond|name2 = Theodor Schneider|cat = Gelfond|cat2 = Schneider

Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Sequence: The sequence of Bernoulli numbers begins: {{begin-eqn B_0 1 ; B_1 | ro= - \dfrac 1 2 ; B_2 \dfrac 1 6 ; B_4 | ro= - \dfrac 1 {30} ; B_6 \dfrac 1 {42} ; B_8 | ro= - \dfrac 1 {30} ; B_{10} \dfrac 5 {66} ; B_{12} | ro= - \dfrac {691} {2730} ; {{end-eqn The odd index Bernoulli numbers, apart from B_1, are all equal to 0.
Definition:Hypocycloid: Let a circle C_1 roll around the inside of another (larger) circle C_2. The locus of a given point on the circumference of C_1 is known as a hypocycloid.
Definition:Epicycloid: Let a circle C_1 roll around the outside of another circle C_2. The locus of a given point on the circumference of C_1 is known as an epicycloid.
Definition:Astroid: An astroid is a hypocycloid with 4 cusps. :400px
Definition:Tusi Couple: A Tusi couple is a hypocycloid with 2 cusps. :400px

Definition:Hypocycloid/Generator: The circles C_1 and C_2 can be referred to as the generators of the hypocycloid. === Stator === {{Definition:Hypocycloid/Generator/Stator === Rotor === {{Definition:Hypocycloid/Generator/Rotor
Definition:Hypocycloid/Generator/Rotor: The circle C_1 can be referred to as the rotor of the hypocycloid.
Definition:Hypocycloid/Generator/Stator: The circle C_2 can be referred to as the stator of the hypocycloid.

Definition:Epicycloid/Generator: The circles C_1 and C_2 can be referred to as the generators of the epicycloid. === Stator === {{Definition:Epicycloid/Generator/Stator === Rotor === {{Definition:Epicycloid/Generator/Rotor
Definition:Epicycloid/Generator/Stator: The circle C_2 can be referred to as the stator of the epicycloid.
Definition:Epicycloid/Generator/Rotor: The circle C_1 can be referred to as the rotor of the epicycloid.
Definition:Deltoid: A deltoid is a hypocycloid with 3 cusps. :400px

The oscillation of f on (or over) A is defined as: : \map {\omega_f} A := \sup_{x, y \mathop \in A} \size {\map f x - \map f y} where the supremum is taken in the extended real numbers \overline \R.

Definition:Nephroid: A nephroid is an epicycloid with 2 cusps. :600px

Definition:Curvature: Let C be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. The curvature of a C is the reciprocal of the radius of the osculating circle to C and is often denoted \kappa (Greek kappa).
Definition:Radius of Curvature: The radius of curvature of a curve C at a point P is defined as the reciprocal of the absolute value of its curvature: :\rho = \dfrac 1 {\size k}

Definition:Normal to Curve: Let C be a curve embedded in the plane. The normal to C at a point P is defined as the straight line which lies perpendicular to the tangent at P and in the same plane as P.

Definition:Center of Curvature: Let C be a curve embedded in the plane. Let N be the normal to C at a point P. Let \rho be the radius of curvature of C at P. Let Q be the point on N which is at a distance \rho from P on the concave side of C. Q is known as the center of curvature of C at P.

Definition:Curvature/Cartesian Form: Let C be embedded in a cartesian plane. The curvature \kappa of C at a point P = \tuple {x, y} is given by: :\kappa = \dfrac {y} {\paren {1 + y'^2}^{3/2} } where: :y' = \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} is the derivative of y {{WRT|Differentiation x at P :y = \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} is the second derivative of y {{WRT|Differentiation x at P.

Definition:Intrinsic Equation: Let C be a curve. An intrinsic equation of C is an equation that defines C using a relation between the intrinsic properties of C. Thus an intrinsic equation defines the shape of C without specifying its position relative to an arbitrarily defined coordinate system. === Natural Equation === {{:Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Natural Equation === Cesàro Equation === {{:Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Cesàro Equation === Whewell Equation === {{:Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Whewell Equation
Definition:Intrinsic Property: Let C be a curve. The intrinsic properties of C are those properties that do not depend on the nature of the embedding of C in a coordinate system.
Definition:Intrinsic Property/Examples: Examples of the intrinsic properties of a curve include: :Arc length s :Curvature \kappa :Turning angle \psi :Torsion \tau :Radius of curvature \rho

Definition:Turning Angle: Let C be a curve. The turning angle \psi of C at a point P is defined by the differential equation: :\kappa = \dfrac {\d \psi} {\d s} where: :\kappa is the curvature at P :\dfrac {\d \psi} {\d s} is the derivative of \psi {{WRT|Differentiation the arc length s. That is, the turning angle is a measure of how sharply a curve changes direction. The turning angle is an intrinsic property of C.

Definition:Intrinsic Equation/Whewell Equation: A Whewell equation is an intrinsic equation for a curve C such that C is expressed in terms of its intrinsic properties: :Arc length s :Turning angle \psi

Definition:Curvature/Whewell Form: The curvature \kappa of C at a point P can be expressed in the form of a Whewell equation as: :\kappa = \dfrac {\d \psi} {\d s} where: :\psi is the turning angle of C :s is the arc length of C.
Definition:Astronomical Unit/Approximate Values: The astronomical unit is approximately 150 \, 000 \, 000 \, \mathrm {k m}, or 93 million (international) miles.

Definition:Astronomical Unit: The astronomical unit is a derived unit of length. It is defined as being 149 \, 597 \, 870 \, 700 metres. The astronomical unit is the standard unit of measurement used by astronomers when discussing distances within the solar system. It is derived as the approximate mean distance from the Earth to the Sun. === Approximate Values === {{:Definition:Astronomical Unit/Approximate Values === Symbol === {{:Definition:Astronomical Unit/Symbol

Definition:Division Algebra/Definition 1: \left({A_F, \oplus}\right) is a division algebra {{iff: : \forall a, b \in A_F, b \ne \mathbf 0_A: \exists_1 x \in A_F, y \in A_F: a = b \oplus x, a = y \oplus b

Definition:Conjugate Quaternion/Matrix Form: Let \mathbf x be a quaternion defined in matrix form as: :\mathbf x = \begin{bmatrix} a + bi & c + di \\ -c + di & a - bi \end{bmatrix} The conjugate quaternion of \mathbf x is defined as: :\overline {\mathbf x} = \begin{bmatrix} a - bi & -c - di \\ c - di & a + bi \end{bmatrix}

Definition:Conjugate Quaternion/Ordered Pair: Let \mathbf x be a quaternion defined as an ordered pair \left({a, b}\right) of complex numbers. The conjugate quaternion of \mathbf x is defined as: :\overline {\mathbf x} = \overline {\left({a, b}\right)} = \left({\overline a, -b}\right)

Definition:Field Norm of Quaternion: Let \mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k be a quaternion. Let \overline {\mathbf x} be the conjugate of \mathbf x. The norm of \mathbf x is the real number defined as: :n \left({\mathbf x}\right) := \left\vert{\mathbf x \overline {\mathbf x} }\right\vert = \left\vert{\overline {\mathbf x} \mathbf x }\right\vert = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2

Definition:Positive Definite (Ring): Let \struct {R, +, \times} be a ring whose zero is denoted 0_R. Let f: R \to \R be a (real-valued) function on R. Then f is positive definite {{iff: :\forall x \in R: \begin {cases} \map f x = 0 & : x = 0_R \\ \map f x > 0 & : x \ne 0_R \end {cases} Category:Definitions/Ring Theory p3oa3bgzq9l393gfnrxy925ltk362pq

Definition:Nonassociative Algebra: Let \left({A_R, \oplus}\right) be an algebra over a ring. Then \left({A_R, \oplus}\right) is a nonassociative algebra {{iff it is not necessarily the case that \oplus is associative.

Definition:Lie Algebra: Let \struct {A_R, \oplus} be an algebra over a ring. Then \struct {A_R, \oplus} is a Lie algebra {{iff: :\forall a \in A_R: a^2 = 0 :\forall a, b, c \in A_R: a \paren {b c} + b \paren {c a} + c \paren {a b} = 0
Definition:Lie Group: A Lie group is a group which is also a smooth manifold.
Definition:Cayley Algebra: The Cayley algebra is the nonassociative division algebra formed by the Octonions under octonion multiplication.

Definition:Normal Family: Let X = \left({M_1, d_1}\right) and Y = \left({M_2, d_2}\right) be complete metric spaces. Let \mathcal F = \left \langle{f_i}\right \rangle_{i \mathop \in I} be a family of continuous mappings f_i: X \to Y. Then \mathcal F is a normal family {{iff: : every sequence of mappings in \mathcal F contains a subsequence which converges uniformly on compact subsets of X to a continuous function f: X \to Y.

Definition:Locally Bounded/Mapping: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let f be a mapping defined on M. Then f is said to be locally bounded {{iff: :for all x \in A, there is some neighbourhood N of x such that f \left[{N}\right] is bounded.

Definition:Uniformly Bounded: Let X be a set and let Y = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let \mathcal F = \left \langle{f_i}\right \rangle_{i \mathop \in I} be a family of mappings f_i: X \to Y. Then \mathcal F is said to be uniformly bounded if every mapping f \in \mathcal F can be bounded by the same constant. That is, if there exists some M \in \R such that: :\forall x, y \in X, i \in I : d \left({f_i \left({x}\right), f_i \left({y}\right)}\right) \le M Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces Category:Definitions/Boundedness 9v1jbgvwtmrcsgrniksvg1s7rlg2f48

Definition:Locally Bounded/Family of Mappings: Let M = \left({A, d}\right) be a metric space. Let \mathcal F = \left \langle{f_i}\right \rangle_{i \mathop \in I} be a family of mappings defined on M. Then \mathcal F is said to be locally bounded {{iff: : for all x \in A, there is some neighbourhood N of x such that \mathcal F is uniformly bounded on N.

Definition:Mechanical Curve: A mechanical curve is a curve which cannot be constructed using a compass and straightedge. Note that while it is not possible to construct such a curve in this manner, it may well be possible to construct as many points on it as required.

Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Degenerate Hyperbola: Let \phi < \theta, that is: so as to make K a hyperbola. However, let D pass through the apex of C. Then K degenerates into a pair of intersecting straight lines.
Definition:Geometric Curve: A geometric curve is a curve which can be constructed using a compass and straightedge.

Definition:Number Theory/Also known as: Older sources refer to number theory variously as: :theory of numbers :the higher arithmetic :arithmetic. {{AuthorRef|Carl Friedrich Gauss himself used the term arithmetic, after the manner of the ancient Greeks. Number theory can also be seen described by the fanciful name the Queen of Mathematics for various whimsical reasons.

Definition:Ore Graph: Let G = \struct {V, E} be an undirected simple graph. Then G is an Ore graph {{iff: :the sum of the degrees of every pair of non-adjacent vertices is greater than or equal to the order of G. That is, {{iff: :\forall u, v \in V: \set {u, v} \notin E \implies \map {\deg_G} u + \map {\deg_G} v \ge \card V {{NamedforDef|Øystein Ore|cat = Ore

Definition:Derivative/Higher Derivatives/Second Derivative/Notation: The second derivative is variously denoted as: :\map {f} \xi :D^2 \map f \xi :D_{xx} \map f \xi :\map {\dfrac {\d^2} {\d x^2} } \xi If y = \map f x, then it can also expressed as y: :y := \map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} } and written: :\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2}
