Definition:Series/Real: A real series S_n is the limit to infinity of the sequence of partial sums of a real sequence \sequence {a_n}: {{begin-eqn S_n \lim_{N \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^N a_n ; r = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n ; r = a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots ; {{end-eqn
Definition:Non-Archimedean/Norm (Division Ring): === Definition 1 === {{:Definition:Non-Archimedean/Norm (Division Ring)/Definition 1
Definition:Non-Archimedean/Norm (Division Ring)/Archimedean: A norm \norm {\, \cdot \,} on a division ring R is Archimedean {{iff it is not non-Archimedean.
Definition:Bell Number/Sequence: The sequence of Bell numbers begins: :(1), 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, 877, 4140, 21 \, 147, \ldots where the first (1) is the zeroth Bell number B_0.
Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Also known as: A divisor can also be referred to as a factor.

Definition:Ring of Sequences: Let \struct {R, +, \circ} be a ring. Given the natural numbers \N, the ring of sequences over R is the ring of mappings \struct {R^\N, +', \circ'} where: :(1): \quad R^\N is the set of sequences in R :(2): \quad +' and \circ' are the (pointwise) operations induced by + and \circ.

Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation/Definition 1: The inverse image mapping of \mathcal R is the mapping \mathcal R^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S that sends a subset Y \subseteq T to its preimage \map {\mathcal R^{-1} } Y under \mathcal R: :\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {\mathcal R^\gets} Y = \begin {cases} \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \tuple {t, s} \in \mathcal R^{-1} } & : \Img {\mathcal R} \cap Y \ne \O \\ \O & : \Img {\mathcal R} \cap Y = \O \end {cases}

Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation/Definition 2: The inverse image mapping of \mathcal R is the direct image mapping of the inverse \mathcal R^{-1} of \mathcal R: :\mathcal R^\gets = \paren {\mathcal R^{-1} }^\to: \powerset T \to \powerset S That is: :\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {\mathcal R^\gets} Y = \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \tuple {t, s} \in \mathcal R^{-1} }

Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping/Definition 1: The inverse image mapping of f is the mapping f^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S that sends a subset Y \subseteq T to its preimage f^{-1} \paren T under f: :\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {f^\gets} Y = \begin {cases} \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \map f s = t} & : \Img f \cap Y \ne \O \\ \O & : \Img f \cap Y = \O \end {cases}

Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping/Definition 2: The inverse image mapping of f is the direct image mapping of the inverse f^{-1} of f: :f^\gets = \paren {f^{-1} }^\to: \powerset T \to \powerset S: That is: :\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {f^\gets} Y = \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \map f s = t}

Definition:Surjection/Also known as: The phrase f is surjective is often used for f is a surjection. Authors who prefer to limit the jargon of mathematics tend to use the term an onto mapping for a surjection, and onto for surjective. A mapping which is not surjective is thence described as into. A surjection f from S to T is sometimes denoted: :f: S \twoheadrightarrow T to emphasize surjectivity. {{LatexFor|for = f: S \twoheadrightarrow T
Definition:Cauchy Functional Equation: Let f: \R \to \R be a real function. Then the Cauchy functional equation is: :\forall x, y \in \R: f \paren {x + y} = f \paren x + f \paren y

Definition:Subtraction/Real Numbers: Let \struct {\R, +, \times} be the field of real numbers. The operation of subtraction is defined on \R as: :\forall a, b \in \R: a - b := a + \paren {-b} where -b is the negative of b in \R.

Definition:Subtraction/Rational Numbers: Let \struct {\Q, +, \times} be the field of rational numbers. The operation of subtraction is defined on \Q as: :\forall a, b \in \Q: a - b := a + \paren {-b} where -b is the negative of b in \Q.
Definition:Self-Inverse Element/Definition 1: x is a self-inverse element of \struct {S, \circ} {{iff x \circ x = e.
Definition:Self-Inverse Element/Definition 2: x is a self-inverse element of \struct {S, \circ} {{iff: :x is invertible and: :x = x^{-1}, where x^{-1} is the inverse of x.

Definition:Symmetric Group/n Letters: Let S_n denote the set of permutations on n letters. Let \struct {S_n, \circ} denote the symmetric group on S_n. Then \struct {S_n, \circ} is referred to as the symmetric group on n letters.

Definition:Symmetric Group/Notation: In order not to make notation for operations on a symmetric group overly cumbersome, product notation is usually used for mapping composition. Thus \pi \circ \rho is written \pi \rho. Also, for the same reason, rather than using I_{S_n} for the identity mapping, the symbol e is usually used.

Definition:Rotation (Geometry): A rotation in the context of Euclidean geometry is an isometry from a Euclidean Space \R^n as follows. A rotation is defined usually for either: :n = 2, representing the plane or: :n = 3, representing ordinary space. === Rotation in the Plane === {{:Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Plane === Rotation in Space === {{:Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Space

Definition:Rotation (Geometry)/Axis: Let r_\theta be a rotation in the Euclidean Space \Gamma = \R^n. The set A of points in \Gamma such that: :\forall P \in A: \map {r_\theta} P = P is called the axis of rotation of r_\theta.

Definition:Reflection (Geometry): A reflection in the context of Euclidean geometry is an isometry from a Euclidean Space \R^n as follows. A reflection is defined usually for either: :n = 2, representing the plane or: :n = 3, representing ordinary space. === Reflection in the Plane === {{:Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Plane === Reflection in Space === {{:Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Space === Point Reflection in Space === {{:Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Point

Definition:Translation Mapping/Abelian Group: Let \struct {G, +} be an abelian group. Let g \in G. Then translation by g is the mapping \tau_g: G \to G defined by: :\forall h \in G: \map {\tau_g} h = h + \paren {-g} where -g is the inverse of g with respect to + in G.

Definition:Translation Mapping/Euclidean Space: A translation \tau_\mathbf x is an isometry on the Euclidean Space \Gamma = \R^n defined as: :\forall \mathbf y \in \R^n: \map {\tau_\mathbf x} {\mathbf y} = \mathbf y - \mathbf x where \mathbf x is a vector in \R^n.

Definition:Aleph Number: The aleph numbers are a sequence of numbers used to represent the cardinality (or size) of infinite sets that can be well-ordered. The cardinality of the natural numbers is \aleph_0. The next larger cardinality is \aleph_1. Then \aleph_2 and so on.
Definition:Order of Group Element/Also known as: Some sources refer to the order of an element of a group as its period.
Definition:Order of Group Element/Also denoted as: The order of an element x in a group is sometimes seen as \map o x. Some sources render it as \map {\operatorname {Ord} } x.
Definition:Cyclic Group/Definition 1: The group G is cyclic {{iff every element of G can be expressed as the power of one element of G: :\exists g \in G: \forall h \in G: h = g^n for some n \in \Z.
Definition:Cyclic Group/Definition 2: The group G is cyclic {{iff it is generated by one element g \in G: :G = \gen g
Definition:Generator of Group: Let \struct {G, \circ} be a group. Let S \subseteq G. Then S is a generator of G, denoted G = \gen S, {{iff G is the subgroup generated by S.
Definition:Cyclic Group/Generator: Let a \in G be an element of G such that \gen a = G. Then a is a generator of G.

Definition:Multiplicative Group of Reduced Residues: Let m \in \Z_{> 0} be a (strictly) positive integer. Let \Z'_m denote the reduced residue system modulo m. Consider the algebraic structure: :\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m} where \times_m denotes multiplication modulo m. Then \struct {\Z'_m, \times_m} is referred to as the multiplicative group of reduced residues modulo m.
Definition:Congruence Modulo Subgroup/Left Congruence/Also known as: When \tuple {x, y} \in \mathcal R^l_H, we write: : x \equiv^l y \pmod H which is read: x is left congruent to y modulo H.
Definition:Congruence Modulo Subgroup/Right Congruence/Also known as: When \tuple {x, y} \in \mathcal R^r_H, we write: : x \equiv^r y \pmod H which is read: x is right congruent to y modulo H.

Definition:Existential Quantifier/Unique/Also denoted as: The symbol \exists_1 is also found for the same concept, being an instance of the exact existential quantifier \exists_n. Some sources, for example {{BookReference|Axiomatic Set Theory|1972|Patrick Suppes, use \operatorname E !, which is idiosyncratic, considering the use in the same source of \exists for the general existential quantifier.
Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite/Definition 1: x is of infinite order, or has infinite order {{iff there exists no k \in \Z_{> 0} such that x^k = e_G: :\order x = \infty
Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite/Definition 2: x is of infinite order, or has infinite order {{iff the powers x, x^2, x^3, \ldots of x are all distinct: :\order x = \infty
Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite/Also known as: An element of finite order of G is also known as a torsion element of G.
Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite/Definition 1: x is of finite order, or has finite order {{iff there exists k \in \Z_{> 0} such that x^k = e_G.
Definition:Order of Group Element/Finite/Definition 2: x is of finite order, or has finite order {{iff there exist m, n \in \Z_{> 0} such that m \ne n but x^m = x^n.

Definition:Complete Normed Division Ring: A normed division ring \struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} } is complete {{iff the metric space \struct {R, d} is a complete metric space where d is the metric induced by the norm 
orm {\, \cdot \,}. That is, a normed division ring \struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} } is complete {{iff every Cauchy sequence is convergent.

Definition:Order of Group Element/Infinite/Definition 3: x is of infinite order, or has infinite order {{iff the group \gen x generated by x is of infinite order. :\order x = \infty \iff \order {\gen x} = \infty

Definition:Cardinality/Infinite: Let S be an infinite set. The cardinality \card S of S can be indicated as: :\card S = \infty However, it needs to be noted that this just means that the cardinality of S cannot be assigned a number n \in \N. It means that \card S is at least \aleph_0 (aleph null).

Definition:Field of Integers Modulo Prime: Let p \in \Bbb P be a prime number. Let \Z_p be the set of integers modulo p. Let +_p and \times_p denote addition modulo p and multiplication modulo p respectively. The algebraic structure \struct {\Z_p, +_p, \times_p} is the field of integers modulo p.
Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Element/Also known as: Some sources refer to the conjugate of x as the transform of x. Some sources refer to conjugacy as conjugation.

Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Element/Also defined as: Some sources define the conjugate of x by a in G as: :x \sim y \iff \exists a \in G: x \circ a = a \circ y or: :x \sim y \iff \exists a \in G: a^{-1} \circ x \circ a = y
Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Element/Definition 1: The conjugacy relation \sim is defined on G as: :\forall \tuple {x, y} \in G \times G: x \sim y \iff \exists a \in G: a \circ x = y \circ a

Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Element/Definition 2: The conjugacy relation \sim is defined on G as: :\forall \tuple {x, y} \in G \times G: x \sim y \iff \exists a \in G: a \circ x \circ a^{-1} = y

Definition:Ring (Abstract Algebra)/Historical Note: According to {{AuthorRef|Ian Stewart, in his {{BookLink|Galois Theory|Ian Stewart|ed = 3rd|edpage = Third Edition of 2004, the ring axioms were first formulated by {{AuthorRef|Heinrich Martin Weber in 1893.

Definition:Norm/Ring: Let \struct {R, +, \circ} be a ring whose zero is denoted 0_R. A (submultiplicative) norm on R is a mapping from R to the non-negative reals: {{:Definition:Submultiplicative Norm on Ring

Definition:Norm/Division Ring: Let \struct {R, +, \circ} be a division ring whose zero is denoted 0_R. A (multiplicative) norm on R is a mapping from R to the non-negative reals: {{:Definition:Multiplicative Norm on Ring

Definition:Norm/Vector Space: Let \struct {R, +, \circ} be a division ring with norm \norm {\,\cdot\,}_R. Let V be a vector space over R, with zero 0_V. A norm on V is a map from V to the nonnegative reals: :\norm{\,\cdot\,}: V \to \R_{\ge 0} satisfying the (vector space) norm axioms: {{Definition:Norm Axioms (Vector Space)

Definition:Norm/Unital Algebra: Let A be an unital algebra over R with unit e. A norm on A is an algebra norm \norm{\,\cdot\,}: A \to \R_{\ge 0} such that: :\norm e = 1
Definition:Norm/Bounded Linear Functional/Definition 1: The norm of L is the real number defined as the supremum: :\norm L = \sup \set {\size {L h}: \norm h_H \le 1}

Definition:Group Direct Product/Finite Product: Let \struct {G_1, \circ_1}, \struct {G_2, \circ_2}, \ldots, \struct {G_n, \circ_n} be groups. Let G = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n G_k be their cartesian product. Let \circ be the operation defined on G as: :\circ := \tuple {g_1, g_2, \ldots, g_n} \circ \tuple {h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n} = \tuple {g_1 \circ_1 h_1, g_2 \circ_2 h_2, \ldots, g_n \circ_n h_n} for all ordered n-tuples in G. The group \struct {G, \circ} is called the (external) direct product of \struct {G_1, \circ_1}, \struct {G_2, \circ_2}, \ldots, \struct {G_n, \circ_n}.

Definition:Bilateral Symmetry/Axis: Let F be a plane geometric figure. Let \map R F be a reflection in an axis of reflection AB which is a symmetry. Then AB is referred to as an axis of symmetry of F.
Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Subset/Also defined as: S^a := \set {y \in G: \exists x \in S: y = a^{-1} \circ x \circ a} = a^{-1} \circ S \circ a

Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Roots of Unity: Let n \in \Z be an integer such that n > 0. Let U_n := \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1} denote the set of complex nth roots of unity. Let \struct {U_n, \times} be the algebraic structure formed by U_n under complex multiplication. Then \struct {U_n, \times} is the multiplicative group of complex nth roots of unity.

Definition:Isolated Zero: Let f: \C \to \C be a complex function. Let \map f {z_0} = 0 for some z_0 \in \C. We say z_0 is an isolated zero of f if there exists an open ball B containing z_0, such that \map f w \ne 0 for all w \in B \setminus \set {z_0}.

Definition:Conjugacy Action/Subsets: Let \powerset G be the power set of G. The (left) conjugacy action on subsets is the group action * : G \times \powerset G \to \powerset G: :g * S = g \circ S \circ g^{-1} The right conjugacy action on subsets is the group action * : \powerset G \times G \to \powerset G: :S * g = g^{-1} \circ S \circ g

Definition:Subgroup Action: Let \struct {G, \circ} be a group. Let \struct {H, \circ} be a subgroup of G. Let *: H \times G \to G be the operation defined as: :\forall h \in H, g \in G: h * g := h \circ g This is the subgroup action of H on G.
Definition:Norm/Ring/Multiplicative: \norm {\,\cdot\,}: R \to \R_{\ge 0} satisfying the (ring) multiplicative norm axioms: {{:Definition:Multiplicative Norm Axioms
Definition:Norm/Ring/Submultiplicative: \norm {\,\cdot\,}: R \to \R_{\ge 0} satisfying the (ring) submultiplicative norm axioms: {{:Definition:Submultiplicative Norm Axioms

Definition:Cartesian Product/Cartesian Space/Two Dimensions: The cartesian 2nd power of S is: :S^2 = S \times S = \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2}: x_1, x_2 \in S} The set S^2 called a cartesian space of 2 dimensions.

Definition:Square/Mapping: Let \struct {S, \circ} be an algebraic structure. Let f: S \to S be the mapping from S to S defined as: :\forall x \in S: \map f x := x \circ x This is usually denoted x^2: :x^2 := x \circ x
Definition:Square/Mapping/Element: A square (element of S) is an element y of S for which: :\exists x \in S: y = x^2 Such a y = x^2 is referred to as the square of x.
Definition:Square/Function/Definition 1: The square (function) on \F is the mapping f: \F \to \F defined as: :\forall x \in \F: \map f x = x \times x where \times denotes multiplication.

Definition:Square/Function: Let \F denote one of the standard classes of numbers: \N, \Z, \Q, \R, \C. === Definition 1 === {{:Definition:Square/Function/Definition 1 === Definition 2 === {{:Definition:Square/Function/Definition 2
Definition:Square/Function/Definition 2: The square (function) on \F is the mapping f: \F \to \F defined as: :\forall x \in \F: \map f x = x^2 where x^2 denotes the 2nd power of x.
Definition:Square/Function/Integer: The (integer) square function is the integer function f: \Z \to \Z defined as: :\forall x \in \Z: \map f x = x^2
Definition:Ultrametric Space: An ultrametric space is a metric space \struct {X, d} where d is non-Archimedean.

Definition:Unique up to Isomorphism: Let \mathbf C be a category. Let S \subseteq \operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf C) be a subclass of its objects. The class S is unique up to isomorphism {{iff for all objects s,t \in S there is a isomorphism from s to t.
Definition:Power of Element/Also defined as: Some treatments do not define the power of an element for a magma whose operation is non-associative.

Definition:Subset Product Action/Left: The (left) subset product action of G is the group action *: G \times \powerset G \to \powerset G: :\forall g \in G, S \in \powerset G: g * S = g \circ S

Definition:Subset Product Action: Let \struct {G, \circ} be a group. Let \HH be the set of subgroups of G. === Left Subset Product Action === {{:Definition:Subset Product Action/Left === Right Subset Product Action === {{:Definition:Subset Product Action/Right
Definition:Subset Product Action/Right: The (right) subset product action of G is the group action *: G \times \powerset G \to \powerset G: :\forall g \in G, S \in \powerset G: g * S = S \circ g
Definition:Generated Subgroup/Definition 2: The subgroup generated by S is the intersection of all subgroups of G containing S.

Definition:Group Action on Coset Space: Let G be a group. Let H be a subgroup of G. The mapping *: G \times G / H \to G / H by the rule: :\forall g \in G, \forall g' H \in G / H: g * \paren {g' H} := \paren {g g'} H is the group action on the (left) coset space G / H.

Definition:Trivial Quotient Group: Let G be a group. The quotient group: :G / \set {e_G} \cong G where: :\cong denotes group isomorphism :e_G denotes the identity element of G. is known as the trivial quotient group.

Definition:Inner Automorphism Group: Let G be a group. The inner automorphism group of G is the algebraic structure: :\struct {\Inn G, \circ} where: :\Inn G is the set of inner automorphisms of G :\circ denotes composition of mappings.

Definition:Generator of Subgroup/Definition by Predicate: A generator of a subgroup can be defined by a predicate. For example: :\gen {x \in G: x^2 = e} defines the subgroup of G generated by the elements of G of order 2.
Definition:Generated Normal Subgroup/Definition 3: The normal subgroup generated by S, denoted \gen {S^G}, is the smallest normal subgroup of G containing S: :\gen {S^G} = \gen {x G x^{-1}: x \in G}

Definition:Nu Function/Sequence: The sequence of values of \nu function: \map \nu n for n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots begins: :1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 5, 2, 2, 1, 5, 1, 2, 1, 14, 1, 5, 1, 5, 2, 2, 1, 15, 2, 2, 5, 4, 1, 4, 1, 51, 1, 2, 1, 14, 1, 2, 2, 14, \ldots

Definition:Extension Problem: Let H and K be groups. The extension problem is to determine all groups G such that: :K \trianglelefteq G :G / K \cong H where: :K \trianglelefteq G denotes that K is a normal subgroup of G :G / K denotes the quotient group of G by K :\cong denotes group isomorphism.

Definition:Involution (Mapping)/Definition 1: f: A \to A is an involution precisely when: :\forall x \in A: \map f {\map f x} = x That is: :f \circ f = I_A where I_A denotes the identity mapping on A.

Definition:Involution (Mapping)/Definition 3: Let f: A \to A be a mapping on A. Then f is an involution {{iff f is both a bijection and a symmetric relation. That is, {{iff f is a bijection such that f = f^{-1}.
Definition:Self-Inverse Element/Also known as: The definition of a self-inverse element is usually made in the context of a group. Some sources refer to such an element as an involution.

Definition:Characterization Theorem: Let E be a non-abelian finite simple group. Let u \in E be a self-inverse element of E. Let H = \map {C_E} u be the centralizer of u in E. Let G be a finite simple group with a self-inverse element t such that H \cong \map {C_G} t. A characterization theorem is a theorem that proves there is only one such group type G. That is, that G \cong E necessarily.

Definition:Group of Units/Ring: Let \struct {R, +, \circ} be a ring with unity. Then the set U_R of units of \struct {R, +, \circ} is called the group of units of \struct {R, +, \circ}. This can be denoted explicitly as \struct {U_R, \circ}.

The space \struct {S, \tau} is said to be completely metrizable {{iff there exists a metric d such that: :\struct {S, d} is a complete metric space and: :\tau is the topological space induced by the metric d. == Also see == {{refactor|Trivial, but the following statement needs to be justified in its own page All completely metrizable topologies are in particular metrizable topologies.

Definition:Null Sequence/Normed Division Ring: Let \struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} } be a normed division ring with zero 0_R. Let \sequence {x_n} be a sequence in R which converges to the limit 0_R: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = 0_R Then \sequence {x_n} is called a null sequence.

Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime/Base 4: Let q be a composite number such that 4^q \equiv 4 \pmod q. Then q is a Fermat pseudoprime to base 4.
Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime/Base 5: Let q be a composite number such that 5^q \equiv 5 \pmod q. Then q is a Fermat pseudoprime to base 5.

Definition:Null Sequence/Complex Numbers: Let \sequence {z_n} be a sequence in \C which converges to a limit of 0: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} z_n = 0 Then \sequence {z_n} is called a (complex) null sequence.

Definition:Null Sequence/Real Numbers: Let \sequence {x_n} be a sequence in \R which converges to a limit of 0: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = 0 Then \sequence {x_n} is called a (real) null sequence.

Definition:Null Sequence/Rational Numbers: Let \sequence {x_n} be a sequence in \Q which converges to a limit of 0: : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = 0 Then \sequence {x_n} is called a (rational) null sequence.

Definition:Floating Point Representation: Floating point representation is a technique whereby numbers are held in a computer in standard scientific notation.

Definition:Scientific Notation: Scientific notation is a technique for representing approximations to (usually large) numbers by presenting them in the form: :n \approx m \times 10^e where: :m is a rational number such that 1 \le m < 10, expressed in decimal notation :e is an integer.
Definition:Megaflop: A megaflop is a measure of calculation speed of a computer. :1 megaflop = 1 million floating point operations per second.

Definition:Group Presentation/Relation: The standard form of a relation in a group presentation is: :w = e where w is a word in the group.

Definition:International Standard Book Number: An international standard book number is an index number used to uniquely identify a published {{WP|Book|book. === ISBN-10 === {{:Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-10 === ISBN-13 === {{:Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-13

Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-10: The ISBN-10 format consists of a string of 9 digits followed by a check digit in the set \set {0, 1, \ldots, 9, X}. The check digit d is calculated as follows. Let c be calculated as: :c = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^9 k d_k \pmod {11} where d_k denotes the kth digit in the ISBN-10. Then the check digit d is defined as: :d = \begin{cases} c & : c \le 9 \\ X &: c = 10 \end{cases}

Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-13: The ISBN-13 format consists of a string of 12 digits followed by a check digit. The check digit d is calculated as: :d = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^{12} k d_k \pmod {10}

Definition:International Standard Book Number/Linguistic Note: When referring to an international standard book number by its abbreviation ISBN, beware not to vocalise it as "ISBN number". The word number is already included in the abbreviation ISBN, so does not need to be repeated.

Definition:Check Digit: A check digit is a digit or other symbol used as an aid to identifying whether a mistake has been made transmitting a codeword. It is calculated from the symbols in the codeword itself, and appended to the codeword as an extra symbol. If a mistake is made transmitting the codeword, the check digit will then be incompatible with the rest of the contents of the codeword, and reveal that a transmission error is present.

Definition:Error-Correcting Code: An error-correcting code is a technique whereby a transmitted codeword contains extra characters whose purpose is to detect whether the codeword has been corrupted during transmission.

Definition:Linear Code: Let p be a prime number. Let \Z_p be the set of residue classes modulo p. Let \map V {n, p} denote the set of sequences of length n of elements of \Z_p. A linear \tuple {n, k}-code is a k-dimensional subspace C of \map V {n, p} considered as a vector space over \Z_p of n dimensions.
Definition:Linear Code/Master Code: \map V {n, p} is itself a linear \tuple {n, n}-code, and is referred to on {{ProofWiki as a master code (for a linear \tuple {n, k}-code over \Z_p).
Definition:Codeword: === Codeword of Linear Code === {{:Definition:Linear Code/Codeword

Definition:Linear Code/Codeword: The elements of \map V {n, p} are referred to as codewords. A codeword is usually written without punctuation, so that, for example: :\tuple {\eqclass 1 p, \eqclass 0 p, \eqclass 1 p} is presented as: :101
Definition:Weight of Linear Codeword: Let C be a codeword of a linear code. The weight of C is the number of non-zero terms of C.
Definition:Distance between Linear Codewords: Let u and v be two codewords of a linear code. The distance between u and v is the number of corresponding terms at which u and v are different.

Definition:Minimum Distance of Linear Code: Let C be a linear code whose master code is \map V {n, p}. The minimum distance d of C is defined as: :\map d C := \min_{u, v \mathop \in C: u \mathop \ne v} \set {\map d {u, v} } where \map d {u, v} denotes the distance between u and v.

Definition:Standard Generator Matrix for Linear Code: Let n, k \in \Z_{>0} be strictly positive integers such that n > k. Let p be a prime number. Let \Z_p denote the set of residue classes modulo p. A (standard) generator matrix G over \Z_p is a k \times n matrix such that: :The elements of G are elements of \Z_p :The first k columns form the k \times k identity matrix.

Definition:Transmission Error: Let c be a transmitted codeword of a message sent over a transmission line T. Let c' be the corresponding word received across T. Each term of c' may or may not match the corresponding term of c. Each term of c' which does not match the corresponding term of c is referred to as an instance of a transmission error. Category:Definitions/Information Theory hx64fvv2g0bag2ytqohht7jnyphtbmj

Definition:Transmitted Codeword: Let M be a message sent over a transmission line T. Let M consist of a number of codewords. Each of the codewords comprising M, as it is before it has been transmitted across T, is referred to as a transmitted codeword.

Definition:Received Word: Let M be a message sent over a transmission line T. Let M consist of a number of codewords. Each of the codewords comprising M, as it is after it has been transmitted across T, is referred to as a received word. Note that if a received word c' does not match its corresponding transmitted codeword c, then it is possible that c' is not actually a codeword. Definition:Absolute Galois Group/Definition 1: The absolute Galois group of K is the Galois group \Gal {K^{\operatorname{sep} } \mid K} of its separable closure.
Definition:Absolute Galois Group/Definition 2: The absolute Galois group of K is the automorphism group \Aut {\overline K \mid K} of its algebraic closure.

Definition:Group Action/Left Group Action: A (left) group action is an operation \phi: G \times X \to X such that: :\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X in such a way that the group action axioms are satisfied: {{:Definition:Group Action Axioms

Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Definition 1: The orbit of an element x \in X is defined as: :\Orb x := \set {y \in X: \exists g \in G: y = g * x} where * denotes the group action. That is, \Orb x = G * x. Thus the orbit of an element is all its possible destinations under the group action.

Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Definition 2: Let \mathcal R be the relation on X defined as: :\forall x, y \in X: x \mathrel {\mathcal R} y \iff \exists g \in G: y = g * x where * denotes the group action. From Group Action Induces Equivalence Relation, \mathcal R is an equivalence relation. The orbit of x, denoted \Orb x, is the equivalence class of x under \mathcal R.
Definition:Gillion: Gillion is a rarely-used word for 10^9.
Definition:Gazillion: Gazillion is a rhetorical flourish to mean a very large number, generally understood to be of the order of an unspecified power of 10.

Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition 1: The group \struct {G, \circ} is the internal group direct product of H_1 and H_2 {{iff the mapping: :C: H_1 \times H_2 \to G: \map C {h_1, h_2} = h_1 \circ h_2 is a group isomorphism from the (group) direct product \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } } \times \struct {H_2, \circ {\restriction_{H_2} } } onto \struct {G, \circ}.

Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition 2: The group \struct {G, \circ} is the internal group direct product of H_1 and H_2 {{iff: :(1): \quad \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } } and \struct {H_2, \circ {\restriction_{H_2} } } are both normal subgroups of \struct {G, \circ} :(2): \quad every element of G can be expressed uniquely in the form: ::::g = h_1 \circ h_2

Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition/Definition 1: The group \struct {G, \circ} is the internal group direct product of \sequence {H_n} {{iff the mapping: : C: \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n H_k \to G: \map C {h_1, \ldots, h_n} = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n h_k is a group isomorphism from the group direct product \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } } \times \cdots \times \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } } onto \struct {G, \circ}.

Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition/Definition 2: (1): \quad Each H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n is a normal subgroup of G :(2): \quad Each element g of G can be expressed uniquely in the form: ::::g = h_1 \circ h_2 \circ \cdots \circ h_n :::where h_i \in H_i for all i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}.

Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition 3: The group \struct {G, \circ} is the internal group direct product of H_1 and H_2 {{iff: :(1): \quad \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } } and \struct {H_2, \circ {\restriction_{H_2} } } are both normal subgroups of \struct {G, \circ} :(2): \quad G is the subset product of H_1 and H_2, that is: G = H_1 \circ H_2 :(3): \quad H_1 \cap H_2 = \set e where e is the identity element of G.
Definition:Even Integer/Definition 1: An integer n \in \Z is even {{iff it is divisible by 2.
Definition:Even Integer/Definition 3: An integer n \in \Z is even {{iff: :x \equiv 0 \pmod 2 where the notation denotes congruence modulo 2.
Definition:Even Integer/Definition 2: An integer n \in \Z is even {{iff it is of the form: :n = 2 r where r \in \Z is an integer.
Definition:Odd Integer/Definition 3: An integer n \in \Z is odd {{iff: :x \equiv 1 \pmod 2 where the notation denotes congruence modulo 2.

Definition:Balanced Ternary Representation: Let n \in \Z be an integer. Balanced ternary representation is the unique representation of n in the form: :\sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0} such that: : n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m r_j 3^j where: :m \in \Z_{>0} is a strictly positive integer such that 3^m \le \size n < 3^{m + 1} :all the r_j are such that r_j \in \set {\underline 1, 0, 1}, where \underline 1 := -1.

Definition:Integral Ideal: Let J \subseteq \Z be a non-empty subset of the set of integers. Let J fulfil the following conditions: :(1): \quad n, m \in J \implies m + n \in J, m - n \in J :(2): \quad n \in J, r \in \Z \implies r n \in J Then J is an integral ideal.
Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integers/Definition 1: The greatest common divisor of a and b is defined as: :the largest d \in \Z_{>0} such that d \divides a and d \divides b

Definition:Greatest Common Divisor/Integers/Definition 2: The greatest common divisor of a and b is defined as the (strictly) positive integer d \in \Z_{>0} such that: :(1): \quad d \divides a \land d \divides b :(2): \quad c \divides a \land c \divides b \implies c \divides d

Definition:Lowest Common Multiple/Also known as: The lowest common multiple is also known as the least common multiple. It is usually abbreviated LCM, lcm or l.c.m. The notation \lcm \set {a, b} can be found written as \sqbrk {a, b}. This usage is not recommended as it can cause confusion.

Definition:Open Ball/Normed Division Ring: Let \struct{R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } be a normed division ring. Let a \in R. Let \epsilon \in \R_{>0} be a strictly positive real number. The open \epsilon-ball of a in \struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } is defined as: :\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in R: 
orm{x - a} < \epsilon} If it is necessary to show the norm itself, then the notation \map {B_\epsilon} {a; 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } can be used.
Definition:Open Ball/Normed Division Ring/Radius: In \map {B_\epsilon} a, the value \epsilon is referred to as the radius of the open \epsilon-ball.
Definition:Open Ball/Normed Division Ring/Center: In \map {B_\epsilon} a, the value a is referred to as the center of the open \epsilon-ball.

Definition:Closed Ball/Normed Division Ring: Let \struct{R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } be a normed division ring. Let a \in R. Let \epsilon \in \R_{>0} be a strictly positive real number. The closed \epsilon-ball of a in \struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } is defined as: :\map { {B_\epsilon}^-} a = \set {x \in R: 
orm {x - a} \le \epsilon} If it is necessary to show the norm itself, then the notation \map { {B_\epsilon}^-} {a; 
orm {\,\cdot\,} } can be used.
Definition:Closed Ball/Normed Division Ring/Radius: In \map { {B_\epsilon}^-} a, the value \epsilon is referred to as the radius of the closed \epsilon-ball.
Definition:Closed Ball/Normed Division Ring/Center: In \map { {B_\epsilon}^-} a, the value a is referred to as the center of the closed \epsilon-ball.

Definition:Lattice Point: Let \CC be a cartesian coordinate system of n dimensions. Let P = \tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} be a point in \CC. Then P is a lattice point of \CC {{iff a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n are all integers. === Rational Lattice Point === {{:Definition:Lattice Point/Rational

Definition:Intercept: Let \mathcal C be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. An intercept of \mathcal C is a point where \mathcal C intersects one of the coordinate axes. In particular: === x-Intercept === {{:Definition:Intercept/X-Intercept === y-Intercept === {{:Definition:Intercept/Y-Intercept
Definition:Intercept/X-Intercept: An x-intercept of \mathcal C is a point where \mathcal C intersects the x-axis.
Definition:Intercept/Y-Intercept: A y-intercept of \mathcal C is a point where \mathcal C intersects the y-axis.

Definition:Perpendicular Distance: Let \mathcal L be a straight line. Let P be a point not on \mathcal L. Let a perpendicular be dropped from P to \mathcal L, intersecting \mathcal L at A. The perpendicular distance from P to \mathcal L is defined as being the length of the line AP. :300px

Definition:Lowest Common Multiple/Integers/General Definition: Let S = \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \subseteq \Z such that \prod_{a \mathop \in S} a = 0 (that is, all elements of S are non-zero). Then the lowest common multiple of S: :\lcm \paren S = \lcm \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} is defined as the smallest m \in \Z_{>0} such that: :\forall x \in S: x \divides m

Definition:Sphere/Metric Space: Let M = \struct{A, d} be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let a \in A. Let \epsilon \in \R_{>0} be a strictly positive real number. The \epsilon-sphere of a in M is defined as: :\map {S_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in A: \map d {x, a} = \epsilon}
Definition:Sphere/Metric Space/Center: In S_\epsilon \paren{a}, the value a is referred to as the center of the \epsilon-sphere.
Definition:Sphere/Metric Space/Radius: In S_\epsilon \paren{a}, the value \epsilon is referred to as the radius of the \epsilon-sphere.

Definition:Sphere/Normed Division Ring: Let \struct{R, 
orm{\,\cdot\, be a normed division ring. Let a \in R. Let \epsilon \in \R_{>0} be a strictly positive real number. The \epsilon-sphere of a in \struct{R, 
orm{\,\cdot\, is defined as: :S_\epsilon \paren{a} = \set {x \in R: 
orm{x - a} = \epsilon}
Definition:Sphere/Normed Division Ring/Radius: In \map {S_\epsilon} a, the value \epsilon is referred to as the radius of the \epsilon-sphere.
Definition:Sphere/Normed Division Ring/Center: In \map {S_\epsilon} a, the value a is referred to as the center of the \epsilon-sphere.

Definition:Stellation/Polygon/Regular: A regular stellated polygon is a stellated polygon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: :300px
Definition:Triskaidecagon: A triskaidecagon is a polygon with exactly 13 sides. :300px === Regular Triskaidecagon === {{:Definition:Triskaidecagon/Regular
